abstract: MURPHY consists of a camera looking at a robot arm, with a connectionist network architecture situated in between. By moving its arm through a small, representative sample of the 1 billion possible joint configurations, MURPHY learns the relationships, backwards and forwards, between the positions of its joints and the state of its visual field. MURPHY can use its internal model in the forward direction to "envision" sequences of actions for planning purposes, such as in grabbing a visually presented object, or in the reverse direction to "imitate", with its arm, autonomous activity in its visual field. Furthermore, by taking explicit advantage of continuity in the mappings between visual space and joint space, MURPHY is able to learn non-linear mappings with only a single layer of modifiable weights.

paragraphs: MURPHY connects a camera and robot arm through a neural architecture that learns from the arm's own movement. By exploring a small representative sample of a billion possible joint configurations, it learns relationships between joint positions and the visual scene. The relationships can be used in both directions.

In the forward direction, the internal model predicts visual consequences from arm configurations. This lets MURPHY envision sequences of actions for planning, including reaching for a visually presented object. In the reverse direction, it uses visual activity to guide its arm, allowing it to imitate activity occurring in the camera's view.

The learning method explicitly uses continuity in the relationship between visual space and joint space. With that structure, MURPHY learns nonlinear mappings using only one layer of adjustable weights. The significance is that the system's learned model supports both prediction and action selection, while the continuity of the task helps make learning possible from a limited sample of its many possible configurations.
summary.tldr: MURPHY learns bidirectional relationships between arm positions and camera views to support action planning and imitation.

title: MURPHY: A Robot that Learns by Doing

abstract: The performance sensitivity of Albus' CMAC network was studied for the scenario in which faults are introduced into the adjustable weights after training has been accomplished. It was found that fault sensitivity was reduced with increased generalization when "loss of weight" faults were considered, but sensitivity was increased for "saturated weight" faults.
originalAbstract: The performance sensitivity of Albus' CMAC network was studied for the scenario in which faults are introduced into the adjustable weights after training has been accomplished. It was found that fault sensitivity was reduced with increased generalization when "loss of weight" faults were considered, but sensitivity was increased for "saturated weight" faults.

paragraphs: A trained neural system can encounter hardware faults after its weights have been learned. This paper examines that operational setting for Albus’ CMAC network, asking how its configuration affects sensitivity to damaged adjustable weights. The study distinguishes faults by what they do to the stored value.

For loss-of-weight faults, increasing the network’s generalization reduces sensitivity. For saturated-weight faults, the same change increases sensitivity. The two cases therefore reveal opposite responses to one design choice, rather than a single overall notion of fault tolerance.

The finding matters because a configuration that handles one failure mode well may be worse under another. Evaluating only an average or generic fault model could conceal that difference. The paper’s contribution is a fault-specific characterization of CMAC behavior after training, showing that robustness decisions need to reflect the kind of weight corruption expected during operation.
summary.tldr: Increasing CMAC generalization improves tolerance to lost weights but worsens sensitivity to saturated weights.

title: Operational Fault Tolerance of CMAC Networks

paragraphs: The paper presents two working analog vision chips that compute properties of pixel groups. The goal is to move visual processing toward object-level descriptions, where a shared electrical value can represent something about an entire collection of image points. Both circuits are built from networks of resistors and switches.

The first chip implements the dynamic wires model. It establishes dedicated communication among pixels sharing a property and uses that organization to compute contour arclength, the distance along a visual boundary. This produces a collective measurement that depends on how pixels form a contour.

The second chip separates the inside of a contour from its surroundings by assigning the two regions different voltages. Small contour gaps are automatically closed, making its figure-ground separation robust in noisy conditions. Together, the circuits demonstrate hardware operations that organize pixels into meaningful groups and encode group properties electrically. Their stated contribution is a practical step toward object-based processing within analog vision circuitry.
summary.tldr: Two analog vision chips compute contour length and robust figure-ground separation through electrical representations of pixel groups.

title: Object-Based Analog VLSI Vision Circuits

abstract: This paper describes some of the interactions of model learning algorithms and planning algorithms we have found in exploring model-based reinforcement learning. The paper focuses on how lo(cid:173) cal trajectory optimizers can be used effectively with learned non(cid:173) parametric models. We find that trajectory planners that are fully consistent with the learned model often have difficulty finding rea(cid:173) sonable plans in the early stages of learning. Trajectory planners that balance obeying the learned model with minimizing cost (or maximizing reward) often do better, even if the plan is not fully consistent with the learned model.

paragraphs: In model-based reinforcement learning, an agent learns how its environment behaves and uses that model to plan. This paper examines the interaction between those two activities when local trajectory optimizers work with learned nonparametric models. The practical question is how closely a planner should follow a model that is still being learned.

The authors find that strict consistency can be problematic early in learning. A trajectory planner that fully obeys the learned model may struggle to find reasonable plans. This makes the planner's treatment of the model an important design choice, alongside the choice of model-learning algorithm itself.

Planners often do better when they balance agreement with the model against reducing cost or increasing reward, even when the resulting trajectory is not completely model-consistent. The finding concerns planning during learning, when the model is still developing. Its significance is that the planner and learner must be considered together: insisting on perfect adherence to the current model can hinder the search for useful behavior.
summary.tldr: Early in model-based learning, trajectory planners can perform better by trading strict model consistency against cost or reward.

title: Nonparametric Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We replace the commonly used Gaussian noise model in nonlinear regression by a more flexible noise model based on the Student-t(cid:173) distribution. The degrees of freedom of the t-distribution can be chosen such that as special cases either the Gaussian distribution or the Cauchy distribution are realized. The latter is commonly used in robust regres(cid:173) sion. Since the t-distribution can be interpreted as being an infinite mix(cid:173) ture of Gaussians, parameters and hyperparameters such as the degrees of freedom of the t-distribution can be learned from the data based on an EM-learning algorithm. We show that modeling using the t-distribution leads to improved predictors on real world data sets. In particular, if outliers are present, the t-distribution is superior to the Gaussian noise model. In effect, by adapting the degrees of freedom, the system can "learn" to distinguish between outliers and non-outliers. Especially for online learning tasks, one is interested in avoiding inappropriate weight changes due to measurement outliers to maintain stable online learn(cid:173) ing capability. We show experimentally that using the t-distribution as a noise model leads to stable online learning algorithms and outperforms state-of-the art online learning methods like the extended Kalman filter algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper makes nonlinear regression more robust by replacing a Gaussian noise model with a Student-t distribution. Its degrees-of-freedom parameter controls the distribution's form, connecting Gaussian behavior with the Cauchy distribution used in robust regression. This flexibility lets the noise model adapt to data containing unusually large errors.

The authors use the interpretation of the t-distribution as an infinite mixture of Gaussians to develop EM-based learning. Model parameters and hyperparameters, including degrees of freedom, can be estimated from data. By adapting this parameter, the system can effectively distinguish outliers from other observations and reduce inappropriate responses to extreme measurements.

Experiments on real-world datasets show improved predictors, particularly when outliers are present. The paper also examines online learning, where an unusual measurement can otherwise trigger an unsuitable weight update. In the reported experiments, the t-based noise model supports stable online learning and outperforms methods including the extended Kalman filter. These findings link the noise assumption directly to prediction quality and the stability of ongoing adaptation.
summary.tldr: Learning a Student-t noise model improves regression robustness and produces stable online learning in the reported experiments.

title: Robust Neural Network Regression for Offline and Online Learning

abstract: Recent neurophysiological evidence suggests the ability to interpret biological motion is facilitated by a neuronal "mirror system" which maps visual inputs to the pre-motor cortex. If the common architecture and circuitry of the cortices is taken to imply a common computation across multiple perceptual and cognitive modalities, this visual-motor interaction might be expected to have a unified computational basis. Two essential tasks underlying such visual-motor cooperation are shown here to be simply expressed and directly solved as transformation-discovery inverse problems: (a) discriminating and determining the pose of a primed 3D object in a real-world scene, and (b) interpreting the 3D configuration of an articulated kinematic object in an image. paragraphs: This paper connects two visual recognition tasks through a common computational problem: finding transformations that explain an observed image. One task is recognizing a previously specified three-dimensional object and determining its pose in a real scene. The other is interpreting the three-dimensional arrangement of an articulated object, whose parts can move relative to one another.

The proposed formulation treats both tasks as inverse problems. Instead of starting with an object configuration and generating its appearance, the method searches for a composition of transformations connecting two patterns. The map-seeking method makes this search tractable by exploiting an ordering property of superposed patterns and decomposing transformation spaces according to the processes that generate the observations.

The neuroscience motivation comes from visual interactions with motor-related cortex and the possibility of shared computations across cortical regions. The contribution is a computationally unified, cortically plausible account of these recognition tasks. That plausibility supports a possible computational basis for visual-motor cooperation; it does not establish that cortical circuits actually implement the proposed method.
summary.tldr: A map-seeking method expresses object recognition and articulated pose interpretation as tractable searches for compositions of transformations.

title: A Cortically-Plausible Inverse Problem Solving Method Applied to Recognizing Static and Kinematic 3D Objects

abstract: Pyramid intersection is an efﬁcient method for computing an approximate partial matching between two sets of feature vectors. We introduce a novel pyramid em- bedding based on a hierarchy of non-uniformly shaped bins that takes advantage of the underlying structure of the feature space and remains accurate even for sets with high-dimensional feature vectors. The matching similarity is computed in linear time and forms a Mercer kernel. Whereas previous matching approxima- tion algorithms suffer from distortion factors that increase linearly with the fea- ture dimension, we demonstrate that our approach can maintain constant accuracy even as the feature dimension increases. When used as a kernel in a discrimina- tive classiﬁer, our approach achieves improved object recognition results over a state-of-the-art set kernel.

paragraphs: Comparing two sets of feature vectors can involve finding a partial matching between their members. Pyramid intersection approximates this comparison efficiently. This paper changes the pyramid representation so that it can take advantage of structure in the feature space, addressing the loss of matching accuracy that can accompany high-dimensional vectors.

The proposed embedding uses a hierarchy of bins with nonuniform shapes. These bins provide a structured representation for computing matching similarity, and the resulting computation takes linear time. The similarity also satisfies the requirements of a Mercer kernel, allowing it to be used directly in a kernel-based discriminative classifier.

The authors demonstrate that their approach can maintain constant accuracy as feature dimensionality increases, whereas earlier approximations have distortion factors that grow linearly with dimension. In object recognition experiments, the proposed kernel improves results over a state-of-the-art set kernel. Together, these findings support adapting the pyramid to the feature space as a way to combine efficient matching with useful high-dimensional comparisons.
summary.tldr: A pyramid embedding with nonuniform bins supports efficient set matching that can retain accuracy as feature dimensionality grows.

title: Approximate Correspondences in High Dimensions

abstract: Cognitive control refers to the flexible deployment of memory and attention in response to task demands and current goals. Control is often studied experimentally by presenting sequences of stimuli, some demanding a response, and others modulating the stimulus-response mapping. In these tasks, participants must maintain information about the current stimulus-response mapping in working memory. Prominent theories of cognitive control use recurrent neural nets to implement working memory, and optimize memory utilization via reinforcement learning. We present a novel perspective on cognitive control in which working memory representations are intrinsically probabilistic, and control operations that maintain and update working memory are dynamically determined via probabilistic inference. We show that our model provides a parsimonious account of behavioral and neuroimaging data, and suggest that it offers an elegant conceptualization of control in which behavior can be cast as optimal, subject to limitations on learning and the rate of information processing. Moreover, our model provides insight into how task instructions can be directly translated into appropriate behavior and then efficiently refined with subsequent task experience.

paragraphs: Cognitive control allows memory and attention to adapt to changing goals and task demands. In tasks where instructions alter which response belongs to a stimulus, people must retain the current mapping in working memory. This paper proposes that those memory representations are inherently probabilistic and that control operations follow from inference over them.

Within this perspective, maintaining and updating working memory are dynamically determined through probabilistic inference. The authors present the model as a compact account of behavioral and neuroimaging data. They suggest that behavior can be understood as optimal subject to limits on learning and the rate of information processing, making those constraints part of the explanation.

The framework also addresses how task instructions can produce appropriate behavior immediately and how experience can subsequently refine that behavior. Instructions and practice thus enter a common account of control over time. The contribution is a probabilistic perspective on the changing contents and use of working memory, supported by its reported ability to account for both behavioral observations and neuroimaging findings.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic working-memory model explains cognitive control through inference constrained by learning and information-processing limits.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Cognitive Control

abstract: We introduce the first temporal-difference learning algorithm that is stable with linear function approximation and off-policy training, for any finite Markov decision process, target policy, and exciting behavior policy, and whose complexity scales linearly in the number of parameters. We consider an i.i.d.\ policy-evaluation setting in which the data need not come from on-policy experience. The gradient temporal-difference (GTD) algorithm estimates the expected update vector of the TD(0) algorithm and performs stochastic gradient descent on its L_2 norm. Our analysis proves that its expected update is in the direction of the gradient, assuring convergence under the usual stochastic approximation conditions to the same least-squares solution as found by the LSTD, but without its quadratic computational complexity. GTD is online and incremental, and does not involve multiplying by products of likelihood ratios as in importance-sampling methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses policy evaluation when experience comes from a different policy than the one being evaluated. It introduces gradient temporal-difference learning, or GTD, combining stability under linear function approximation with computational cost that grows linearly with the number of parameters. This makes convergence and inexpensive incremental updates part of the same algorithmic result.

GTD estimates the expected update that ordinary TD(0) would make, then uses stochastic gradient descent to reduce the size of that update vector. The analysis establishes that its expected update follows the gradient direction. Under the usual stochastic approximation conditions, it converges to the same least-squares solution as LSTD, while avoiding that method's quadratic computational complexity.

The result concerns an independent, identically distributed policy-evaluation setting, a finite Markov decision process, and an exciting behavior policy. These qualifications define the scope of the convergence claim. Within that setting, GTD processes information online and incrementally, without multiplying products of likelihood ratios as importance-sampling methods do. The contribution is a stable route to off-policy evaluation with linear computational scaling.
summary.tldr: GTD achieves convergent off-policy evaluation with linear function approximation and linear computational cost under the stated sampling and convergence conditions.

title: A Convergent $O(n)$ Temporal-difference Algorithm for Off-policy Learning with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Research in animal learning and behavioral neuroscience has distinguished between two forms of action control: a habit-based form, which relies on stored action values, and a goal-directed form, which forecasts and compares action outcomes based on a model of the environment. While habit-based control has been the subject of extensive computational research, the computational principles underlying goal-directed control in animals have so far received less attention. In the present paper, we advance a computational framework for goal-directed control in animals and humans. We take three empirically motivated points as founding premises: (1) Neurons in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex represent action policies, (2) Neurons in orbitofrontal cortex represent rewards, and (3) Neural computation, across domains, can be appropriately understood as performing structured probabilistic inference. On a purely computational level, the resulting account relates closely to previous work using Bayesian inference to solve Markov decision problems, but extends this work by introducing a new algorithm, which provably converges on optimal plans. On a cognitive and neuroscientific level, the theory provides a unifying framework for several different forms of goal-directed action selection, placing emphasis on a novel form, within which orbitofrontal reward representations directly drive policy selection.

paragraphs: Goal-directed action control forecasts possible outcomes using a model of the environment and compares them before choosing an action. This paper develops a computational account of that process in animals and humans. It addresses a form of control that, according to the abstract, had received less computational attention than habit-based choices relying on stored action values.

The framework starts from three empirically motivated premises. Dorsolateral prefrontal neurons represent action policies, orbitofrontal neurons represent rewards, and neural computation can be understood as structured probabilistic inference. Together, these premises connect representations of possible behavior and desirable outcomes through an inference process.

Computationally, the account relates to Bayesian approaches for solving Markov decision problems and introduces an algorithm proved to converge to optimal plans. At the cognitive and neural level, it organizes several forms of goal-directed selection within one framework. A particularly emphasized form lets orbitofrontal reward representations directly drive policy selection. The convergence result belongs to the proposed algorithm, while the neural account rests on the stated representational and computational premises.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic-inference framework links prefrontal policy and reward representations to goal-directed control and an algorithm that converges to optimal plans.

title: Goal-directed decision making in prefrontal cortex: a computational framework

abstract: Many statistical $M$-estimators are based on convex optimization problems formed by the weighted sum of a loss function with a norm-based regularizer. We analyze the convergence rates of first-order gradient methods for solving such problems within a high-dimensional framework that allows the data dimension $d$ to grow with (and possibly exceed) the sample size $n$. This high-dimensional structure precludes the usual global assumptions---namely, strong convexity and smoothness conditions---that underlie classical optimization analysis. We define appropriately restricted versions of these conditions, and show that they are satisfied with high probability for various statistical models. Under these conditions, our theory guarantees that Nesterov's first-order method~\cite{Nesterov07} has a globally geometric rate of convergence up to the statistical precision of the model, meaning the typical Euclidean distance between the true unknown parameter $\theta^*$ and the optimal solution $\widehat{\theta}$. This globally linear rate is substantially faster than previous analyses of global convergence for specific methods that yielded only sublinear rates. Our analysis applies to a wide range of $M$-estimators and statistical models, including sparse linear regression using Lasso ($\ell_1$-regularized regression), group Lasso, block sparsity, and low-rank matrix recovery using nuclear norm regularization. Overall, this result reveals an interesting connection between statistical precision and computational efficiency in high-dimensional estimation.
originalAbstract: Many statistical $M$-estimators are based on convex optimization problems formed by the weighted sum of a loss function with a norm-based regularizer. This high-dimensional structure precludes the usual global assumptions---namely, strong convexity and smoothness conditions---that underlie classical optimization analysis. We define appropriately restricted versions of these conditions, and show that they are satisfied with high probability for various statistical models. Under these conditions, our theory guarantees that Nesterov's first-order method~\cite{Nesterov07} has a globally geometric rate of convergence up to the statistical precision of the model, meaning the typical Euclidean distance between the true unknown parameter $\theta^*$ and the optimal solution $\widehat{\theta}$. Our analysis applies to a wide range of $M$-estimators and statistical models, including sparse linear regression using Lasso ($\ell_1$-regularized regression), group Lasso, block sparsity, and low-rank matrix recovery using nuclear norm regularization. Overall, this result reveals an interesting connection between statistical precision and computational efficiency in high-dimensional estimation.

This paper examines how quickly gradient methods solve such problems when the number of variables can grow with, or exceed, the number of observations. In this setting, the global curvature assumptions used in classical optimization analysis may be unavailable.

The authors introduce restricted versions of strong convexity and smoothness and show that these hold with high probability for several statistical models. Under those conditions, Nesterov's first-order method converges geometrically until it reaches the model's statistical precision. That precision is measured by the typical distance between the estimated parameter and the unknown true parameter.

The guarantee ties useful computational accuracy to the accuracy supported by the data. Within that range, the geometric rate is substantially faster than the sublinear rates in previous analyses cited by the authors. The framework covers examples including Lasso, group sparsity, and nuclear-norm-based matrix recovery, making the connection relevant across several forms of high-dimensional estimation.
summary.tldr: Under restricted curvature conditions, a first-order method converges geometrically to the statistical precision of several high-dimensional estimators.

title: Fast global convergence rates of gradient methods for high-dimensional statistical recovery

abstract: In Learning Using Privileged Information (LUPI) paradigm, along with the standard training data in the decision space, a teacher supplies a learner with the privileged information in the correcting space. The goal of the learner is to find a classifier with a low generalization error in the decision space. We consider a new version of empirical risk minimization algorithm, called Privileged ERM, that takes into account the privileged information in order to find a good function in the decision space. We outline the conditions on the correcting space that, if satisfied, allow Privileged ERM to have much faster learning rate in the decision space than the one of the regular empirical risk minimization.

paragraphs: Learning Using Privileged Information gives a learner additional guidance from a teacher alongside its ordinary training data. The extra information belongs to a correcting space, while the classifier ultimately operates in the decision space. This paper examines when that additional training guidance can improve how quickly the learner acquires a classifier with low generalization error.

The authors introduce Privileged ERM, a version of empirical risk minimization that uses the privileged information when selecting a function in the decision space. The two spaces have distinct roles: one contains the information used for the final prediction problem, and the other supplies guidance that influences the training procedure.

The theoretical contribution outlines conditions on the correcting space under which Privileged ERM can learn much faster than ordinary empirical risk minimization. The acceleration is conditional on those properties of the additional information. This makes the quality and structure of the teacher's guidance central to the result: providing extra information can help when it satisfies the stated theoretical conditions.
summary.tldr: Privileged ERM can achieve much faster learning than ordinary ERM when the teacher's additional information satisfies suitable conditions.

title: On the Theory of Learnining with Privileged Information

abstract: Applications of Brain-Machine-Interfaces typically estimate user intent based on biological signals that are under voluntary control. For example, we might want to estimate how a patient with a paralyzed arm wants to move based on residual muscle activity. To solve such problems it is necessary to integrate obtained information over time. To do so, state of the art approaches typically use a probabilistic model of how the state, e.g. position and velocity of the arm, evolves over time – a so-called trajectory model. We wanted to further develop this approach using two intuitive insights: (1) At any given point of time there may be a small set of likely movement targets, potentially identified by the location of objects in the workspace or by gaze information from the user. (2) The user may want to produce movements at varying speeds. We thus use a generative model with a trajectory model incorporating these insights. Approximate inference on that generative model is implemented using a mixture of extended Kalman filters. We find that the resulting algorithm allows us to decode arm movements dramatically better than when we use a trajectory model with linear dynamics.

Because individual observations provide information over time, a decoder needs a model of how movement evolves. This paper develops that trajectory model using two ideas: the user may be choosing among a small set of likely targets, and the same movement may occur at different speeds.

The authors incorporate both ideas into a generative model. Candidate targets could be suggested by objects in the workspace or by the user's gaze, while time warping accommodates variation in movement speed. Approximate inference uses a mixture of extended Kalman filters, bringing multiple trajectory possibilities into the decoding procedure.

The resulting algorithm decodes arm movements dramatically better than a decoder using a trajectory model with linear dynamics in the reported comparison. The finding supports the value of representing plausible destinations and flexible timing when integrating biological signals. It shows that assumptions about intended movement can materially affect decoding quality, alongside the information carried by the observed signals.
summary.tldr: A trajectory model combining likely movement targets with variable speeds improves arm-movement decoding over the tested linear-dynamics model.

title: Mixture of time-warped trajectory models for movement decoding

abstract: We propose a new supervised learning framework for visual object counting tasks, such as estimating the number of cells in a microscopic image or the number of humans in surveillance video frames. We focus on the practically-attractive case when the training images are annotated with dots (one dot per object). Our goal is to accurately estimate the count. However, we evade the hard task of learning to detect and localize individual object instances. Instead, we cast the problem as that of estimating an image density whose integral over any image region gives the count of objects within that region. Learning to infer such density can be formulated as a minimization of a regularized risk quadratic cost function. We introduce a new loss function, which is well-suited for such learning, and at the same time can be computed efficiently via a maximum subarray algorithm. The learning can then be posed as a convex quadratic program solvable with cutting-plane optimization. The proposed framework is very flexible as it can accept any domain-specific visual features. Once trained, our system provides accurate object counts and requires a very small time overhead over the feature extraction step, making it a good candidate for applications involving real-time processing or dealing with huge amount of visual data.

The resulting learning problem is a convex quadratic program solved through cutting-plane optimization. summary.tldr: Learning an image density from dot annotations enables accurate regional object counts with little overhead beyond feature extraction.

title: Learning To Count Objects in Images

abstract: In recent years, a rich variety of shrinkage priors have been proposed that have great promise in addressing massive regression problems. In general, these new priors can be expressed as scale mixtures of normals, but have more complex forms and better properties than traditional Cauchy and double exponential priors. We first propose a new class of normal scale mixtures through a novel generalized beta distribution that encompasses many interesting priors as special cases. This encompassing framework should prove useful in comparing competing priors, considering properties and revealing close connections. We then develop a class of variational Bayes approximations through the new hierarchy presented that will scale more efficiently to the types of truly massive data sets that are now encountered routinely.

paragraphs: The paper develops a common mathematical representation for shrinkage priors used in large regression problems. These priors control how strongly regression coefficients are pulled toward smaller values. Many promising constructions can be written as normal distributions whose scales are themselves random, but their different forms can obscure the relationships among them.

The authors introduce a new generalized beta distribution that generates a broad class of these normal scale mixtures. Several existing priors become special cases of the same construction. This encompassing hierarchy is intended to make it easier to compare competing priors, examine their properties, and identify connections that are less apparent when each prior is presented separately.

The hierarchy also provides a basis for a class of variational Bayes approximations. These are designed to make inference scale more efficiently to very large datasets. The paper thus connects a modeling contribution with a computational one: a shared family organizes shrinkage choices, while approximate inference methods use that organization to support large regression applications.
summary.tldr: A generalized beta hierarchy unifies many Gaussian scale-mixture shrinkage priors and supports scalable variational Bayesian inference.

title: Generalized Beta Mixtures of Gaussians

abstract: This paper studies the problem of semi-supervised learning from the vector field perspective. Many of the existing work use the graph Laplacian to ensure the smoothness of the prediction function on the data manifold. However, beyond smoothness, it is suggested by recent theoretical work that we should ensure second order smoothness for achieving faster rates of convergence for semi-supervised regression problems. To achieve this goal, we show that the second order smoothness measures the linearity of the function, and the gradient field of a linear function has to be a parallel vector field. Consequently, we propose to find a function which minimizes the empirical error, and simultaneously requires its gradient field to be as parallel as possible. We give a continuous objective function on the manifold and discuss how to discretize it by using random points. The discretized optimization problem turns out to be a sparse linear system which can be solved very efficiently. The experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised regression uses both labeled and unlabeled data to learn a prediction function. Many approaches encourage the function to vary smoothly over the data manifold using a graph Laplacian. This paper pursues second-order smoothness, motivated by theoretical work suggesting that it can help achieve faster convergence rates.

The authors connect second-order smoothness to the function's linearity and connect linearity to a parallel gradient field. Their objective therefore balances agreement with observed labels against making the gradient field as parallel as possible. The regularization concerns how the function's changes vary across the manifold, going beyond smoothness of the predictions alone.

The paper first formulates this objective continuously on the manifold, then explains how to discretize it with random points. The resulting optimization is a sparse linear system that can be solved efficiently. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach. Its contribution combines a geometric motivation for the regularizer with a computational formulation that makes the proposed regression procedure practical.
summary.tldr: Parallel-field regularization encourages second-order smoothness in semi-supervised regression and leads to an efficient sparse linear system.

title: Semi-supervised Regression via Parallel Field Regularization

abstract: The dominant visual search paradigm for object class detection is sliding windows. Although simple and effective, it is also wasteful, unnatural and rigidly hardwired. We propose strategies to search for objects which intelligently explore the space of windows by making sequential observations at locations decided based on previous observations. Our strategies adapt to the class being searched and to the content of a particular test image. Their driving force is exploiting context as the statistical relation between the appearance of a window and its location relative to the object, as observed in the training set. In addition to being more elegant than sliding windows, we demonstrate experimentally on the PASCAL VOC 2010 dataset that our strategies evaluate two orders of magnitude fewer windows while at the same time achieving higher detection accuracy.

paragraphs: Object detectors often search an image by evaluating many sliding windows. This straightforward approach can spend substantial effort on uninformative locations. The paper develops sequential search strategies that choose the next window based on what earlier windows revealed, making the search responsive to both the object category and the particular image.

The guiding information is context learned from training data. Specifically, the method uses statistical relationships between a window’s appearance and its position relative to an object. An observation can therefore help direct attention toward other locations, even as the search proceeds. Window selection becomes an adaptive process informed by accumulated visual evidence.

On PASCAL VOC 2010, the authors report evaluating two orders of magnitude fewer windows while also achieving higher detection accuracy. This combines a reduction in search effort with improved detection in the reported experiment. The finding supports the idea that learning where to look can be as consequential as evaluating what appears at a predetermined set of locations.
summary.tldr: Context-guided sequential search evaluates roughly 100 times fewer windows while improving detection accuracy on PASCAL VOC 2010.

title: Searching for objects driven by context

abstract: Stochastic differential equations (SDE) are a natural tool for modelling systems that are inherently noisy or contain uncertainties that can be modelled as stochastic processes. Crucial to the process of using SDE to build mathematical models is the ability to estimate parameters of those models from observed data. Over the past few decades, significant progress has been made on this problem, but we are still far from having a definitive solution. We describe a novel method of approximating a diffusion process that we show to be useful in Markov chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) inference algorithms. We take the ‘white’ noise that drives a diffusion process and decompose it into two terms. The first is a ‘coloured noise’ term that can be deterministically controlled by a set of auxilliary variables. The second term is small and enables us to form a linear Gaussian ‘small noise’ approximation. The decomposition allows us to take a diffusion process of interest and cast it in a form that is amenable to sampling by MCMC methods. We explain why many state-of-the-art inference methods fail on highly nonlinear inference problems. We demonstrate experimentally that our method performs well in such situations. Our results show that this method is a promising new tool for use in inference and parameter estimation problems.

paragraphs: Stochastic differential equations model systems driven by noise, but using them requires estimating parameters from observations. This paper develops an approximation of diffusion processes designed to help Markov chain Monte Carlo inference. The goal is to express a noisy process in a form that sampling algorithms can handle effectively, including in highly nonlinear inference problems.

The method splits the driving white noise into two components. A colored-noise component is deterministically controlled by auxiliary variables. Its practical significance is the connection between a particular approximation of the noise and a more workable sampling formulation.
summary.tldr: Decomposing diffusion noise into controlled colored noise and a small residual enables an MCMC-friendly approximation for nonlinear parameter inference.

title: The Coloured Noise Expansion and Parameter Estimation of Diffusion Processes

abstract: Designing a principled and effective algorithm for learning deep architectures is a challenging problem. The current approach involves two training phases: a fully unsupervised learning followed by a strongly discriminative optimization. We suggest a deep learning strategy that bridges the gap between the two phases, resulting in a three-phase learning procedure. We propose to implement the scheme using a method to regularize deep belief networks with top-down information. The network is constructed from building blocks of restricted Boltzmann machines learned by combining bottom-up and top-down sampled signals. A global optimization procedure that merges samples from a forward bottom-up pass and a top-down pass is used. Experiments on the MNIST dataset show improvements over the existing algorithms for deep belief networks. Object recognition results on the Caltech-101 dataset also yield competitive results.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the transition between two stages of training deep belief networks: unsupervised learning and strongly discriminative optimization. The authors propose a three-phase procedure that adds a bridge between them. Its purpose is to connect the learning signals used across the training process more closely.

Their implementation regularizes deep belief networks using top-down information. The network is assembled from restricted Boltzmann machines trained with a combination of bottom-up and top-down sampled signals. A global optimization procedure merges samples from a forward bottom-up pass with samples from a top-down pass, allowing both directions to participate in learning the network.

Experiments on MNIST show improvements over existing deep belief network algorithms. On Caltech-101, the method produces competitive object-recognition results. These are distinct empirical claims: the abstract reports improvement in the first setting and competitiveness in the second. Together, they support the usefulness of introducing top-down regularization into a staged training procedure for the deep belief networks studied.
summary.tldr: A three-phase training procedure uses top-down signals to regularize deep belief networks, improving MNIST results and remaining competitive on Caltech-101.

title: Top-Down Regularization of Deep Belief Networks

abstract: A predictor that is deployed in a live production system may perturb the features it uses to make predictions. Such a feedback loop can occur, for example, when a model that predicts a certain type of behavior ends up causing the behavior it predicts, thus creating a self-fulfilling prophecy. In this paper we analyze predictor feedback detection as a causal inference problem, and introduce a local randomization scheme that can be used to detect non-linear feedback in real-world problems. We conduct a pilot study for our proposed methodology using a predictive system currently deployed as a part of a search engine.
originalAbstract: A predictor that is deployed in a live production system may perturb the features it uses to make predictions. Such a feedback loop can occur, for example, when a model that predicts a certain type of behavior ends up causing the behavior it predicts, thus creating a self-fulfilling prophecy. In this paper we analyze predictor feedback detection as a causal inference problem, and introduce a local randomization scheme that can be used to detect non-linear feedback in real-world problems. We conduct a pilot study for our proposed methodology using a predictive system currently deployed as a part of a search engine.

paragraphs: A predictor deployed in a production system can change the features it later uses to make predictions. For example, predicting a behavior may help cause that behavior, creating a self-fulfilling pattern. The paper studies how to detect this feedback when a predictive model is already operating within a live system.

The authors formulate feedback detection as a causal inference problem. The question concerns whether the deployed predictor influences its inputs, making the direction of influence central to the analysis. They introduce a local randomization scheme designed to detect nonlinear feedback, extending the proposed detection approach to relationships that need not follow a simple linear pattern.

The methodology is examined in a pilot study involving a predictive system deployed within a search engine. This provides an application of the proposed causal approach in a real production setting. The paper's contribution is a way to investigate whether a live predictor participates in creating the signals it subsequently observes, with the pilot study illustrating its practical use.
summary.tldr: A causal inference approach uses local randomization to detect nonlinear feedback from deployed predictors into their own input features.

title: Feedback Detection for Live Predictors

abstract: Linear regression models have been successfully used to function estimation and model selection in high-dimensional data analysis. However, most existing methods are built on least squares with the mean square error (MSE) criterion, which are sensitive to outliers and their performance may be degraded for heavy-tailed noise. In this paper, we go beyond this criterion by investigating the regularized modal regression from a statistical learning viewpoint. A new regularized modal regression model is proposed for estimation and variable selection, which is robust to outliers, heavy-tailed noise, and skewed noise. On the theoretical side, we establish the approximation estimate for learning the conditional mode function, the sparsity analysis for variable selection, and the robustness characterization. On the application side, we applied our model to successfully improve the cognitive impairment prediction using the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) cohort data.

Its target is the conditional mode: the most likely response value for given inputs. Changing that target provides an alternative basis for estimation in difficult noise conditions.

The proposed model performs both function estimation and variable selection. The authors characterize its robustness to outliers, heavy-tailed noise, and skewed noise. Their theoretical analysis covers approximation of the conditional mode function, sparsity in the selected variables, and robustness, linking the predictive target with the ability to identify a smaller set of relevant inputs.

The method is also applied to cognitive impairment prediction using data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, where the authors report an improvement. This application demonstrates the approach in the studied prediction setting. The broader methodological contribution is a statistically analyzed alternative to squared-error regression that combines a modal prediction target with regularization and variable selection.
summary.tldr: Regularized modal regression combines robust estimation and variable selection, with a reported improvement in cognitive impairment prediction.

title: Regularized Modal Regression with Applications in Cognitive Impairment Prediction

abstract: Given samples lying on any of a number of subspaces, subspace clustering is the task of grouping the samples based on the their corresponding subspaces. Many subspace clustering methods operate by assigning a measure of affinity to each pair of points and feeding these affinities into a graph clustering algorithm. This paper proposes a new paradigm for subspace clustering that computes affinities based on the corresponding conic geometry. The proposed conic subspace clustering (CSC) approach considers the convex hull of a collection of normalized data points and the corresponding tangent cones. The union of subspaces underlying the data imposes a strong association between the tangent cone at a sample $x$ and the original subspace containing $x$. In addition to describing this novel geometric perspective, this paper provides a practical algorithm for subspace clustering that leverages this perspective, where a tangent cone membership test is used to estimate the affinities. This algorithm is accompanied with deterministic and stochastic guarantees on the properties of the learned affinity matrix, on the true and false positive rates and spread, which directly translate into the overall clustering accuracy.

paragraphs: Subspace clustering groups points according to which underlying subspace they occupy. Many methods first assign pairwise affinities and then cluster the resulting graph. This paper proposes a geometric way to construct those affinities, using tangent cones associated with the convex hull of normalized data points.

A tangent cone describes the local directions available from a point within this convex geometry. The paper argues that the collection of underlying subspaces creates a strong association between a sample's tangent cone and its original subspace. Its conic subspace clustering algorithm uses a tangent-cone membership test to estimate how strongly pairs of samples should be connected.

The authors provide deterministic and stochastic guarantees for the learned affinity matrix, including its true-positive and false-positive rates and spread. These properties translate directly into overall clustering accuracy. The contribution therefore connects a geometric view of the data to both a practical clustering procedure and an analysis of the relationships it constructs, making affinity estimation the bridge between subspace structure and final groups.
summary.tldr: Conic subspace clustering uses tangent-cone geometry to estimate pairwise affinities, with guarantees connecting those affinities to clustering accuracy.

title: Subspace Clustering via Tangent Cones

abstract: We consider the problem of estimating multiple related functions computed by weighted automata~(WFA). We first present a natural notion of relatedness between WFAs by considering to which extent several WFAs can share a common underlying representation. We then introduce the model of vector-valued WFA which conveniently helps us formalize this notion of relatedness. Finally, we propose a spectral learning algorithm for vector-valued WFAs to tackle the multitask learning problem. By jointly learning multiple tasks in the form of a vector-valued WFA, our algorithm enforces the discovery of a representation space shared between tasks. The benefits of the proposed multitask approach are theoretically motivated and showcased through experiments on both synthetic and real world datasets.

Its starting question is what makes the corresponding learning tasks related in a way an algorithm can exploit. The authors answer by considering how much of an underlying representation the automata can share.

To express that relationship, they introduce vector-valued weighted automata. A single model represents multiple task outputs, providing a formal setting for shared structure. They then develop a spectral learning algorithm for this model. Learning the tasks jointly enforces the discovery of a common representation space, making sharing an explicit property of the learning procedure.

This matters because the method connects a definition of task relatedness with a concrete mechanism for learning related tasks together. The authors provide theoretical motivation for the benefits and demonstrate them on synthetic and real-world datasets. The stated contribution is therefore both a modeling framework for shared automaton representations and an algorithm whose multitask benefits are supported by analysis and experiments.
summary.tldr: A spectral algorithm learns related weighted automata jointly by representing their tasks in a shared vector-valued model.

title: Multitask Spectral Learning of Weighted Automata

abstract: Most distributed machine learning systems nowadays, including TensorFlow and CNTK, are built in a centralized fashion. One bottleneck of centralized algorithms lies on high communication cost on the central node. Motivated by this, we ask, can decentralized algorithms be faster than its centralized counterpart? Although decentralized PSGD (D-PSGD) algorithms have been studied by the control community, existing analysis and theory do not show any advantage over centralized PSGD (C-PSGD) algorithms, simply assuming the application scenario where only the decentralized network is available. In this paper, we study a D-PSGD algorithm and provide the first theoretical analysis that indicates a regime in which decentralized algorithms might outperform centralized algorithms for distributed stochastic gradient descent. This is because D-PSGD has comparable total computational complexities to C-PSGD but requires much less communication cost on the busiest node. We further conduct an empirical study to validate our theoretical analysis across multiple frameworks (CNTK and Torch), different network configurations, and computation platforms up to 112 GPUs. On network configurations with low bandwidth or high latency, D-PSGD can be up to one order of magnitude faster than its well-optimized centralized counterparts.

paragraphs: Distributed training can concentrate communication at a central node, making that node a bottleneck. This paper asks whether decentralized parallel stochastic gradient descent can outperform a centralized implementation even when both arrangements are available. The question concerns training efficiency, rather than decentralization being the only possible network arrangement.

The theoretical analysis identifies a regime where decentralized training might be faster. Its total computational complexity is comparable to that of centralized training, while its busiest node handles much less communication. This separates the amount of computation from the communication burden concentrated at a particular location, explaining how similar computational requirements can lead to different runtimes.

The authors test this argument using CNTK and Torch, multiple network configurations, and platforms with up to 112 GPUs. On networks with low bandwidth or high latency, decentralized training can be up to an order of magnitude faster than well-optimized centralized counterparts. The result supports a conditional advantage: the communication environment matters substantially to whether decentralization improves speed.
summary.tldr: Decentralized stochastic gradient descent can outperform centralized training when communication bottlenecks dominate, with reported speedups up to an order of magnitude.

title: Can Decentralized Algorithms Outperform Centralized Algorithms? A Case Study for Decentralized Parallel Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: Converting an n-dimensional vector to a probability distribution over n objects is a commonly used component in many machine learning tasks like multiclass classification, multilabel classification, attention mechanisms etc. For this, several probability mapping functions have been proposed and employed in literature such as softmax, sum-normalization, spherical softmax, and sparsemax, but there is very little understanding in terms how they relate with each other. Further, none of the above formulations offer an explicit control over the degree of sparsity. To address this, we develop a unified framework that encompasses all these formulations as special cases. This framework ensures simple closed-form solutions and existence of sub-gradients suitable for learning via backpropagation. Within this framework, we propose two novel sparse formulations, sparsegen-lin and sparsehourglass, that seek to provide a control over the degree of desired sparsity. We further develop novel convex loss functions that help induce the behavior of aforementioned formulations in the multilabel classification setting, showing improved performance. We also demonstrate empirically that the proposed formulations, when used to compute attention weights, achieve better or comparable performance on standard seq2seq tasks like neural machine translation and abstractive summarization.

paragraphs: Many learning systems convert a vector of scores into probabilities, whether for classification or attention. This paper studies the relationship among several such mappings, including softmax, sum-normalization, spherical softmax, and sparsemax. It focuses particularly on controlling sparsity: how many entries receive zero probability.

The authors develop a common framework containing these existing mappings as special cases. It provides simple closed-form solutions and subgradients suitable for backpropagation. Within it, they introduce sparsegen-lin and sparsehourglass, two formulations intended to offer control over the desired degree of sparsity. This makes sparsity a property the mapping is designed to regulate.

The paper also develops convex losses to encourage the proposed mappings' behavior in multilabel classification, where experiments show improved performance. When used for attention in machine translation and abstractive summarization, the formulations achieve better or comparable results on the reported tasks. The findings support controllable sparse mappings as useful alternatives, without claiming that greater sparsity always improves a model.
summary.tldr: A unified framework connects probability mappings and introduces sparse alternatives with explicit control over sparsity and competitive empirical performance.

title: On Controllable Sparse Alternatives to Softmax

abstract: Given samples from a probability distribution, anomaly detection is the problem of determining if a given point lies in a low-density region. This paper concerns calibrated anomaly detection, which is the practically relevant extension where we additionally wish to produce a confidence score for a point being anomalous. Building on a classification framework for anomaly detection, we show how minimisation of a suitably modified proper loss produces density estimates only for anomalous instances. We then show how to incorporate quantile control by relating our objective to a generalised version of the pinball loss. Finally, we show how to efficiently optimise the objective with kernelised scorer, by leveraging a recent result from the point process literature. The resulting objective captures a close relative of the one-class SVM as a special case.

paragraphs: Anomaly detection asks whether a point falls in a region where the data distribution has little probability density. Calibrated anomaly detection adds another requirement: the system should also produce a confidence score for calling that point unusual. The paper develops a learning objective that connects these two outputs, so detection and confidence estimation can be addressed within one framework.

Starting from a classification approach to anomaly detection, the authors modify a proper loss function. Minimizing the resulting loss produces density estimates specifically for anomalous instances. This targeted estimation is central to the approach: the objective supplies density information in the part of the distribution relevant to identifying anomalies.

The framework also supports quantile control through a connection to a generalized pinball loss. For scoring functions built with kernels, the authors derive an efficient optimization approach using a result from point process theory. A close relative of the one-class support vector machine appears as a special case, connecting the proposed calibrated objective to an established anomaly-detection formulation.
summary.tldr: A modified classification loss combines anomaly detection with confidence estimation, quantile control, and efficient kernel-based optimization.

title: A loss framework for calibrated anomaly detection

abstract: The growing importance of massive datasets with the advent of deep learning makes robustness to label noise a critical property for classifiers to have. Sources of label noise include automatic labeling for large datasets, non-expert labeling, and label corruption by data poisoning adversaries. In the latter case, corruptions may be arbitrarily bad, even so bad that a classifier predicts the wrong labels with high confidence. To protect against such sources of noise, we leverage the fact that a small set of clean labels is often easy to procure. We demonstrate that robustness to label noise up to severe strengths can be achieved by using a set of trusted data with clean labels, and propose a loss correction that utilizes trusted examples in a data-efficient manner to mitigate the effects of label noise on deep neural network classifiers. Across vision and natural language processing tasks, we experiment with various label noises at several strengths, and show that our method significantly outperforms existing methods.

paragraphs: Large training datasets can contain incorrect labels from automatic annotation, nonexpert annotators, or deliberate poisoning. Severe corruption can lead a classifier to predict incorrect labels with high confidence. This paper examines how a small collection of trusted, correctly labeled examples can help train deep networks despite substantial noise in the broader dataset.

The proposed method uses trusted examples to construct a correction to the training loss. The goal is to use clean labels efficiently so that their information reduces the influence of corrupted supervision. Its practical premise is that obtaining a small clean set is often feasible even when ensuring the quality of every label in a large dataset is difficult.

Experiments span vision and natural-language tasks, several types of label noise, and multiple noise strengths. The method significantly outperforms existing approaches in those evaluations, including under severe noise. These findings support using trusted data as a resource for correcting noisy training, with the evidence demonstrating robustness across the tested conditions rather than establishing success against every possible corruption.
summary.tldr: A loss correction uses a small trusted set of clean labels to improve deep-network robustness under tested severe label-noise conditions.

title: Using Trusted Data to Train Deep Networks on Labels Corrupted by Severe Noise

abstract: We propose a new type of generative model for high-dimensional data that learns a manifold geometry of the data, rather than density, and can generate points evenly along this manifold. This is in contrast to existing generative models that represent data density, and are strongly affected by noise and other artifacts of data collection. We demonstrate how this approach corrects sampling biases and artifacts, thus improves several downstream data analysis tasks, such as clustering and classification. Finally, we demonstrate that this approach is especially useful in biology where, despite the advent of single-cell technologies, rare subpopulations and gene-interaction relationships are affected by biased sampling. We show that SUGAR can generate hypothetical populations, and it is able to reveal intrinsic patterns and mutual-information relationships between genes on a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset of hematopoiesis.

paragraphs: The frequency with which observations appear in a dataset can reflect collection biases as well as the underlying phenomenon. This paper proposes a generative model that learns the geometry of the manifold along which high-dimensional data lie. It then generates points evenly along that manifold, rather than aiming to reproduce the observed data density.

This geometric objective matters when uneven sampling and collection artifacts distort analysis. The authors demonstrate that their approach can correct such biases and improve downstream tasks, including clustering and classification. The generated points serve as a way to explore the learned data structure with a different distribution of coverage.

The paper highlights biology, where biased sampling can affect rare cell populations and relationships between genes. On a single-cell RNA sequencing dataset of hematopoiesis, the method, called SUGAR, generates hypothetical populations and reveals intrinsic patterns and mutual-information relationships between genes. These findings illustrate how geometry-based generation can support analysis of biological structure obscured by sampling.
summary.tldr: SUGAR generates points evenly along learned data geometry to address sampling biases and reveal patterns in downstream analyses.

title: Geometry Based Data Generation

abstract: Vulnerability identification is crucial to protect the software systems from attacks for cyber security. It is especially important to localize the vulnerable functions among the source code to facilitate the fix. However, it is a challenging and tedious process, and also requires specialized security expertise. Inspired by the work on manually-defined patterns of vulnerabilities from various code representation graphs and the recent advance on graph neural networks, we propose Devign, a general graph neural network based model for graph-level classification through learning on a rich set of code semantic representations. It includes a novel Conv module to efficiently extract useful features in the learned rich node representations for graph-level classification. The model is trained over manually labeled datasets built on 4 diversified large-scale open-source C projects that incorporate high complexity and variety of real source code instead of synthesis code used in previous works. The results of the extensive evaluation on the datasets demonstrate that Devign outperforms the state of the arts significantly with an average of 10.51% higher accuracy and 8.68% F1 score, increases averagely 4.66% accuracy and 6.37% F1 by the Conv module.

paragraphs: Finding vulnerable functions in source code helps developers identify where repairs are needed, but manual inspection is demanding and requires security expertise. Devign approaches this task through graph-level classification. It learns from rich graph representations of program semantics, drawing on the idea that code relationships can reveal vulnerability patterns.

The model uses a graph neural network to learn node representations and introduces a Conv module to extract useful features from them for classifying whole graphs. The training datasets are manually labeled and drawn from four diverse, large open-source C projects. This grounds the evaluation in complex real source code with varied behavior.

The reported evaluation shows average improvements over prior leading methods of 10.51% in accuracy and 8.68% in F1 score. The Conv module contributes average gains of 4.66% in accuracy and 6.37% in F1. These findings support both the overall use of learned program representations and the feature-extraction module's contribution on the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Devign learns graph representations of program semantics to identify vulnerable functions, improving reported performance on real C-project datasets.

title: Devign: Effective Vulnerability Identification by Learning Comprehensive Program Semantics via Graph Neural Networks

abstract: Conformal prediction is a technique for constructing prediction intervals that attain valid coverage in finite samples, without making distributional assumptions. Despite this appeal, existing conformal methods can be unnecessarily conservative because they form intervals of constant or weakly varying length across the input space. In this paper we propose a new method that is fully adaptive to heteroscedasticity. It combines conformal prediction with classical quantile regression, inheriting the advantages of both. We establish a theoretical guarantee of valid coverage, supplemented by extensive experiments on popular regression datasets. We compare the efficiency of conformalized quantile regression to other conformal methods, showing that our method tends to produce shorter intervals.

In this paper we propose a new method that is fully adaptive to heteroscedasticity. It combines conformal prediction with classical quantile regression, inheriting the advantages of both. paragraphs: Prediction intervals express uncertainty by giving a range of plausible outcomes around a prediction. Conformal prediction offers finite-sample coverage guarantees without requiring a specified distributional form. However, the paper observes that existing approaches can produce intervals whose lengths change too little across inputs, making them unnecessarily conservative where uncertainty is smaller.

The proposed method combines conformal prediction with quantile regression. Quantile regression provides a way to model different parts of the outcome distribution, allowing interval widths to respond to changing uncertainty. This is useful under heteroscedasticity, where the variability of outcomes differs across the input space. The conformal component supplies the coverage guarantee.

The authors establish valid coverage theoretically and evaluate the method on popular regression datasets. Compared with other conformal approaches, their intervals tend to be shorter. This is an efficiency improvement: the method aims to give informative ranges while preserving the stated coverage property. The empirical wording matters, because the abstract reports a tendency toward shorter intervals rather than a universal advantage on every prediction.
summary.tldr: Conformalized quantile regression adapts prediction intervals to varying uncertainty, guarantees valid coverage, and tends to produce shorter intervals.

title: Conformalized Quantile Regression

abstract: Min-cost flow has been a widely used paradigm for solving data association problems in multi-object tracking (MOT). However, most existing methods of solving min-cost flow problems in MOT are either direct adoption or slight modifications of generic min-cost flow algorithms, yielding sub-optimal computation efficiency and holding the applications back from larger scale of problems. In this paper, by exploiting the special structures and properties of the graphs formulated in MOT problems, we develop an efficient min-cost flow algorithm, namely, minimum-update Successive Shortest Path (muSSP). muSSP is proved to provide exact optimal solution and we demonstrated its efficiency through 40 experiments on five MOT datasets with various object detection results and a number of graph designs. muSSP is always the most efficient in each experiment compared to the three peer solvers, improving the efficiency by 5 to 337 folds relative to the best competing algorithm and averagely 109 to 4089 folds to each of the three peer methods.

paragraphs: Multi-object tracking requires associating detections across observations so that they form consistent object tracks. One widely used formulation expresses this association problem as a minimum-cost flow problem on a graph. This paper targets the computational burden of solving those graphs, which can limit the scale of tracking problems that are practical to process.

The authors develop minimum-update Successive Shortest Path, or muSSP, by exploiting structural properties specific to tracking graphs. The approach specializes the solver to this setting rather than relying on a generic flow algorithm with only small modifications. They prove that muSSP returns an exact optimal solution to the formulated flow problem.

The evaluation includes 40 experiments across five tracking datasets, with different detection results and graph designs. muSSP is the fastest of the compared solvers in every experiment, with reported improvements of 5 to 337 times over the best competitor. These findings demonstrate substantial computational gains in the tested settings while retaining exact optimization. The optimality guarantee concerns the flow objective used for association.
summary.tldr: muSSP exploits tracking-graph structure to solve minimum-cost flow exactly, with large speedups across the reported experiments.

title: muSSP: Efficient Min-cost Flow Algorithm for Multi-object Tracking

abstract: Many classic tasks in vision -- such as the estimation of optical flow or stereo disparities -- can be cast as dense correspondence matching. Well-known techniques for doing so make use of a cost volume, typically a 4D tensor of match costs between all pixels in a 2D image and their potential matches in a 2D search window. State-of-the-art (SOTA) deep networks for flow/stereo make use of such volumetric representations as internal layers. However, such layers require significant amounts of memory and compute, making them cumbersome to use in practice. As a result, SOTA networks also employ various heuristics designed to limit volumetric processing, leading to limited accuracy and overfitting. Instead, we introduce several simple modifications that dramatically simplify the use of volumetric layers - (1) volumetric encoder-decoder architectures that efficiently capture large receptive fields, (2) multi-channel cost volumes that capture multi-dimensional notions of pixel similarities, and finally, (3) separable volumetric filtering that significantly reduces computation and parameters while preserving accuracy. Our innovations dramatically improve accuracy over SOTA on standard benchmarks while being significantly easier to work with - training converges in 10X fewer iterations, and most importantly, our networks generalize across correspondence tasks. On-the-fly adaptation of search windows allows us to repurpose optical flow networks for stereo (and vice versa), and can also be used to implement adaptive networks that increase search window sizes on-demand.

paragraphs: Optical flow and stereo estimation both involve finding corresponding image locations. Cost volumes represent possible matches and their costs, but their four-dimensional structure can consume substantial memory and computation. This paper seeks to make volumetric processing more practical, addressing the reliance on restrictive heuristics that the authors associate with reduced accuracy and overfitting.

The proposed network makes three changes. A volumetric encoder-decoder captures information over large receptive fields. Multiple cost-volume channels represent different notions of pixel similarity. Separable volumetric filtering reduces computation and parameter count while preserving accuracy. These components improve how the network represents and processes candidate correspondences.

The contribution therefore combines more efficient volumetric computation with a correspondence representation that can be adapted across the two tasks.
summary.tldr: More efficient volumetric correspondence layers improve accuracy and training convergence while allowing networks to adapt between optical flow and stereo.

title: Volumetric Correspondence Networks for Optical Flow

abstract: We study the robustness verification problem of tree based models, including random forest (RF) and gradient boosted decision tree (GBDT). Formal robustness verification of decision tree ensembles involves finding the exact minimal adversarial perturbation or a guaranteed lower bound of it. Existing approaches cast this verification problem into a mixed integer linear programming (MILP) problem, which finds the minimal adversarial distortion in exponential time so is impractical for large ensembles. Although this verification problem is NP-complete in general, we give a more precise complexity characterization. We show that there is a simple linear time algorithm for verifying a single tree, and for tree ensembles the verification problem can be cast as a max-clique problem on a multi-partite boxicity graph. For low dimensional problems when boxicity can be viewed as constant, this reformulation leads to a polynomial time algorithm. For general problems, by exploiting the boxicity of the graph, we devise an efficient verification algorithm that can give tight lower bounds on robustness of decision tree ensembles, and allows iterative improvement and any-time termination. On RF/GBDT models trained on a variety of datasets, we significantly outperform the lower bounds obtained by relaxing the MILP formulation into a linear program (LP), and are hundreds times faster than solving MILPs to get the exact minimal adversarial distortion. Our proposed method is capable of giving tight robustness verification bounds on large GBDTs with hundreds of deep trees.

For tree ensembles, verification can seek the exact smallest change or a guaranteed lower bound. This paper studies random forests and gradient-boosted trees, where exact mixed-integer optimization becomes impractical for large ensembles.
