The method also produces tight bounds for large boosted ensembles containing hundreds of deep trees.
summary.tldr: A graph-based formulation enables efficient robustness bounds for large tree ensembles and polynomial-time verification under a constant-boxicity condition.

title: Robustness Verification of Tree-based Models

abstract: Recently, deep feedforward neural networks have achieved considerable success in modeling biological sensory processing, in terms of reproducing the input-output map of sensory neurons. However, such models raise profound questions about the very nature of explanation in neuroscience. Are we simply replacing one complex system (a biological circuit) with another (a deep network), without understanding either? Moreover, beyond neural representations, are the deep network's computational mechanisms for generating neural responses the same as those in the brain? Without a systematic approach to extracting and understanding computational mechanisms from deep neural network models, it can be difficult both to assess the degree of utility of deep learning approaches in neuroscience, and to extract experimentally testable hypotheses from deep networks. We develop such a systematic approach by combining dimensionality reduction and modern attribution methods for determining the relative importance of interneurons for specific visual computations. We apply this approach to deep network models of the retina, revealing a conceptual understanding of how the retina acts as a predictive feature extractor that signals deviations from expectations for diverse spatiotemporal stimuli. For each stimulus, our extracted computational mechanisms are consistent with prior scientific literature, and in one case yields a new mechanistic hypothesis. Thus overall, this work not only yields insights into the computational mechanisms underlying the striking predictive capabilities of the retina, but also places the framework of deep networks as neuroscientific models on firmer theoretical foundations, by providing a new roadmap to go beyond comparing neural representations to extracting and understand computational mechanisms.

The approach combines dimensionality reduction with attribution methods that assess the relative importance of interneurons for particular visual computations. Applied to retinal models, it yields an interpretation of the retina as a predictive feature extractor. In this account, responses signal departures from expectations across a variety of stimuli that change over space and time.

For each stimulus examined, the extracted mechanisms agree with prior scientific literature, and one case produces a new mechanistic hypothesis. Agreement provides support for the interpretation, while the new hypothesis offers a direction for experimental investigation. The broader contribution is a route from a successful predictive network to specific explanations of its computations, extending analysis beyond comparisons of neural representations alone.
summary.tldr: Dimensionality reduction and attribution reveal interpretable predictive mechanisms in retinal networks, including one new mechanistic hypothesis.

title: From deep learning to mechanistic understanding in neuroscience: the structure of retinal prediction

abstract: A central problem in learning from sequential data is representing cumulative history in an incremental fashion as more data is processed. We introduce a general framework (HiPPO) for the online compression of continuous signals and discrete time series by projection onto polynomial bases. Given a measure that specifies the importance of each time step in the past, HiPPO produces an optimal solution to a natural online function approximation problem. As special cases, our framework yields a short derivation of the recent Legendre Memory Unit (LMU) from first principles, and generalizes the ubiquitous gating mechanism of recurrent neural networks such as GRUs. This formal framework yields a new memory update mechanism (HiPPO-LegS) that scales through time to remember all history, avoiding priors on the timescale. HiPPO-LegS enjoys the theoretical benefits of timescale robustness, fast updates, and bounded gradients. By incorporating the memory dynamics into recurrent neural networks, HiPPO RNNs can empirically capture complex temporal dependencies. On the benchmark permuted MNIST dataset, HiPPO-LegS sets a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 98.3%. Finally, on a novel trajectory classification task testing robustness to out-of-distribution timescales and missing data, HiPPO-LegS outperforms RNN and neural ODE baselines by 25-40% accuracy.

title: HiPPO: Recurrent Memory with Optimal Polynomial Projections

abstract: Neural Networks can perform poorly when the training label distribution is heavily imbalanced, as well as when the testing data differs from the training distribution. In order to deal with shift in the testing label distribution, which imbalance causes, we motivate the problem from the perspective of an optimal Bayes classifier and derive a prior rebalancing technique that can be solved through a KL-divergence based optimization. This method allows a flexible post-training hyper-parameter to be efficiently tuned on a validation set and effectively modify the classifier margin to deal with this imbalance. We further combine this method with existing likelihood shift methods, re-interpreting them from the same Bayesian perspective, and demonstrating that our method can deal with both problems in a unified way. The resulting algorithm can be conveniently used on probabilistic classification problems agnostic to underlying architectures. Our results on six different datasets and five different architectures show state of art accuracy, including on large-scale imbalanced datasets such as iNaturalist for classification and Synthia for semantic segmentation. Please see https://github.com/GT-RIPL/UNO-IC.git for implementation.

paragraphs: Neural classifiers can struggle when some labels dominate the training data or when the testing distribution differs from training. This paper approaches label imbalance and shifts in label frequency through the perspective of an optimal Bayes classifier. It derives a prior rebalancing method formulated as a Kullback–Leibler divergence optimization problem.

The method includes a flexible hyperparameter that can be tuned efficiently on validation data after training. Adjusting it changes the classifier margin to address imbalance. The authors also combine prior rebalancing with existing methods for likelihood shift, interpreting both through the same Bayesian framework. This produces a unified approach to the two problems that can be used with probabilistic classifiers across different architectures.

Evaluations span six datasets and five architectures, with reported state-of-the-art accuracy. They include large-scale imbalanced classification on iNaturalist and semantic segmentation on Synthia. These findings support the practical usefulness of post-training recalibration and its combination with likelihood-shift methods, while showing applicability across both image-level classification and pixel-level prediction.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian post-training recalibration method rebalances class priors and combines with likelihood-shift methods to improve predictions on imbalanced datasets.

title: Posterior Re-calibration for Imbalanced Datasets

abstract: Many inference problems in structured prediction can be modeled as maximizing a score function on a space of labels, where graphs are a natural representation to decompose the total score into a sum of unary (nodes) and pairwise (edges) scores. Given a generative model with an undirected connected graph G and true vector of binary labels $\bar{y}$, it has been previously shown that when G has good expansion properties, such as complete graphs or d-regular expanders, one can exactly recover $\bar{y}$ (with high probability and in polynomial time) from a single noisy observation of each edge and node. We analyze the previously studied generative model by Globerson et al. (2015) under a notion of statistical parity. That is, given a fair binary node labeling, we ask the question whether it is possible to recover the fair assignment, with high probability and in polynomial time, from single edge and node observations. We find that, in contrast to the known trade-offs between fairness and model performance, the addition of the fairness constraint improves the probability of exact recovery. We effectively explain this phenomenon and empirically show how graphs with poor expansion properties, such as grids, are now capable of achieving exact recovery. Finally, as a byproduct of our analysis, we provide a tighter minimum-eigenvalue bound than that which can be derived from Weyl's inequality.

paragraphs: Structured prediction can involve assigning labels to graph nodes using noisy evidence about individual nodes and their connections. Previous results showed that certain well-connected graphs permit recovery of every true binary label with high probability and in polynomial time. This paper asks how that recovery problem changes when the true labeling satisfies a statistical-parity fairness condition.

The analysis considers a particular generative model on an undirected connected graph, with one noisy observation per node and edge. Within this setting, adding the fairness constraint improves the probability of recovering the complete true assignment. The result demonstrates a case where a known fairness property supplies useful information for inference, rather than merely introducing a competing prediction requirement.

The authors explain this improvement theoretically and provide experiments showing exact recovery on graphs with weak expansion, including grids. The scope matters: the result concerns recovering an already fair assignment under the studied model. As an additional mathematical contribution, the analysis yields a tighter lower bound on the minimum eigenvalue than one obtainable from Weyl’s inequality.
summary.tldr: Under a studied graph-based generative model, a statistical-parity constraint improves the probability of exactly recovering a fair binary labeling.

title: Fairness constraints can help exact inference in structured prediction

abstract: Total Variation (TV) is a popular regularization strategy that promotes piece-wise constant signals by constraining the ℓ1-norm of the first order derivative of the estimated signal. The resulting optimization problem is usually solved using iterative algorithms such as proximal gradient descent, primal-dual algorithms or ADMM. However, such methods can require a very large number of iterations to converge to a suitable solution. In this paper, we accelerate such iterative algorithms by unfolding proximal gradient descent solvers in order to learn their parameters for 1D TV regularized problems. While this could be done using the synthesis formulation, we demonstrate that this leads to slower performances. The main difficulty in applying such methods in the analysis formulation lies in proposing a way to compute the derivatives through the proximal operator. As our main contribution, we develop and characterize two approaches to do so, describe their benefits and limitations, and discuss the regime where they can actually improve over iterative procedures. We validate those findings with experiments on synthetic and real data.

paragraphs: Total variation regularization encourages a recovered signal to consist of relatively constant segments separated by changes. It does this by penalizing the size of first-order differences through an L1 constraint. Solving the resulting optimization problem with standard iterative methods can require many steps. This paper explores learning solver parameters to accelerate the process for one-dimensional signals.

The authors unfold proximal gradient descent into a trainable sequence of operations. They examine two formulations of the underlying problem and find that using the synthesis formulation leads to slower performance. The analysis formulation presents a different obstacle: training requires derivatives through the proximal operator, the operation that handles the regularization within each iteration.

The main contribution is the development and characterization of two ways to compute those derivatives. The authors describe their respective benefits and limitations and identify the regime where the learned approach can improve on iterative procedures. Experiments on synthetic and real data support those findings. The work makes differentiating through the solver a central part of understanding when learned acceleration is useful.
summary.tldr: Two approaches to differentiating through the total-variation proximal operator enable learned acceleration of one-dimensional solvers in the studied regimes.

title: Learning to solve TV regularised problems with unrolled algorithms

abstract: We investigate the sample efficiency of reinforcement learning in a $\gamma$-discounted infinite-horizon Markov decision process (MDP) with state space S and action space A, assuming access to a generative model. Despite a number of prior work tackling this problem, a complete picture of the trade-offs between sample complexity and statistical accuracy is yet to be determined. In particular, prior results suffer from a sample size barrier, in the sense that their claimed statistical guarantees hold only when the sample size exceeds at least $ |S| |A| / (1-\gamma)^2 $ (up to some log factor). The current paper overcomes this barrier by certifying the minimax optimality of model-based reinforcement learning as soon as the sample size exceeds the order of $ |S| |A| / (1-\gamma) $ (modulo some log factor). More specifically, a perturbed model-based planning algorithm provably finds an $\epsilon$-optimal policy with an order of $ |S| |A| / ((1-\gamma)^3\epsilon^2 ) $ samples (up to log factor) for any $0< \epsilon < 1/(1-\gamma)$. Along the way, we derive improved (instance-dependent) guarantees for model-based policy evaluation. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first minimax-optimal guarantee in a generative model that accommodates the entire range of sample sizes (beyond which finding a meaningful policy is information theoretically impossible).

paragraphs: This paper studies how many samples reinforcement learning needs to find a good policy in a discounted, infinite-horizon Markov decision process. It assumes access to a generative model for obtaining samples. Earlier statistical guarantees required a sample count of at least roughly |S||A|/(1−γ)², ignoring logarithmic factors, leaving a gap in understanding smaller sample budgets.

The authors lower that threshold to roughly |S||A|/(1−γ) and establish minimax optimality for model-based reinforcement learning there. Their perturbed planning algorithm finds an ε-optimal policy using on the order of |S||A|/((1−γ)³ε²) samples, up to logarithmic factors. The guarantee covers every accuracy level satisfying 0 < ε < 1/(1−γ).

Minimax optimality means that the guarantee matches the best achievable worst-case sample requirements at the stated level of precision. The work also improves policy-evaluation guarantees that depend on the particular problem instance. Its central advance is extending optimal statistical guarantees across the meaningful sample-size range under the generative-model assumption.
summary.tldr: A perturbed model-based planning algorithm achieves minimax-optimal sample guarantees across the meaningful sample-size range under generative-model access.

title: Breaking the Sample Size Barrier in Model-Based Reinforcement Learning with a Generative Model

abstract: This work studies the problem of sequential control in an unknown, nonlinear dynamical system, where we model the underlying system dynamics as an unknown function in a known Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space. This framework yields a general setting that permits discrete and continuous control inputs as well as non-smooth, non-differentiable dynamics. Our main result, the Lower Confidence-based Continuous Control (LC3) algorithm, enjoys a near-optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound against the optimal controller in episodic settings, where $T$ is the number of episodes. The bound has no explicit dependence on dimension of the system dynamics, which could be infinite, but instead only depends on information theoretic quantities. We empirically show its application to a number of nonlinear control tasks and demonstrate the benefit of exploration for learning model dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper considers an agent controlling an unknown nonlinear dynamical system over repeated episodes. The dynamics are assumed to belong to a known reproducing kernel Hilbert space, although the particular function governing the system is unknown. That modeling framework accommodates discrete or continuous control inputs and can include dynamics that are neither smooth nor differentiable.

The authors introduce LC3, a lower-confidence-based control algorithm, and establish a near-optimal regret bound growing as the square root of the number of episodes. Regret measures accumulated performance loss relative to the optimal controller. The result describes how the cost of learning the unknown system grows as the agent gains experience.

A central feature is that the bound depends on information-theoretic quantities rather than explicitly on the dimension of the dynamics, which may be infinite. This makes the guarantee meaningful for the function-space formulation used in the paper. Experiments on nonlinear control tasks illustrate the algorithm’s application and demonstrate benefits from exploration when learning dynamics. The theoretical claim remains tied to the specified modeling framework and episodic setting.
summary.tldr: LC3 achieves near-optimal episodic regret for unknown nonlinear dynamics in a known kernel function space, using information-theoretic complexity.

title: Information Theoretic Regret Bounds for Online Nonlinear Control

abstract: This paper studies the problem of approximately unlearning a Bayesian model from a small subset of the training data to be erased. We frame this problem as one of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the approximate posterior belief of model parameters after directly unlearning from erased data vs. the exact posterior belief from retraining with remaining data. Using the variational inference (VI) framework, we show that it is equivalent to minimizing an evidence upper bound which trades off between fully unlearning from erased data vs. not entirely forgetting the posterior belief given the full data (i.e., including the remaining data); the latter prevents catastrophic unlearning that can render the model useless. In model training with VI, only an approximate (instead of exact) posterior belief given the full data can be obtained, which makes unlearning even more challenging. We propose two novel tricks to tackle this challenge. We empirically demonstrate our unlearning methods on Bayesian models such as sparse Gaussian process and logistic regression using synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Bayesian unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training examples from a model's posterior beliefs. This paper studies approximate removal of a small subset of data. Its reference target is the exact posterior that would result from retraining on the remaining data, and it measures the discrepancy using KL divergence.

Within variational inference, the authors show that this objective is equivalent to minimizing an evidence upper bound. The bound balances removing information associated with erased data against retaining the posterior learned from the full dataset. Retention matters because that posterior also contains information from examples that should remain; excessive forgetting can make the model unusable.

A further difficulty is that variational training supplies only an approximate full-data posterior to begin with. The authors propose two techniques to address this complication and demonstrate their methods on sparse Gaussian process and logistic regression models using synthetic and real-world datasets. The contribution is a principled objective for approximate unlearning that explicitly balances deletion with preservation of useful remaining knowledge.
summary.tldr: Variational Bayesian unlearning balances removing selected data's influence with retaining useful posterior knowledge, targeting the posterior from retraining on remaining data.

title: Variational Bayesian Unlearning

abstract: Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have shown promising results in modeling graph-structured data. However, they have difficulty with processing digraphs because of two reasons: 1) transforming directed to undirected graph to guarantee the symmetry of graph Laplacian is not reasonable since it not only misleads message passing scheme to aggregate incorrect weights but also deprives the unique characteristics of digraph structure; 2) due to the fixed receptive field in each layer, GCNs fail to obtain multi-scale features that can boost their performance. In this paper, we theoretically extend spectral-based graph convolution to digraphs and derive a simplified form using personalized PageRank. Specifically, we present the Digraph Inception Convolutional Networks (DiGCN) which utilizes digraph convolution and kth-order proximity to achieve larger receptive fields and learn multi-scale features in digraphs. We empirically show that DiGCN can encode more structural information from digraphs than GCNs and help achieve better performance when generalized to other models. Moreover, experiments on various benchmarks demonstrate its superiority against the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Directed graphs carry information in the orientation of their connections. Converting them to undirected graphs so that a graph Laplacian becomes symmetric can discard this information and distort the weights used in message passing. The paper also identifies a separate problem: a fixed receptive field in each graph convolution layer limits the collection of features at different scales.

The authors extend spectral graph convolution theoretically to directed graphs and derive a simplified form using personalized PageRank. Their Digraph Inception Convolutional Network, or DiGCN, combines directed convolution with higher-order proximity. This lets the network use larger receptive fields and learn from graph relationships at multiple scales while retaining directed structure.

Experiments indicate that DiGCN captures more structural information from directed graphs than conventional GCNs. The authors also report improvements when their approach is extended to other models and superior performance against state-of-the-art methods across the evaluated benchmarks. The contribution connects a directed spectral formulation with an architecture designed to use both direction and scale as sources of information.
summary.tldr: DiGCN extends spectral convolution to directed graphs and combines multiple neighborhood scales to improve structural representations and benchmark performance.

title: Digraph Inception Convolutional Networks

abstract: Training models with discrete latent variables is challenging due to the difficulty of estimating the gradients accurately. Much of the recent progress has been achieved by taking advantage of continuous relaxations of the system, which are not always available or even possible. The Augment-REINFORCE-Merge (ARM) estimator provides an alternative that, instead of relaxation, uses continuous augmentation. Applying antithetic sampling over the augmenting variables yields a relatively low-variance and unbiased estimator applicable to any model with binary latent variables. However, while antithetic sampling reduces variance, the augmentation process increases variance. We show that ARM can be improved by analytically integrating out the randomness introduced by the augmentation process, guaranteeing substantial variance reduction. Our estimator, DisARM, is simple to implement and has the same computational cost as ARM. We evaluate DisARM on several generative modeling benchmarks and show that it consistently outperforms ARM and a strong independent sample baseline in terms of both variance and log-likelihood. Furthermore, we propose a local version of DisARM designed for optimizing the multi-sample variational bound, and show that it outperforms VIMCO, the current state-of-the-art method.

paragraphs: Models with binary latent variables are difficult to train because their gradients can be hard to estimate accurately. Continuous relaxations offer one route, but are not always available. The ARM estimator instead introduces continuous auxiliary randomness and uses antithetic sampling to obtain an unbiased gradient estimate with relatively low variance.

This paper identifies a tension within ARM: antithetic sampling reduces variance, while introducing auxiliary randomness increases it. DisARM analytically integrates out randomness introduced by the augmentation process. The authors establish a substantial variance reduction from this change, while retaining the same computational cost as ARM and a simple implementation.

The authors also develop a local version for optimizing a variational bound that uses multiple samples, reporting improvements over VIMCO. The work shows how removing analytically manageable randomness can improve learning without increasing the estimator's computational cost.
summary.tldr: DisARM removes auxiliary randomness from ARM gradient estimates, reducing variance at the same computational cost and improving generative-model benchmarks.

title: DisARM: An Antithetic Gradient Estimator for Binary Latent Variables

abstract: In this work, we identify a novel set of conditions that ensure convergence with probability 1 of Q-learning with linear function approximation, by proposing a two time-scale variation thereof. In the faster time scale, the algorithm features an update similar to that of DQN, where the impact of bootstrapping is attenuated by using a Q-value estimate akin to that of the target network in DQN. The slower time-scale, in turn, can be seen as a modified target network update. We establish the convergence of our algorithm, provide an error bound and discuss our results in light of existing convergence results on reinforcement learning with function approximation. Finally, we illustrate the convergent behavior of our method in domains where standard Q-learning has previously been shown to diverge.

In the faster time scale, the algorithm features an update similar to that of DQN, where the impact of bootstrapping is attenuated by using a Q-value estimate akin to that of the target network in DQN. The slower time-scale, in turn, can be seen as a modified target network update. We establish the convergence of our algorithm, provide an error bound and discuss our results in light of existing convergence results on reinforcement learning with function approximation. Finally, we illustrate the convergent behavior of our method in domains where standard Q-learning has previously been shown to diverge.

paragraphs: Q-learning with linear function approximation can diverge, so representing action values with a linear model does not by itself ensure stable learning. This paper introduces a variant that separates learning into two time scales and identifies conditions under which it converges with probability one.

The faster update resembles the update used in DQN. It reduces the influence of bootstrapping by using a separate Q-value estimate analogous to a target network. Bootstrapping means that a current update depends on another estimated value, so controlling how that estimate changes is central to the design. The slower update modifies the target-like estimate on a different time scale.

The authors establish convergence for their algorithm, provide an error bound, and relate the result to existing theory for reinforcement learning with function approximation. They also illustrate convergence in domains where standard Q-learning has been shown to diverge. The guarantee applies under the identified conditions; it is a result about this particular two-time-scale method, rather than a general guarantee for target networks.
summary.tldr: A two-time-scale variant of linear Q-learning has almost-sure convergence guarantees under identified conditions and converges in examples where standard Q-learning diverges.

title: A new convergent variant of Q-learning with linear function approximation

abstract: A common problem in neuroscience is to elucidate the collective neural representations of behaviorally important variables such as head direction, spatial location, upcoming movements, or mental spatial transformations. Often, these latent variables are internal constructs not directly accessible to the experimenter. Here, we propose a new probabilistic latent variable model to simultaneously identify the latent state and the way each neuron contributes to its representation in an unsupervised way. In contrast to previous models which assume Euclidean latent spaces, we embrace the fact that latent states often belong to symmetric manifolds such as spheres, tori, or rotation groups of various dimensions. We therefore propose the manifold Gaussian process latent variable model (mGPLVM), where neural responses arise from (i) a shared latent variable living on a specific manifold, and (ii) a set of non-parametric tuning curves determining how each neuron contributes to the representation. Cross-validated comparisons of models with different topologies can be used to distinguish between candidate manifolds, and variational inference enables quantification of uncertainty. We demonstrate the validity of the approach on several synthetic datasets, as well as on calcium recordings from the ellipsoid body of Drosophila melanogaster and extracellular recordings from the mouse anterodorsal thalamic nucleus. These circuits are both known to encode head direction, and mGPLVM correctly recovers the ring topology expected from neural populations representing a single angular variable.
originalAbstract: A common problem in neuroscience is to elucidate the collective neural representations of behaviorally important variables such as head direction, spatial location, upcoming movements, or mental spatial transformations. Often, these latent variables are internal constructs not directly accessible to the experimenter. Here, we propose a new probabilistic latent variable model to simultaneously identify the latent state and the way each neuron contributes to its representation in an unsupervised way. In contrast to previous models which assume Euclidean latent spaces, we embrace the fact that latent states often belong to symmetric manifolds such as spheres, tori, or rotation groups of various dimensions. We therefore propose the manifold Gaussian process latent variable model (mGPLVM), where neural responses arise from (i) a shared latent variable living on a specific manifold, and (ii) a set of non-parametric tuning curves determining how each neuron contributes to the representation. Cross-validated comparisons of models with different topologies can be used to distinguish between candidate manifolds, and variational inference enables quantification of uncertainty. We demonstrate the validity of the approach on several synthetic datasets, as well as on calcium recordings from the ellipsoid body of Drosophila melanogaster and extracellular recordings from the mouse anterodorsal thalamic nucleus. These circuits are both known to encode head direction, and mGPLVM correctly recovers the ring topology expected from neural populations representing a single angular variable.

paragraphs: Neural populations can represent variables such as head direction or spatial location even when those variables are not directly accessible to an experimenter. This paper introduces an unsupervised probabilistic model that jointly estimates the hidden state and how individual neurons represent it. Its central choice is to allow hidden states to occupy non-Euclidean spaces.

The manifold Gaussian process latent variable model, or mGPLVM, places a shared latent variable on a specified manifold, such as a sphere, torus, or rotation group. Non-parametric tuning curves describe each neuron's response to that shared state. Cross-validation can compare models with different candidate topologies, and variational inference provides a way to quantify uncertainty in the inferred representation.

The authors validate the approach using synthetic datasets and neural recordings from fruit-fly and mouse circuits known to encode head direction. In both biological settings, the model recovers the expected ring topology for a single angular variable. This demonstrates why latent geometry matters: a circular behavioral quantity can be represented using its corresponding structure while the model also learns how neurons participate in encoding it.
summary.tldr: mGPLVM infers hidden neural representations on non-Euclidean manifolds and recovers the expected ring structure in head-direction recordings.

title: Manifold GPLVMs for discovering non-Euclidean latent structure in neural data

abstract: In this paper, we aim to create generalizable and controllable neural signed distance fields (SDFs) that represent clothed humans from monocular depth observations. Recent advances in deep learning, especially neural implicit representations, have enabled human shape reconstruction and controllable avatar generation from different sensor inputs. However, to generate realistic cloth deformations from novel input poses, watertight meshes or dense full-body scans are usually needed as inputs. Furthermore, due to the difficulty of effectively modeling pose-dependent cloth deformations for diverse body shapes and cloth types, existing approaches resort to per-subject/cloth-type optimization from scratch, which is computationally expensive. In contrast, we propose an approach that can quickly generate realistic clothed human avatars, represented as controllable neural SDFs, given only monocular depth images. We achieve this by using meta-learning to learn an initialization of a hypernetwork that predicts the parameters of neural SDFs. The hypernetwork is conditioned on human poses and represents a clothed neural avatar that deforms non-rigidly according to the input poses. Meanwhile, it is meta-learned to effectively incorporate priors of diverse body shapes and cloth types and thus can be much faster to fine-tune, compared to models trained from scratch. We qualitatively and quantitatively show that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art approaches that require complete meshes as inputs while our approach requires only depth frames as inputs and runs orders of magnitudes faster. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our meta-learned hypernetwork is very robust, being the first to generate avatars with realistic dynamic cloth deformations given as few as 8 monocular depth frames.

The authors also demonstrate realistic dynamic clothing deformation from as few as eight monocular depth frames. The central finding is that a learned initialization can make sparse observations sufficient for the demonstrated avatar reconstructions while retaining pose-dependent control.
summary.tldr: MetaAvatar uses a meta-learned, pose-conditioned hypernetwork to create animatable clothed avatars from as few as eight depth frames.

title: MetaAvatar: Learning Animatable Clothed Human Models from Few Depth Images

abstract: We study the problem of active pure exploration with fixed confidence in generic stochastic bandit environments. The goal of the learner is to answer a query about the environment with a given level of certainty while minimizing her sampling budget. For this problem, instance-specific lower bounds on the expected sample complexity reveal the optimal proportions of arm draws an Oracle algorithm would apply. These proportions solve an optimization problem whose tractability strongly depends on the structural properties of the environment, but may be instrumental in the design of efficient learning algorithms. We devise Frank-Wolfe-based Sampling (FWS), a simple algorithm whose sample complexity matches the lower bounds for a wide class of pure exploration problems. The algorithm is computationally efficient as, to learn and track the optimal proportion of arm draws, it relies on a single iteration of Frank-Wolfe algorithm applied to the lower-bound optimization problem. We apply FWS to various pure exploration tasks, including best arm identification in unstructured, thresholded, linear, and Lipschitz bandits. Despite its simplicity, FWS is competitive compared to state-of-art algorithms.

paragraphs: In fixed-confidence pure exploration, a learner samples a stochastic environment to answer a question with a specified level of certainty. The goal is to use as few samples as possible. Lower bounds on the required sampling reveal ideal proportions for drawing different arms, but finding those proportions can itself be computationally demanding.

Frank-Wolfe-based Sampling, or FWS, learns and tracks these proportions through a single iteration of the Frank-Wolfe optimization algorithm applied to the lower-bound problem. This gives the learner an inexpensive way to update its sampling allocation. The method connects the mathematical description of optimal exploration to a practical rule for deciding which observations to collect.

The authors show that FWS matches sample-complexity lower bounds for a wide class of pure-exploration problems. They apply it to tasks including best-arm identification in unstructured, thresholded, linear, and Lipschitz bandits, and report competitive performance against state-of-the-art algorithms. The result combines sampling efficiency with computational simplicity across the studied settings, rather than requiring a complicated allocation procedure.
summary.tldr: FWS uses lightweight Frank-Wolfe updates to achieve sample-efficient exploration with theoretical guarantees across a wide class of bandit problems.

title: Fast Pure Exploration via Frank-Wolfe

abstract: It is well known that modern deep neural networks are powerful enough to memorize datasets even when the labels have been randomized. Recently, Vershynin(2020) settled a long standing question by Baum(1988), proving that deep threshold networks can memorize $n$ points in $d$ dimensions using $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(e^{1/\delta^2}+\sqrt{n})$ neurons and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(e^{1/\delta^2}(d+\sqrt{n})+n)$ weights, where $\delta$ is the minimum distance between the points. In this work, we improve the dependence on $\delta$ from exponential to almost linear, proving that $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{1}{\delta}+\sqrt{n})$ neurons and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\frac{d}{\delta}+n)$ weights are sufficient. Our construction uses Gaussian random weights only in the first layer, while all the subsequent layers use binary or integer weights. We also prove new lower bounds by connecting memorization in neural networks to the purely geometric problem of separating $n$ points on a sphere using hyperplanes.

paragraphs: This paper asks how large a deep threshold network must be to memorize labeled data. The relevant quantities are the number of points n, their dimension d, and their minimum separation δ. Earlier bounds had an exponential dependence on inverse separation, making the stated sufficient network size grow rapidly as points became closer.

The authors construct networks with a much milder dependence on separation. Up to logarithmic factors, they show that 1/δ + √n neurons and d/δ + n weights are sufficient. These are upper bounds on resources needed for memorization, rather than claims that every dataset requires networks of exactly those sizes.

The construction also restricts where complicated weights are needed: only the first layer uses Gaussian random weights, while later layers use binary or integer weights. Alongside these upper bounds, the paper proves new lower bounds by connecting memorization to separating points on a sphere with hyperplanes. Together, the results sharpen the relationship between dataset geometry and network memorization capacity.
summary.tldr: A new construction greatly reduces the sufficient size of deep threshold networks for memorization, replacing exponential separation dependence with nearly linear dependence.

title: An Exponential Improvement on the Memorization Capacity of Deep Threshold Networks

abstract: Text-to-Image generation in the general domain has long been an open problem, which requires both a powerful generative model and cross-modal understanding. We propose CogView, a 4-billion-parameter Transformer with VQ-VAE tokenizer to advance this problem. We also demonstrate the finetuning strategies for various downstream tasks, e.g. style learning, super-resolution, text-image ranking and fashion design, and methods to stabilize pretraining, e.g. eliminating NaN losses. CogView achieves the state-of-the-art FID on the blurred MS COCO dataset, outperforming previous GAN-based models and a recent similar work DALL-E.

We propose CogView, a 4-billion-parameter Transformer with VQ-VAE tokenizer to advance this problem. We also demonstrate the finetuning strategies for various downstream tasks, e.g. style learning, super-resolution, text-image ranking and fashion design, and methods to stabilize pretraining, e.g. eliminating NaN losses. CogView achieves the state-of-the-art FID on the blurred MS COCO dataset, outperforming previous GAN-based models and a recent similar work DALL-E.

paragraphs: Generating images from unrestricted text requires both an image-generation capability and an understanding of how language relates to visual content. CogView addresses this combination with a four-billion-parameter Transformer and a VQ-VAE tokenizer.

The tokenizer supplies a token-based representation for images, allowing the proposed system to bring image generation into a Transformer framework. The paper presents this large model as an approach to the broad text-to-image problem, where the requested content is not restricted to a narrow domain.

The work also addresses making the model usable beyond its initial training objective. It demonstrates fine-tuning strategies for learning styles, increasing image resolution, ranking text-image pairs, and fashion design. Methods for stabilizing pretraining, including eliminating NaN losses, address practical difficulties in training the system.

CogView achieves the reported best FID on the blurred MS COCO dataset, outperforming previous GAN-based models and DALL-E in that evaluation. This is evidence for its generation quality on the stated benchmark, while the fine-tuning demonstrations show the range of downstream tasks explored with the model.
summary.tldr: CogView combines a large Transformer with image tokenization, stable pretraining, and task-specific fine-tuning to advance text-to-image generation.

title: CogView: Mastering Text-to-Image Generation via Transformers

abstract: Program synthesis from input-output (IO) examples has been a long-standing challenge. While recent works demonstrated limited success on domain-specific languages (DSL), it remains highly challenging to apply them to real-world programming languages, such as C. Due to complicated syntax and token variation, there are three major challenges: (1) unlike many DSLs, programs in languages like C need to compile first and are not executed via interpreters; (2) the program search space grows exponentially when the syntax and semantics of the programming language become more complex; and (3) collecting a large-scale dataset of real-world programs is non-trivial. As a first step to address these challenges, we propose LaSynth and show its efficacy in a restricted-C domain (i.e., C code with tens of tokens, with sequential, branching, loop and simple arithmetic operations but no library call). More specifically, LaSynth learns the latent representation to approximate the execution of partially generated programs, even if they are incomplete in syntax (addressing (1)). The learned execution significantly improves the performance of next token prediction over existing approaches, facilitating search (addressing (2)). Finally, once trained with randomly generated ground-truth programs and their IO pairs, LaSynth can synthesize more concise programs that resemble human-written code. Furthermore, retraining our model with these synthesized programs yields better performance with fewer samples for both Karel and C program synthesis, indicating the promise of leveraging the learned program synthesizer to improve the dataset quality for input-output program synthesis (addressing (3)). When evaluating on whether the program execution outputs match the IO pairs, LaSynth achieves 55.2% accuracy on generating simple C code with tens of tokens including loops and branches, outperforming existing approaches without executors by around 20%.

paragraphs: Generating programs from input-output examples becomes difficult in languages such as C. Incomplete programs may not compile, complex syntax expands the search space, and suitable training programs are hard to collect. LaSynth takes a first step in a restricted C domain: programs with tens of tokens, simple arithmetic, sequences, branches, and loops, without library calls.

This learned execution improves prediction of the next token and helps guide program search. It gives the synthesizer execution-related information before an ordinary complete program is available to run.

On the restricted C task, it achieves 55.2% accuracy measured by matching execution outputs to the supplied examples, with a reported improvement of around 20% over approaches without executors. The results support both latent execution and synthesized training-data refinement.
summary.tldr: LaSynth approximates execution of incomplete programs in latent space, improving synthesis and training-data quality in restricted C and Karel.

title: Latent Execution for Neural Program Synthesis Beyond Domain-Specific Languages

abstract: Explaining the influence of training data on deep neural network predictions is a critical tool for debugging models through data curation. A recent tractable and appealing approach for this task was provided via the concept of Representer Point Selection (RPS), i.e. a method the leverages the dual form of $l_2$ regularized optimization in the last layer of the neural network to identify the contribution of training points to the prediction. However, two key drawbacks of RPS are that they (i) lead to disagreement between the originally trained network and the RP regularized network modification and (ii) often yield a static ranking of training data for the same class, independent of the data being classified. Inspired by the RPS approach, we propose an alternative method based on a local Jacobian Taylor expansion (LJE) of the Jacobian.We empirically compared RPS-LJE with the original RPS-$l_2$ on image classification (with ResNet), text classification recurrent neural networks (with Bi-LSTM), and tabular classification (with XGBoost) tasks.Quantitatively, we show that RPS-LJE slightly outperforms RPS-$l_2$ and other state-of-the-art data explanation methods by up to 3\% on a data debugging task. Qualitatively, we observe that RPS-LJE provides individualized explanations for each test data point rather than the class-specific static ranking of points in the original approach. Overall, RPS-LJE represents a novel approach to RPS that provides a powerful tool for data-oriented explanation and debugging.

paragraphs: Explaining which training examples contribute to a prediction can help identify problematic data. Representer Point Selection addresses this by expressing contributions through a regularized last-layer formulation. However, the resulting modified network can disagree with the original, and explanations can become a fixed ranking for a class rather than changing with each test example.

The paper proposes RPS-LJE, an alternative based on a local Jacobian Taylor expansion. Its goal is to retain training-data explanations while providing a different foundation for calculating them. The authors compare it with the original regularized approach on image classification using ResNet, text classification using Bi-LSTM, and tabular classification using XGBoost.

On a data-debugging task, RPS-LJE slightly outperforms the original method and other leading explanation methods, with improvements of up to 3%. Qualitatively, it produces explanations individualized to test examples instead of class-wide static rankings. The findings support its usefulness for data-oriented debugging across several model types, with a modest reported quantitative improvement and a meaningful difference in explanation specificity.
summary.tldr: RPS-LJE uses a local Jacobian expansion to produce individualized training-data explanations and modestly improve data debugging.

title: Representer Point Selection via Local Jacobian Expansion for Post-hoc Classifier Explanation of Deep Neural Networks and Ensemble Models

abstract: Operating in the real-world often requires agents to learn about a complex environment and apply this understanding to achieve a breadth of goals. This problem, known as goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL), becomes especially challenging for long-horizon goals. Current methods have tackled this problem by augmenting goal-conditioned policies with graph-based planning algorithms. However, they struggle to scale to large, high-dimensional state spaces and assume access to exploration mechanisms for efficiently collecting training data. In this work, we introduce Successor Feature Landmarks (SFL), a framework for exploring large, high-dimensional environments so as to obtain a policy that is proficient for any goal. SFL leverages the ability of successor features (SF) to capture transition dynamics, using it to drive exploration by estimating state-novelty and to enable high-level planning by abstracting the state-space as a non-parametric landmark-based graph. We further exploit SF to directly compute a goal-conditioned policy for inter-landmark traversal, which we use to execute plans to "frontier" landmarks at the edge of the explored state space. We show in our experiments on MiniGrid and ViZDoom that SFL enables efficient exploration of large, high-dimensional state spaces and outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on long-horizon GCRL tasks.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning asks an agent to reach different requested goals, including goals that require long sequences of actions. Existing combinations of policies and graph planning can struggle in large, high-dimensional environments and depend on a separate mechanism for gathering exploratory experience. Successor Feature Landmarks, or SFL, addresses exploration and goal-directed behavior within one framework.

SFL uses successor features to capture transition dynamics. Those features help estimate how novel a state is, guiding exploration, and support a landmark graph that provides a higher-level representation for planning. The same features directly determine a goal-conditioned policy for traveling between landmarks. Plans toward frontier landmarks then take the agent to the edge of the area it has explored.

Experiments in MiniGrid and ViZDoom show efficient exploration of large, high-dimensional state spaces and better performance than state-of-the-art baselines on long-horizon goal-conditioned tasks. The approach matters because its representation supports three connected needs: deciding where to explore, planning through known territory, and executing movement between landmarks. Exploration consequently feeds the structure used for reaching later goals.
summary.tldr: SFL uses successor features for novelty-driven exploration, landmark planning, and travel between landmarks to improve long-horizon goal-reaching.

title: Successor Feature Landmarks for Long-Horizon Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider a sequential setting in which a single dataset of individuals is used to perform adaptively-chosen analyses, while ensuring that the differential privacy loss of each participant does not exceed a pre-specified privacy budget. The standard approach to this problem relies on bounding a worst-case estimate of the privacy loss over all individuals and all possible values of their data, for every single analysis. Yet, in many scenarios this approach is overly conservative, especially for "typical" data points which incur little privacy loss by participation in most of the analyses. In this work, we give a method for tighter privacy loss accounting based on the value of a personalized privacy loss estimate for each individual in each analysis. To implement the accounting method we design a filter for Rényi differential privacy. A filter is a tool that ensures that the privacy parameter of a composed sequence of algorithms with adaptively-chosen privacy parameters does not exceed a pre-specified budget. Our filter is simpler and tighter than the known filter for $(\epsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy by Rogers et al. (2016). We apply our results to the analysis of noisy gradient descent and show that personalized accounting can be practical, easy to implement, and can only make the privacy-utility tradeoff tighter.

paragraphs: When a dataset supports a sequence of adaptively chosen analyses, privacy accounting must ensure that each participant stays within a predetermined privacy budget. Standard accounting bounds every analysis using a worst case across individuals and possible data values. That can be conservative for participants whose data contributes little privacy loss to most analyses.

This paper develops accounting based on a personalized privacy-loss estimate for each individual in each analysis. To make this work across adaptive sequences, the authors design a filter for Rényi differential privacy. The filter controls the cumulative privacy parameter even when the privacy parameters of successive algorithms are chosen adaptively.

The proposed filter is simpler and tighter than the cited existing filter for epsilon-delta differential privacy. Applying the approach to noisy gradient descent, the authors show that personalized accounting can be practical and straightforward to implement. They also establish that it can only tighten the privacy–utility tradeoff. The contribution is more precise tracking of privacy costs while maintaining the required budget, rather than relaxing the protection promised to participants.
summary.tldr: A Rényi privacy filter supports tighter individual privacy accounting across adaptive analyses while keeping each participant within a specified budget.

title: Individual Privacy Accounting via a Rényi Filter

abstract: We theoretically study the fundamental problem of learning a single neuron with a bias term ($\mathbf{x}\mapsto \sigma(\langle\mathbf{w},\mathbf{x}\rangle + b)$) in the realizable setting with the ReLU activation, using gradient descent. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that this is a significantly different and more challenging problem than the bias-less case (which was the focus of previous works on single neurons), both in terms of the optimization geometry as well as the ability of gradient methods to succeed in some scenarios. We provide a detailed study of this problem, characterizing the critical points of the objective, demonstrating failure cases, and providing positive convergence guarantees under different sets of assumptions. To prove our results, we develop some tools which may be of independent interest, and improve previous results on learning single neurons.

Perhaps surprisingly, we show that this is a significantly different and more challenging problem than the bias-less case (which was the focus of previous works on single neurons), both in terms of the optimization geometry as well as the ability of gradient methods to succeed in some scenarios. paragraphs: Even a single neuron can present a nontrivial optimization problem. This paper studies gradient descent for a ReLU neuron with both weights and a bias, where the bias shifts the input to the activation. The analysis assumes a realizable setting, meaning that the target can be represented by a neuron of the form being learned.

The central finding is that including a bias substantially changes the problem compared with learning a neuron without one. It changes the geometry of the optimization objective and can affect whether gradient methods succeed. Consequently, conclusions from the bias-free setting do not automatically describe the behavior of this slightly more general neuron.

The authors characterize the objective's critical points, exhibit situations where learning fails, and establish positive convergence guarantees under different assumptions. These results describe both obstacles and conditions supporting successful optimization, rather than presenting a single unconditional guarantee. The work also develops proof tools and improves earlier single-neuron learning results. Its significance is showing how a basic architectural choice can materially alter the theory of gradient-based learning.
summary.tldr: Adding a bias makes single-ReLU learning substantially harder, with new failure cases and assumption-dependent convergence guarantees.

title: Learning a Single Neuron with Bias Using Gradient Descent

abstract: Automatic Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech systems are primarily trained in a supervised fashion and require high-quality, accurately labeled speech datasets. In this work, we examine common problems with speech data and introduce a toolbox for the construction and interactive error analysis of speech datasets. The construction tool is based on K{\"u}rzinger et al. work, and, to the best of our knowledge, the dataset exploration tool is the world's first open-source tool of this kind. We demonstrate how to apply these tools to create a Russian speech dataset and analyze existing speech datasets (Multilingual LibriSpeech, Mozilla Common Voice). The tools are open sourced as a part of the NeMo framework.

paragraphs: Speech recognition and text-to-speech systems commonly learn from labeled recordings, making dataset quality an important part of their development. This paper examines common problems in speech data and introduces tools for constructing datasets and interactively analyzing errors. Its focus is the data work that supports supervised speech systems.

The toolbox addresses two related activities: assembling a speech dataset and exploring an existing one to investigate problems. The construction component builds on earlier work. The authors also describe the exploration component as, to their knowledge, the first open-source tool of its kind, framing that novelty claim with an explicit qualification.

The paper demonstrates the tools by creating a Russian speech dataset and analyzing Multilingual LibriSpeech and Mozilla Common Voice. These examples cover both building a resource and inspecting established collections. Released within the NeMo framework, the tools provide a reusable way to carry out dataset construction and error analysis, making those activities a concrete part of the speech research workflow.
summary.tldr: An open-source toolbox supports speech dataset construction and interactive error analysis, with demonstrations on Russian and existing multilingual data.

title: A Toolbox for Construction and Analysis of Speech Datasets

abstract: We study the problem of model selection in bandit scenarios in the presence of nested policy classes, with the goal of obtaining simultaneous adversarial and stochastic (``best of both worlds") high-probability regret guarantees. Our approach requires that each base learner comes with a candidate regret bound that may or may not hold, while our meta algorithm plays each base learner according to a schedule that keeps the base learner's candidate regret bounds balanced until they are detected to violate their guarantees. We develop careful mis-specification tests specifically designed to blend the above model selection criterion with the ability to leverage the (potentially benign) nature of the environment. We recover the model selection guarantees of the CORRAL algorithm for adversarial environments, but with the additional benefit of achieving high probability regret bounds. More importantly, our model selection results also hold simultaneously in stochastic environments under gap assumptions. These are the first theoretical results that achieve best-of-both world (stochastic and adversarial) guarantees while performing model selection in contextual bandit scenarios.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to select among nested policy classes in contextual bandit problems while retaining guarantees in both adversarial and stochastic environments. These settings demand different kinds of adaptability: a learner must remain reliable when outcomes are hostile while benefiting when the environment has favorable statistical structure. The goal is to combine both properties with model selection.

Each base learner supplies a candidate regret bound, which is allowed to be incorrect. A meta algorithm schedules the learners so their proposed bounds remain balanced until evidence indicates that a guarantee has been violated. Specially designed misspecification tests connect this selection process with the ability to exploit a potentially benign environment.

For adversarial environments, the resulting model selection guarantees recover those of CORRAL while adding high-probability regret bounds. The guarantees also apply simultaneously to stochastic environments under gap assumptions. That qualification matters: the stochastic result relies on the stated structure. The contribution is a theoretical framework showing that contextual-bandit model selection and these two forms of regret protection can coexist.
summary.tldr: A meta algorithm selects among bandit learners while providing simultaneous high-probability adversarial and, under gap assumptions, stochastic regret guarantees.

title: Best of Both Worlds Model Selection

abstract: Data augmentation is essential to achieve state-of-the-art performance in many deep learning applications. However, the most effective augmentation techniques become computationally prohibitive for even medium-sized datasets. To address this, we propose a rigorous technique to select subsets of data points that when augmented, closely capture the training dynamics of full data augmentation. We first show that data augmentation, modeled as additive perturbations, improves learning and generalization by relatively enlarging and perturbing the smaller singular values of the network Jacobian, while preserving its prominent directions. This prevents overfitting and enhances learning the harder to learn information. Then, we propose a framework to iteratively extract small subsets of training data that when augmented, closely capture the alignment of the fully augmented Jacobian with labels/residuals. We prove that stochastic gradient descent applied to the augmented subsets found by our approach has similar training dynamics to that of fully augmented data. Our experiments demonstrate that our method achieves 6.3x speedup on CIFAR10 and 2.2x speedup on SVHN, and outperforms the baselines by up to 10\% across various subset sizes. Similarly, on TinyImageNet and ImageNet, our method beats the baselines by up to 8%, while achieving up to 3.3x speedup across various subset sizes. Finally, training on and augmenting 50% subsets using our method on a version of CIFAR10 corrupted with label noise even outperforms using the full dataset.

paragraphs: Data augmentation can improve neural network learning, but applying expensive transformations across an entire dataset can be costly. This paper selects small subsets whose augmentation closely reproduces the training dynamics of augmenting all the data. The selection targets the effect that augmented examples have on learning.

The analysis models augmentation as additive perturbations. It shows how these perturbations strengthen and modify smaller singular values of the network Jacobian while preserving its prominent directions, helping with harder-to-learn information and overfitting. The method repeatedly selects subsets that preserve how the augmented Jacobian aligns with labels or prediction residuals. The authors prove similar SGD training dynamics for the selected augmented subsets and the fully augmented data.

Experiments report speedups of 6.3 times on CIFAR10 and 2.2 times on SVHN, with improvements over baselines of up to 10% across subset sizes. Results on TinyImageNet and ImageNet also show gains and speedups. On a label-corrupted CIFAR10 version, training with selected, augmented 50% subsets even outperforms using the full dataset.
summary.tldr: Carefully selected training subsets can preserve the learning dynamics of full-data augmentation while substantially reducing computation in the reported experiments.

title: Data-Efficient Augmentation for Training Neural Networks

abstract: While much progress has been made in understanding the minimax sample complexity of reinforcement learning (RL)---the complexity of learning on the ``worst-case'' instance---such measures of complexity often do not capture the true difficulty of learning. In practice, on an ``easy'' instance, we might hope to achieve a complexity far better than that achievable on the worst-case instance. In this work we seek to understand this ``instance-dependent'' complexity of learning in the setting of RL with linear function approximation. We propose an algorithm, PEDEL, which achieves a fine-grained instance-dependent measure of complexity, the first of its kind in the RL with function approximation setting, thereby capturing the difficulty of learning on each particular problem instance. Through an explicit example, we show that PEDEL yields provable gains over low-regret, minimax-optimal algorithms and that such algorithms are unable to hit the instance-optimal rate. Our approach relies on a novel online experiment design-based procedure which focuses the exploration budget on the ``directions'' most relevant to learning a near-optimal policy, and may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Worst-case reinforcement learning guarantees describe how difficult the hardest problem can be, but they can obscure substantial differences between individual tasks. This paper studies instance-dependent sample complexity with linear function approximation: how much experience is needed to identify a near-optimal policy for the particular problem being solved.

The proposed PEDEL algorithm uses online experiment design to allocate its exploration budget. It focuses on directions that are most relevant to identifying a near-optimal policy. The resulting complexity measure responds to the structure of the individual instance, aiming to capture opportunities that a worst-case analysis alone does not reveal.

An explicit example shows provable gains over algorithms that are both low-regret and minimax-optimal. In that example, those algorithms cannot achieve the instance-optimal rate. This illustrates that good worst-case or regret guarantees need not imply the best sample efficiency for policy identification on a specific problem. The paper’s contribution is both the finer complexity guarantee and the exploration procedure that makes such targeted learning possible.
summary.tldr: PEDEL targets exploration toward policy-relevant directions to obtain sample-complexity guarantees tailored to individual linear reinforcement learning problems.

title: Instance-Dependent Near-Optimal Policy Identification in Linear MDPs via Online Experiment Design

abstract: Comparing the representations learned by different neural networks has recently emerged as a key tool to understand various architectures and ultimately optimize them. In this work, we introduce GULP, a family of distance measures between representations that is explicitly motivated by downstream predictive tasks. By construction, GULP provides uniform control over the difference in prediction performance between two representations, with respect to regularized linear prediction tasks. Moreover, it satisfies several desirable structural properties, such as the triangle inequality and invariance under orthogonal transformations, and thus lends itself to data embedding and visualization. We extensively evaluate GULP relative to other methods, and demonstrate that it correctly differentiates between architecture families, converges over the course of training, and captures generalization performance on downstream linear tasks.

paragraphs: Two neural networks may produce different internal representations, but the practical importance of that difference depends on what predictions those representations support. GULP introduces a family of distances motivated explicitly by downstream prediction. Its goal is to make representation comparison informative about how useful the features are for subsequent learning.

By construction, the distance uniformly controls differences in prediction performance for regularized linear prediction tasks. This gives the comparison a defined predictive scope. GULP also satisfies the triangle inequality and remains unchanged under orthogonal transformations, so rotating a representation does not by itself change the comparison. These properties make it suitable for embedding and visualizing relationships among representations.

The authors evaluate GULP against other comparison methods. They report that it distinguishes architecture families, converges as training proceeds, and captures generalization performance on downstream linear tasks. Together, the theoretical construction and experiments connect representational similarity to a concrete use of the features. The predictive guarantee specifically concerns regularized linear tasks, which is central to interpreting what the distance measures.
summary.tldr: GULP compares neural representations through distances that control performance differences on regularized linear prediction tasks.

title: GULP: a prediction-based metric between representations

abstract: We present a new family of information-theoretic generalization bounds, in which the training loss and the population loss are compared through a jointly convex function. This function is upper-bounded in terms of the disintegrated, samplewise, evaluated conditional mutual information (CMI), an information measure that depends on the losses incurred by the selected hypothesis, rather than on the hypothesis itself, as is common in probably approximately correct (PAC)-Bayesian results. We demonstrate the generality of this framework by recovering and extending previously known information-theoretic bounds. Furthermore, using the evaluated CMI, we derive a samplewise, average version of Seeger's PAC-Bayesian bound, where the convex function is the binary KL divergence. In some scenarios, this novel bound results in a tighter characterization of the population loss of deep neural networks than previous bounds. Finally, we derive high-probability versions of some of these average bounds. We demonstrate the unifying nature of the evaluated CMI bounds by using them to recover average and high-probability generalization bounds for multiclass classification with finite Natarajan dimension.

paragraphs: A generalization bound connects a model's loss on training examples to its loss over the population it is meant to serve. This paper develops a family of such bounds using conditional mutual information, or CMI. Its distinguishing choice is to measure information through the losses produced by the learned hypothesis, rather than through the hypothesis itself.

The framework compares training and population losses with a jointly convex function and bounds that comparison using information evaluated sample by sample. Changing the comparison function lets the framework recover and extend earlier results. One particular choice, binary KL divergence, produces a samplewise average counterpart of Seeger's PAC-Bayesian bound.

In some scenarios, that new bound characterizes deep networks' population loss more tightly than previous bounds. The authors also derive high-probability versions of some average results and recover bounds for multiclass problems with finite Natarajan dimension. These results establish a common framework for several guarantees while keeping the reported improvement conditional on the scenario.
summary.tldr: Measuring information through individual losses yields a unified family of generalization bounds, with tighter results in some deep-learning scenarios.

title: A New Family of Generalization Bounds Using Samplewise Evaluated CMI

abstract: Cross-modal retrieval aims to build correspondence between multiple modalities by learning a common representation space. Typically, an image can match multiple texts semantically and vice versa, which significantly increases the difficulty of this task. To address this problem, probabilistic embedding is proposed to quantify these many-to-many relationships. However, existing datasets (e.g., MS-COCO) and metrics (e.g., Recall@K) cannot fully represent these diversity correspondences due to non-exhaustive annotations. Based on this observation, we utilize semantic correlation computed by CIDEr to find the potential correspondences. Then we present an effective metric, named Average Semantic Precision (ASP), which can measure the ranking precision of semantic correlation for retrieval sets. Additionally, we introduce a novel and concise objective, coined Differentiable ASP Approximation (DAA). Concretely, DAA can optimize ASP directly by making the ranking function of ASP differentiable through a sigmoid function. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, extensive experiments are conducted on MS-COCO, CUB Captions, and Flickr30K, which are commonly used in cross-modal retrieval. The results show that our approach obtains superior performance over the state-of-the-art approaches on all metrics. The code and trained models are released at https://github.com/leolee99/2022-NeurIPS-DAA.

paragraphs: Cross-modal retrieval connects different kinds of data, such as finding text descriptions for an image. A central difficulty is that several descriptions can legitimately match the same image, and vice versa. Probabilistic embeddings address these many-to-many relationships, but incomplete annotations mean that conventional evaluation can overlook semantically valid matches.

The paper uses semantic correlations calculated with CIDEr to identify potential correspondences beyond the annotated ones. It introduces Average Semantic Precision, or ASP, to evaluate how well a retrieved ranking reflects those correlations. This shifts attention toward the semantic quality of the retrieval set rather than relying entirely on whether each result appears among the recorded matches.

The authors also introduce a training objective called Differentiable ASP Approximation. It uses a sigmoid function to make ASP’s ranking operation differentiable, allowing training to directly target an approximation of the metric. Experiments on MS-COCO, CUB Captions, and Flickr30K report improvements over the compared state-of-the-art methods across all evaluated metrics, supporting the combined evaluation and optimization approach.
summary.tldr: A semantic retrieval metric and its differentiable approximation help train models to recognize matches that incomplete annotations may miss.

title: A Differentiable Semantic Metric Approximation in Probabilistic Embedding for Cross-Modal Retrieval

abstract: Although mainstream unsupervised anomaly detection (AD) algorithms perform well in academic datasets, their performance is limited in practical application due to the ideal experimental setting of clean training data. Training with noisy data is an inevitable problem in real-world anomaly detection but is seldom discussed. This paper considers label-level noise in image sensory anomaly detection for the first time. To solve this problem, we proposed a memory-based unsupervised AD method, SoftPatch, which efficiently denoises the data at the patch level. Noise discriminators are utilized to generate outlier scores for patch-level noise elimination before coreset construction. The scores are then stored in the memory bank to soften the anomaly detection boundary. Compared with existing methods, SoftPatch maintains a strong modeling ability of normal data and alleviates the overconfidence problem in coreset. Comprehensive experiments in various noise scenes demonstrate that SoftPatch outperforms the state-of-the-art AD methods on the MVTecAD and BTAD benchmarks and is comparable to those methods under the setting without noise.
