paragraphs: SoftPatch studies image anomaly detection when training data contains label-level noise. This matters because methods evaluated with clean training collections can struggle when their data is contaminated. The paper develops a memory-based unsupervised detector that deals with noise at the patch level while retaining a useful model of normal appearance.

Noise discriminators assign outlier scores to image patches before the method constructs its coreset, a selected collection used by the memory-based detector. Those scores support removal of noisy patches. The method also stores the scores in its memory bank, using them to soften the anomaly detection boundary rather than treating the selected examples with excessive confidence.

The authors report that this combination preserves strong normal-data modeling while reducing overconfidence associated with the coreset. Across several noise scenarios, SoftPatch outperforms state-of-the-art anomaly detectors on MVTecAD and BTAD. Under clean-data conditions, its performance is comparable to those methods. The results support handling contamination explicitly within memory construction and subsequent anomaly decisions.
summary.tldr: SoftPatch uses patch-level outlier scores to clean anomaly-detection memory and reduce overconfidence when training data is noisy.

title: SoftPatch: Unsupervised Anomaly Detection with Noisy Data

abstract: We investigate the robustness of vision transformers (ViTs) through the lens of their special patch-based architectural structure, i.e., they process an image as a sequence of image patches. We find that ViTs are surprisingly insensitive to patch-based transformations, even when the transformation largely destroys the original semantics and makes the image unrecognizable by humans. This indicates that ViTs heavily use features that survived such transformations but are generally not indicative of the semantic class to humans. Further investigations show that these features are useful but non-robust, as ViTs trained on them can achieve high in-distribution accuracy, but break down under distribution shifts. From this understanding, we ask: can training the model to rely less on these features improve ViT robustness and out-of-distribution performance? We use the images transformed with our patch-based operations as negatively augmented views and offer losses to regularize the training away from using non-robust features. This is a complementary view to existing research that mostly focuses on augmenting inputs with semantic-preserving transformations to enforce models' invariance. We show that patch-based negative augmentation consistently improves robustness of ViTs on ImageNet based robustness benchmarks across 20+ different experimental settings. Furthermore, we find our patch-based negative augmentation are complementary to traditional (positive) data augmentation techniques and batch-based negative examples in contrastive learning.

paragraphs: Vision transformers process images as sequences of patches. This paper finds that their predictions can remain surprisingly insensitive to patch transformations that destroy recognizable image meaning. The observation points to reliance on features that survive those changes even though people would not generally use them to identify the image’s semantic class.

Further experiments show that these features can support high accuracy on the training distribution yet fail under distribution shifts. The authors use the transformed images as negative augmentations and introduce training losses that discourage dependence on the surviving non-robust features. This complements conventional augmentation, which usually preserves meaning and encourages predictions to stay consistent.

Across more than twenty experimental settings on ImageNet-based robustness benchmarks, patch-based negative augmentation consistently improves vision transformer robustness. It also complements traditional positive augmentation and batch-based negative examples in contrastive learning. The results show how deliberately damaging semantic content can provide a useful training signal about which features a model should rely on less.
summary.tldr: Patch transformations expose non-robust vision-transformer features and provide negative training examples that improve robustness.

title: Understanding and Improving Robustness of Vision Transformers through Patch-based Negative Augmentation

abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) is the task of using students' historical learning interaction data to model their knowledge mastery over time so as to make predictions on their future interaction performance. Recently, remarkable progress has been made of using various deep learning techniques to solve the KT problem. However, the success behind deep learning based knowledge tracing (DLKT) approaches is still left somewhat unknown and proper measurement and analysis of these DLKT approaches remain a challenge. First, data preprocessing procedures in existing works are often private and custom, which limits experimental standardization. Furthermore, existing DLKT studies often differ in terms of the evaluation protocol and are far away real-world educational contexts. To address these problems, we introduce a comprehensive python based benchmark platform, \textsc{pyKT}, to guarantee valid comparisons across DLKT methods via thorough evaluations. The \textsc{pyKT} library consists of a standardized set of integrated data preprocessing procedures on 7 popular datasets across different domains, and 10 frequently compared DLKT model implementations for transparent experiments. Results from our fine-grained and rigorous empirical KT studies yield a set of observations and suggestions for effective DLKT, e.g., wrong evaluation setting may cause label leakage that generally leads to performance inflation; and the improvement of many DLKT approaches is minimal compared to the very first DLKT model proposed by Piech et al. \cite{piech2015deep}. We have open sourced \textsc{pyKT} and our experimental results at \url{https://pykt.org/}. We welcome contributions from other research groups and practitioners.

paragraphs: Knowledge tracing uses a student's interaction history to model changing knowledge mastery and predict future performance. Many deep-learning methods have been proposed, but their reported success is difficult to compare. Private preprocessing pipelines and inconsistent evaluation protocols can make apparent progress hard to separate from differences in experimental setup.

The paper introduces pyKT, a Python benchmark platform with standardized preprocessing for seven commonly used datasets from different domains and implementations of ten frequently compared models. By integrating these components, the platform supports transparent comparisons under shared procedures. Its purpose is to make the measurement of knowledge-tracing performance more consistent and informative.

The authors' detailed empirical studies show that inappropriate evaluation settings can leak labels and inflate reported performance. They also find that many later deep-learning approaches improve only minimally over the first deep-learning knowledge-tracing model. These observations make evaluation design part of the substantive finding: model comparisons can change when tested rigorously. The library and experimental results are released to support further comparisons and contributions.
summary.tldr: pyKT standardizes knowledge-tracing benchmarks and reveals how label leakage and evaluation choices can exaggerate apparent model improvements.

title: pyKT: A Python Library to Benchmark Deep Learning based Knowledge Tracing Models

abstract: Recent non-contrastive methods for self-supervised representation learning show promising performance. While they are attractive since they do not need negative samples, it necessitates some mechanism to avoid collapsing into a trivial solution. Currently, there are two approaches to collapse prevention. One uses an asymmetric architecture on a joint embedding of input, e.g., BYOL and SimSiam, and the other imposes decorrelation criteria on the same joint embedding, e.g., Barlow-Twins and VICReg. The latter methods have theoretical support from information theory as to why they can learn good representation. However, it is not fully understood why the former performs equally well. In this paper, focusing on BYOL/SimSiam, which uses the stop-gradient and a predictor as asymmetric tricks, we present a novel interpretation of these tricks; they implicitly impose a constraint that encourages feature decorrelation similar to Barlow-Twins/VICReg. We then present a novel non-contrastive method, which replaces the stop-gradient in BYOL/SimSiam with the derived constraint; the method empirically shows comparable performance to the above SOTA methods in the standard benchmark test using ImageNet. This result builds a bridge from BYOL/SimSiam to the decorrelation-based methods, contributing to demystifying their secrets.

In this paper, focusing on BYOL/SimSiam, which uses the stop-gradient and a predictor as asymmetric tricks, we present a novel interpretation of these tricks; they implicitly impose a constraint that encourages feature decorrelation similar to Barlow-Twins/VICReg. We then present a novel non-contrastive method, which replaces the stop-gradient in BYOL/SimSiam with the derived constraint; the method empirically shows comparable performance to the above SOTA methods in the standard benchmark test using ImageNet. This result builds a bridge from BYOL/SimSiam to the decorrelation-based methods, contributing to demystifying their secrets.

paragraphs: Non-contrastive self-supervised learning can learn representations without negative examples, but it needs a way to avoid producing the same uninformative representation for every input. Two successful approaches appear different: BYOL and SimSiam introduce asymmetry into their networks, while Barlow Twins and VICReg explicitly encourage decorrelation among learned features.

The paper offers an interpretation connecting these approaches. Focusing on the predictor and stop-gradient operation used by BYOL and SimSiam, the authors argue that these mechanisms implicitly impose a constraint encouraging feature decorrelation. This links architectural choices whose effectiveness was less understood to a principle with existing information-theoretic support.

The authors also turn the interpretation into a learning method by replacing stop-gradient with the derived constraint. On the standard ImageNet benchmark, the resulting method performs comparably to the leading methods discussed in the paper. This empirical result supports the proposed connection: apparently different ways of preventing collapse can encourage similar representation properties. The finding provides both an explanation of existing methods and a concrete alternative built from that explanation.
summary.tldr: The paper interprets BYOL and SimSiam's asymmetric mechanisms as implicit feature decorrelation and builds a comparably performing method from that connection.

title: Bridging the Gap from Asymmetry Tricks to Decorrelation Principles in Non-contrastive Self-supervised Learning

abstract: Continuous-time dynamic graphs naturally abstract many real-world systems, such as social and transactional networks. While the research on continuous-time dynamic graph representation learning has made significant advances recently, neither graph topological properties nor temporal dependencies have been well-considered and explicitly modeled in capturing dynamic patterns. In this paper, we introduce a new approach, Neural Temporal Walks (NeurTWs), for representation learning on continuous-time dynamic graphs. By considering not only time constraints but also structural and tree traversal properties, our method conducts spatiotemporal-biased random walks to retrieve a set of representative motifs, enabling temporal nodes to be characterized effectively. With a component based on neural ordinary differential equations, the extracted motifs allow for irregularly-sampled temporal nodes to be embedded explicitly over multiple different interaction time intervals, enabling the effective capture of the underlying spatiotemporal dynamics. To enrich supervision signals, we further design a harder contrastive pretext task for model optimization. Our method demonstrates overwhelming superiority under both transductive and inductive settings on six real-world datasets.

The paper introduces Neural Temporal Walks, or NeurTWs, to model these properties explicitly when constructing representations of nodes and their changing interaction patterns.

summary.tldr: NeurTWs combines structure- and time-aware walks, neural differential equations, and contrastive training to improve dynamic-graph representations.

title: Neural Temporal Walks: Motif-Aware Representation Learning on Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs

abstract: Time series forecasting has been a widely explored task of great importance in many applications. However, it is common that real-world time series data are recorded in a short time period, which results in a big gap between the deep model and the limited and noisy time series. In this work, we propose to address the time series forecasting problem with generative modeling and propose a bidirectional variational auto-encoder (BVAE) equipped with diffusion, denoise, and disentanglement, namely D3VAE. Specifically, a coupled diffusion probabilistic model is proposed to augment the time series data without increasing the aleatoric uncertainty and implement a more tractable inference process with BVAE. To ensure the generated series move toward the true target, we further propose to adapt and integrate the multiscale denoising score matching into the diffusion process for time series forecasting. In addition, to enhance the interpretability and stability of the prediction, we treat the latent variable in a multivariate manner and disentangle them on top of minimizing total correlation. Extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world data show that D3VAE outperforms competitive algorithms with remarkable margins. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/PaddlePaddle/PaddleSpatial/tree/main/research/D3VAE.

paragraphs: Time-series forecasting can be difficult when observations cover only a short period and contain substantial noise. The paper addresses this mismatch between limited data and deep models through generative modeling. Its method, D3VAE, combines a bidirectional variational autoencoder with diffusion, denoising, and disentanglement.

A coupled diffusion model augments the time-series data without increasing aleatoric uncertainty, the uncertainty associated with randomness in the observations. The authors incorporate multiscale denoising score matching into the diffusion process to guide generated series toward the true prediction target.

This part of the design aims to improve prediction stability and interpretability by reducing dependence among latent variables. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report substantial gains over competitive algorithms. The approach brings together data augmentation, guidance of generated outputs, and organization of the latent representation to address forecasting from limited, noisy observations.
summary.tldr: D3VAE combines diffusion, denoising, and disentangled latent variables to improve forecasting from limited and noisy time-series data.

title: Generative Time Series Forecasting with Diffusion, Denoise, and Disentanglement

abstract: A desirable objective in self-supervised learning (SSL) is to avoid feature collapse. Whitening loss guarantees collapse avoidance by minimizing the distance between embeddings of positive pairs under the conditioning that the embeddings from different views are whitened. In this paper, we propose a framework with an informative indicator to analyze whitening loss, which provides a clue to demystify several interesting phenomena as well as a pivoting point connecting to other SSL methods. We reveal that batch whitening (BW) based methods do not impose whitening constraints on the embedding, but they only require the embedding to be full-rank. This full-rank constraint is also sufficient to avoid dimensional collapse. Based on our analysis, we propose channel whitening with random group partition (CW-RGP), which exploits the advantages of BW-based methods in preventing collapse and avoids their disadvantages requiring large batch size. Experimental results on ImageNet classification and COCO object detection reveal that the proposed CW-RGP possesses a promising potential for learning good representations. The code is available at https://github.com/winci-ai/CW-RGP.

paragraphs: Self-supervised learning needs representations that preserve useful differences between examples. Feature collapse undermines this goal by making representations lose variation. Whitening losses address collapse by bringing paired views together while conditioning their representations through whitening. This paper investigates what those losses actually require of the learned embeddings.

The authors introduce an analytical framework and an informative indicator for studying whitening loss. Their central finding is that methods based on batch whitening do not force the underlying embeddings themselves to be whitened. Instead, they require full rank, meaning the representation retains independent directions of variation. The analysis identifies this full-rank condition as sufficient to prevent dimensional collapse.

Building on that distinction, the paper proposes channel whitening with random group partition, or CW-RGP. It aims to retain the collapse-prevention benefits of batch whitening while avoiding its requirement for large batches. Experiments on ImageNet classification and COCO object detection suggest promising representation quality. The contribution connects an explanation of existing methods with a design intended to make their useful behavior less dependent on batch size.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies full rank as sufficient for avoiding dimensional collapse and proposes whitening that avoids large-batch requirements.

title: An Investigation into Whitening Loss for Self-supervised Learning

abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning agents must make compromises about which aspects of the environment their models should capture. The value equivalence (VE) principle posits that these compromises should be made considering the model's eventual use in value-based planning. Given sets of functions and policies, a model is said to be order-$k$ VE to the environment if $k$ applications of the Bellman operators induced by the policies produce the correct result when applied to the functions. Prior work investigated the classes of models induced by VE when we vary $k$ and the sets of policies and functions. This gives rise to a rich collection of topological relationships and conditions under which VE models are optimal for planning. Despite this effort, relatively little is known about the planning performance of models that fail to satisfy these conditions. This is due to the rigidity of the VE formalism, as classes of VE models are defined with respect to \textit{exact} constraints on their Bellman operators. This limitation gets amplified by the fact that such constraints themselves may depend on functions that can only be approximated in practice. To address these problems we propose approximate value equivalence (AVE), which extends the VE formalism by replacing equalities with error tolerances. This extension allows us to show that AVE models with respect to one set of functions are also AVE with respect to any other set of functions if we tolerate a high enough error. We can then derive bounds on the performance of VE models with respect to \textit{arbitrary sets of functions}. Moreover, AVE models more accurately reflect what can be learned by our agents in practice, allowing us to investigate previously unexplored tensions between model capacity and the choice of VE model class. In contrast to previous works, we show empirically that there are situations where agents with limited capacity should prefer to learn more accurate models with respect to smaller sets of functions over less accurate models with respect to larger sets of functions.

paragraphs: A model-based reinforcement learning agent needs an environment model that supports useful planning. Value equivalence formalizes this by requiring the model to reproduce particular value updates for chosen functions and policies. Its exact equalities are restrictive, especially when the functions involved can only be approximated during learning.

This paper introduces approximate value equivalence, replacing exact agreement with permitted error. With a sufficiently large tolerance, approximate equivalence relative to one function set extends to another. This connection lets the authors derive planning-performance bounds for value-equivalent models defined using arbitrary function sets, broadening the situations that the theory can address.

The relaxed framework also exposes a practical tradeoff involving model capacity. Learning to match more functions can demand more than a limited model can represent accurately. The authors empirically identify situations where concentrating on a smaller function set produces a better choice than fitting a larger set less accurately. This is a conditional finding about limited-capacity agents, rather than a rule that smaller sets always improve planning.
summary.tldr: Approximate value equivalence allows modeling error and reveals when limited-capacity agents benefit from accurately matching fewer value functions.

title: Approximate Value Equivalence

abstract: Coupling-based normalizing flows (e.g. RealNVP) are a popular family of normalizing flow architectures that work surprisingly well in practice. This calls for theoretical understanding. Existing work shows that such flows weakly converge to arbitrary data distributions. However, they make no statement about the stricter convergence criterion used in practice, the maximum likelihood loss. For the first time, we make a quantitative statement about this kind of convergence: We prove that all coupling-based normalizing flows perform whitening of the data distribution (i.e. diagonalize the covariance matrix) and derive corresponding convergence bounds that show a linear convergence rate in the depth of the flow. Numerical experiments demonstrate the implications of our theory and point at open questions.

paragraphs: Coupling-based normalizing flows, including RealNVP, work well empirically, but explaining their convergence requires more than showing they can approach a distribution in a weak mathematical sense. This paper examines convergence connected to maximum-likelihood loss, the stricter criterion used in practical training.

The authors establish a quantitative result for whitening: making the covariance matrix of the data distribution diagonal. They prove this behavior for coupling-based normalizing flows and derive bounds showing a linear convergence rate with flow depth. This identifies how adding depth relates to progress on a concrete distributional property.

The scope of the result matters: the quantitative guarantee concerns whitening, giving a specific part of the broader convergence picture a rate. It should not be read as an unrestricted rate for matching every aspect of an arbitrary distribution. Numerical experiments illustrate consequences of the theory and point to open questions. The contribution advances understanding beyond weak convergence by analyzing a covariance-level transformation in connection with the likelihood criterion that motivates these models.
summary.tldr: The paper proves whitening guarantees for coupling-based normalizing flows, with a linear convergence rate in flow depth.

title: Whitening Convergence Rate of Coupling-based Normalizing Flows

abstract: Video Semantic Segmentation (VSS) involves assigning a semantic label to each pixel in a video sequence. Prior work in this field has demonstrated promising results by extending image semantic segmentation models to exploit temporal relationships across video frames; however, these approaches often incur significant computational costs. In this paper, we propose an efficient mask propagation framework for VSS, called MPVSS. Our approach first employs a strong query-based image segmentor on sparse key frames to generate accurate binary masks and class predictions. We then design a flow estimation module utilizing the learned queries to generate a set of segment-aware flow maps, each associated with a mask prediction from the key frame. Finally, the mask-flow pairs are warped to serve as the mask predictions for the non-key frames. By reusing predictions from key frames, we circumvent the need to process a large volume of video frames individually with resource-intensive segmentors, alleviating temporal redundancy and significantly reducing computational costs. Extensive experiments on VSPW and Cityscapes demonstrate that our mask propagation framework achieves SOTA accuracy and efficiency trade-offs. For instance, our best model with Swin-L backbone outperforms the SOTA MRCFA using MiT-B5 by 4.0% mIoU, requiring only 26% FLOPs on the VSPW dataset. Moreover, our framework reduces up to 4× FLOPs compared to the per-frame Mask2Former baseline with only up to 2% mIoU degradation on the Cityscapes validation set. Code is available at https://github.com/ziplab/MPVSS.

paragraphs: Video semantic segmentation assigns a category to every pixel across a sequence. Processing each frame with a powerful image model can repeat expensive work on closely related content. MPVSS reduces that repetition by generating detailed predictions on sparse key frames and carrying those predictions forward to other frames.

A query-based image segmentor first produces binary masks and class predictions on key frames. A flow module then uses the learned queries to estimate a separate, segment-aware flow map for each mask. Warping these mask-flow pairs produces predictions for non-key frames, allowing the system to reuse segmentation work while accounting for how individual segments move.

On Cityscapes validation, MPVSS reduces FLOPs by up to fourfold relative to per-frame Mask2Former, with up to 2% mIoU degradation. These comparisons demonstrate the potential of selective segmentation followed by mask propagation.
summary.tldr: MPVSS propagates segment-specific masks from key frames to reduce video segmentation computation while retaining strong reported accuracy.

title: Mask Propagation for Efficient Video Semantic Segmentation

abstract: Coordinate descent methods are popular in machine learning and optimization for their simple sparse updates and excellent practical performance. In the context of large-scale sequential game solving, these same properties would be attractive, but until now no such methods were known, because the strategy spaces do not satisfy the typical separable block structure exploited by such methods.We present the first cyclic coordinate-descent-like method for the polytope of sequence-form strategies, which form the strategy spaces for the players in an extensive-form game (EFG). Our method exploits the recursive structure of the proximal update induced by what are known as dilated regularizers, in order to allow for a pseudo block-wise update.We show that our method enjoys a O(1/T) convergence rate to a two-player zero-sum Nash equilibrium, while avoiding the worst-case polynomial scaling with the number of blocks common to cyclic methods. We empirically show that our algorithm usually performs better than other state-of-the-art first-order methods (i.e., mirror prox), and occasionally can even beat CFR$^+$, a state-of-the-art algorithm for numerical equilibrium computation in zero-sum EFGs. We then introduce a restarting heuristic for EFG solving. We show empirically that restarting can lead to speedups, sometimes huge, both for our cyclic method, as well as for existing methods such as mirror prox and predictive CFR$^+$.

paragraphs: Updating a small part of an optimization problem at a time can make computation efficient. Applying this idea to sequential games is difficult because the components of a player's strategy are linked. Their feasible strategy spaces do not have the separable structure that ordinary coordinate methods typically exploit.

The paper develops a cyclic, coordinate-descent-like method for sequence-form strategies in extensive-form games. It uses the recursive structure of updates associated with dilated regularizers to construct partial updates despite those dependencies. For two-player zero-sum games, the method has an O(1/T) convergence rate to a Nash equilibrium and avoids the worst-case polynomial dependence on block count common to cyclic methods.

Experiments show that the method usually improves on first-order alternatives such as mirror prox and sometimes outperforms CFR+. The authors also introduce a restarting heuristic. Empirically, restarting can accelerate both their method and existing solvers, with very large improvements in some cases. These speedups are experimental findings, while the convergence rate is a theoretical guarantee.
summary.tldr: A cyclic partial-update method offers provable convergence for sequential zero-sum games, while restarting empirically accelerates several game solvers.

title: Block-Coordinate Methods and Restarting for Solving Extensive-Form Games

abstract: In $\mathbb{R}^d$, it is well-known that cumulants provide an alternative to moments that can achieve the same goals with numerous benefits such as lower variance estimators. In this paper we extend cumulants to reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) using tools from tensor algebras and show that they are computationally tractable by a kernel trick. These kernelized cumulants provide a new set of all-purpose statistics; the classical maximum mean discrepancy and Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion arise as the degree one objects in our general construction. We argue both theoretically and empirically (on synthetic, environmental, and traffic data analysis) that going beyond degree one has several advantages and can be achieved with the same computational complexity and minimal overhead in our experiments.

paragraphs: Cumulants offer an alternative to moments for describing probability distributions in ordinary finite-dimensional spaces, with benefits that can include lower-variance estimators. This paper extends that statistical idea to reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces. The aim is to create a richer collection of kernel-based statistics beyond those built around mean embeddings.

The authors use tensor algebra to construct these kernelized cumulants and show that a kernel trick makes them computationally tractable. Two established tools, maximum mean discrepancy and the Hilbert-Schmidt independence criterion, emerge as degree-one cases of the broader construction. Higher-degree statistics therefore extend familiar methods within a shared framework.

The paper supports the advantages of moving beyond degree one through theoretical arguments and experiments on synthetic, environmental, and traffic data. In those experiments, the extensions retain the same computational complexity with little additional overhead. This matters because richer statistics need not entail a different computational scaling in the reported setting. The contribution combines a general mathematical construction with evidence that its higher-degree forms can be practical.
summary.tldr: Kernelized cumulants extend familiar kernel statistics to higher degrees with theoretical advantages and minimal experimental computational overhead.

title: Kernelized Cumulants: Beyond Kernel Mean Embeddings

abstract: Humans write code in a fundamentally interactive manner and rely on constant execution feedback to correct errors, resolve ambiguities, and decompose tasks. While LLMs have recently exhibited promising coding capabilities, current coding benchmarks mostly consider a static instruction-to-code sequence transduction process, which has the potential for error propagation and a disconnect between the generated code and its final execution environment. To address this gap, we introduce InterCode, a lightweight, flexible, and easy-to-use framework of interactive coding as a standard reinforcement learning (RL) environment, with code as actions and execution feedback as observations. Our framework is language and platform agnostic, uses self-contained Docker environments to provide safe and reproducible execution, and is compatible out-of-the-box with traditional seq2seq coding methods, while enabling the development of new methods for interactive code generation. We use InterCode to create three interactive code environments with Bash, SQL, and Python as action spaces, leveraging data from the static NL2Bash, Spider, and MBPP datasets. We demonstrate InterCode’s viability as a testbed by evaluating multiple state-of-the-art LLMs configured with different prompting strategies such as ReAct and Plan & Solve. Our results showcase the benefits of interactive code generation and demonstrate that InterCode can serve as a challenging benchmark for advancing code understanding and generation capabilities. InterCode is designed to be easily extensible and can even be used to create new tasks such as Capture the Flag, a popular coding puzzle that is inherently multi-step and involves multiple programming languages.

paragraphs: Programming usually involves running code, inspecting what happened, and revising the next step. Many coding benchmarks instead evaluate a single conversion from instructions into code. InterCode makes the execution-and-revision loop part of the benchmark, allowing models to respond to errors, clarify behavior, and tackle tasks through multiple interactions.

Self-contained Docker environments support safe, reproducible execution. Their results show benefits from interactive generation while establishing a challenging testbed. The framework is also extensible to tasks such as Capture the Flag, where several steps and programming languages may be needed. Its contribution is a common way to study coding as an ongoing process.
summary.tldr: InterCode benchmarks coding as an interactive process in which models execute code and use feedback to guide subsequent actions.

title: InterCode: Standardizing and Benchmarking Interactive Coding with Execution Feedback

abstract: Existing regression models tend to fall short in both accuracy and uncertainty estimation when the label distribution is imbalanced. In this paper, we propose a probabilistic deep learning model, dubbed variational imbalanced regression (VIR), which not only performs well in imbalanced regression but naturally produces reasonable uncertainty estimation as a byproduct. Different from typical variational autoencoders assuming I.I.D. representations (a data point's representation is not directly affected by other data points), our VIR borrows data with similar regression labels to compute the latent representation's variational distribution; furthermore, different from deterministic regression models producing point estimates, VIR predicts the entire normal-inverse-gamma distributions and modulates the associated conjugate distributions to impose probabilistic reweighting on the imbalanced data, thereby providing better uncertainty estimation. Experiments in several real-world datasets show that our VIR can outperform state-of-the-art imbalanced regression models in terms of both accuracy and uncertainty estimation. Code will soon be available at https://github.com/Wang-ML-Lab/variational-imbalanced-regression.

paragraphs: Regression predicts numerical values, and unevenly distributed target values can cause problems for both accuracy and uncertainty estimates. Variational imbalanced regression, or VIR, addresses these together through a probabilistic deep-learning model. Its design allows information from examples with similar target values to influence how an example is represented.

Specifically, VIR uses nearby regression labels when computing the probability distribution of a latent representation. This differs from treating each representation as unaffected by other examples. It also predicts normal-inverse-gamma distributions rather than only individual numerical estimates. The model adjusts the associated conjugate distributions to reweight imbalanced data probabilistically, linking its treatment of imbalance with its uncertainty output.

Experiments on several real-world datasets show that VIR can outperform leading imbalanced-regression models in both predictive accuracy and uncertainty estimation. The findings support combining information sharing among similar labels with distribution-valued predictions. In this approach, uncertainty estimation is produced within the regression model itself, and the mechanism for addressing label imbalance is incorporated into the same probabilistic formulation.
summary.tldr: VIR combines information from similar labels with probabilistic reweighting to improve regression accuracy and uncertainty estimation under label imbalance.

title: Variational Imbalanced Regression: Fair Uncertainty Quantification via Probabilistic Smoothing

abstract: Conditional score-based diffusion model (SBDM) is for conditional generation of target data with paired data as condition, and has achieved great success in image translation. However, it requires the paired data as condition, and there would be insufficient paired data provided in real-world applications. To tackle the applications with partially paired or even unpaired dataset, we propose a novel Optimal Transport-guided Conditional Score-based diffusion model (OTCS) in this paper. We build the coupling relationship for the unpaired or partially paired dataset based on $L_2$-regularized unsupervised or semi-supervised optimal transport, respectively. Based on the coupling relationship, we develop the objective for training the conditional score-based model for unpaired or partially paired settings, which is based on a reformulation and generalization of the conditional SBDM for paired setting. With the estimated coupling relationship, we effectively train the conditional score-based model by designing a ``resampling-by-compatibility'' strategy to choose the sampled data with high compatibility as guidance. Extensive experiments on unpaired super-resolution and semi-paired image-to-image translation demonstrated the effectiveness of the proposed OTCS model. From the viewpoint of optimal transport, OTCS provides an approach to transport data across distributions, which is a challenge for OT on large-scale datasets. We theoretically prove that OTCS realizes the data transport in OT with a theoretical bound.

paragraphs: Conditional score-based diffusion models generate target data using conditioning examples, but their usual training setup requires paired data. Such pairs may be scarce or unavailable. OTCS addresses both partially paired and unpaired datasets by using optimal transport to estimate a coupling: a relationship connecting examples across the source and target distributions.

The method constructs this relationship with L2-regularized optimal transport, using an unsupervised formulation for unpaired data and a semi-supervised formulation when some pairs exist. It then generalizes the paired diffusion training objective to these settings. A compatibility-based resampling strategy selects examples that fit the estimated relationship well and uses them as training guidance.

Experiments on unpaired super-resolution and semi-paired image translation demonstrate the method's effectiveness. The authors also prove, with a theoretical bound, that OTCS realizes the data transport described by optimal transport. This connects the generation procedure to the estimated distributional relationship and offers an approach to transporting data across distributions at the scale that motivates the work.
summary.tldr: OTCS uses optimal-transport couplings and compatibility-based sampling to train conditional diffusion models with partially paired or unpaired data.

title: Optimal Transport-Guided Conditional Score-Based Diffusion Model

abstract: Existing dataset distillation (DD) techniques typically rely on iterative strategies to synthesize condensed datasets, where datasets before and after distillation are forward and backward through neural networks a massive number of times. Despite the promising results achieved, the time efficiency of prior approaches is still far from satisfactory. Moreover, when different sizes of synthetic datasets are required, they have to repeat the iterative training procedures, which is highly cumbersome and lacks flexibility. In this paper, different from the time-consuming forward-backward passes, we introduce a generative fashion for dataset distillation with significantly improved efficiency. Specifically, synthetic samples are produced by a generator network conditioned on the initialization of DD, while synthetic labels are obtained by solving a least-squares problem in a feature space. Our theoretical analysis reveals that the errors of synthetic datasets solved in the original space and then processed by any conditional generators are upper-bounded. To find a satisfactory generator efficiently, we propose a meta-learning algorithm, where a meta generator is trained on a large dataset so that only a few steps are required to adapt to a target dataset. The meta generator is termed as MGDD in our approach. Once adapted, it can handle arbitrary sizes of synthetic datasets, even for those unseen during adaptation. Experiments demonstrate that the generator adapted with only a limited number of steps performs on par with those state-of-the-art DD methods and yields $22\times$ acceleration.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation creates a small synthetic dataset intended to retain useful training information from a larger one. Existing methods often require many repeated forward and backward passes through neural networks. They can also require repeating the optimization when a different synthetic dataset size is needed, making the process expensive and inflexible.

MGDD replaces much of this iterative synthesis with a generator conditioned on the distillation initialization. Synthetic labels are computed through a least-squares problem in feature space. The paper also develops upper bounds on errors when synthetic datasets solved in the original space are processed by conditional generators, supplying theoretical analysis for the generative approach.

A meta-learning procedure trains the generator on a large dataset so that it can adapt to a target dataset in only a few steps. After adaptation, it can produce arbitrary synthetic dataset sizes, including sizes unseen during adaptation. Experiments report performance on par with state-of-the-art distillation methods and a 22-fold acceleration, supporting the approach's combination of faster adaptation and flexible output size.
summary.tldr: MGDD uses a quickly adapted meta-generator to produce distilled datasets of varying sizes, reporting competitive performance with 22-fold acceleration.

title: MGDD: A Meta Generator for Fast Dataset Distillation

abstract: We investigate theory and algorithms for pool-based active learning for multiclass classification using multinomial logistic regression. Using finite sample analysis, we prove that the Fisher Information Ratio (FIR) lower and upper bounds the excess risk. Based on our theoretical analysis, we propose an active learning algorithm that employs regret minimization to minimize the FIR. To verify our derived excess risk bounds, we conduct experiments on synthetic datasets. Furthermore, we compare FIRAL with five other methods and found that our scheme outperforms them: it consistently produces the smallest classification error in the multiclass logistic regression setting, as demonstrated through experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and 50-class ImageNet.

paragraphs: Pool-based active learning chooses which examples from an available collection should receive labels. This paper studies that choice for multiclass classification with multinomial logistic regression. Its goal is to connect the selection criterion directly to the classifier's excess risk, the extra risk relative to the reference optimum.

Through finite-sample analysis, the authors show that the Fisher Information Ratio provides both lower and upper bounds on excess risk. This makes the ratio a theoretically motivated quantity to optimize when selecting examples. Their algorithm, FIRAL, uses regret minimization to reduce this ratio, translating the statistical analysis into an active learning procedure.

Synthetic-data experiments examine the derived risk bounds. The authors also compare FIRAL against five other methods on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and 50-class ImageNet. FIRAL consistently achieves the smallest classification error in those multiclass logistic regression experiments. The evidence therefore combines a bounded-risk selection principle with empirical support in the specific model setting the paper analyzes.
summary.tldr: FIRAL selects examples by minimizing a Fisher-information criterion that bounds excess risk, achieving the lowest classification error in its reported comparisons.

title: FIRAL: An Active Learning Algorithm for Multinomial Logistic Regression

abstract: Sharpness-aware minimization (SAM) has well documented merits in enhancing generalization of deep neural networks, even without sizable data augmentation. Embracing the geometry of the loss function, where neighborhoods of 'flat minima' heighten generalization ability, SAM seeks 'flat valleys' by minimizing the maximum loss caused by an *adversary* perturbing parameters within the neighborhood.Although critical to account for sharpness of the loss function, such an '*over-friendly* adversary' can curtail the outmost level of generalization. The novel approach of this contribution fosters stabilization of adversaries through *variance suppression* (VaSSO) to avoid such friendliness. VaSSO's *provable* stability safeguards its numerical improvement over SAM in model-agnostic tasks, including image classification and machine translation. In addition, experiments confirm that VaSSO endows SAM with robustness against high levels of label noise. Code is available at https://github.com/BingcongLi/VaSSO.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, trains neural networks by considering how much their loss can increase when parameters are perturbed nearby. It seeks flatter regions of the loss landscape, an approach associated with better generalization. The paper examines a weakness in the adversary that supplies these parameter perturbations during training.

The authors argue that an overly friendly adversary can restrict SAM’s generalization benefits. They propose variance suppression, called VaSSO, to stabilize that adversary. The approach focuses on making the perturbation mechanism more stable, addressing how SAM searches for challenging nearby parameter settings. The paper provides a proof of stability for the proposed method.

Reported experiments show numerical improvements over SAM in image classification and machine translation, illustrating benefits across different model tasks. Additional experiments find improved robustness when training labels contain high levels of noise. Together, these results connect adversary stabilization with better observed generalization and label-noise tolerance, while the stability analysis supplies theoretical support for the mechanism behind the method.
summary.tldr: VaSSO stabilizes SAM’s parameter-perturbation adversary through variance suppression, improving reported performance and robustness to label noise.

title: Enhancing Sharpness-Aware Optimization Through Variance Suppression

abstract: Although the mapping between sound and meaning in human language is assumed to be largely arbitrary, research in cognitive science has shown that there are non-trivial correlations between particular sounds and meanings across languages and demographic groups, a phenomenon known as sound symbolism. Among the many dimensions of meaning, sound symbolism is particularly salient and well-demonstrated with regards to cross-modal associations between language and the visual domain. In this work, we address the question of whether sound symbolism is reflected in vision-and-language models such as CLIP and Stable Diffusion. Using zero-shot knowledge probing to investigate the inherent knowledge of these models, we find strong evidence that they do show this pattern, paralleling the well-known kiki-bouba effect in psycholinguistics. Our work provides a novel method for demonstrating sound symbolism and understanding its nature using computational tools. Our code will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether vision-and-language models reflect sound symbolism: systematic associations between language sounds and meanings. Although sound-to-meaning mappings are often treated as largely arbitrary, cognitive research has found recurring patterns across languages and demographic groups. Associations between linguistic sounds and visual properties provide a particularly clear setting for studying this phenomenon.

The authors investigate models including CLIP and Stable Diffusion using zero-shot knowledge probing. The purpose is to examine patterns already present in the models' knowledge. Their focus is whether these models display associations resembling the well-known kiki-bouba effect, bringing a question from psycholinguistics into the analysis of systems that connect language and visual information.

The study finds strong evidence of sound-symbolic patterns in the examined models. The reported parallel with human findings establishes a behavioral correspondence, without itself specifying how that correspondence arose. The contribution is also methodological: computational probing offers another way to demonstrate sound symbolism and investigate its nature using vision-and-language models as objects of study.
summary.tldr: Zero-shot probing finds sound-symbolic associations in CLIP and Stable Diffusion that parallel the human kiki-bouba effect.

title: Kiki or Bouba? Sound Symbolism in Vision-and-Language Models

abstract: Mean-field variational inference (VI) is computationally scalable, but its highly-demanding independence requirement hinders it from being applied to wider scenarios. Although many VI methods that take correlation into account have been proposed, these methods generally are not scalable enough to capture the correlation among data instances, which often arises in applications with graph-structured data or explicit constraints. In this paper, we developed the Tree-structured Variational Inference (TreeVI), which uses a tree structure to capture the correlation of latent variables in the posterior distribution. We show that samples from the tree-structured posterior can be reparameterized efficiently and parallelly, making its training cost just 2 or 3 times that of VI under the mean-field assumption. To capture correlation with more complicated structure, the TreeVI is further extended to the multiple-tree case. Furthermore, we show that the underlying tree structure can be automatically learned from training data. With experiments on synthetic datasets, constrained clustering, user matching and link prediction, we demonstrate that the TreeVI is superior in capturing instance-level correlation in posteriors and enhancing the performance of downstream applications.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution with a more manageable distribution. Mean-field methods scale well by assuming independence, but that assumption can miss relationships between data instances. Such relationships matter when data have graph structure or when explicit constraints link the latent variables of different instances.

TreeVI represents posterior dependencies using a tree. The authors show that samples from this structured distribution can be reparameterized efficiently and in parallel, allowing training at a reported cost of two or three times that of mean-field variational inference. This makes richer dependence modeling available without the scaling difficulties associated with many existing correlation-aware approaches.

The framework extends to multiple trees for more complicated correlation patterns, and the tree structure itself can be learned automatically from training data. Experiments cover synthetic datasets, constrained clustering, user matching, and link prediction. The reported results show stronger capture of instance-level posterior correlations and improved downstream performance, supporting trees as a useful compromise between independence and more elaborate dependency models.
summary.tldr: TreeVI captures posterior correlations with learnable tree structures while keeping training costs close to mean-field variational inference.

title: TreeVI: Reparameterizable Tree-structured Variational Inference for Instance-level Correlation Capturing

abstract: We propose a novel method for learning representations of poses for 3D deformable objects, which specializes in 1) disentangling pose information from the object's identity, 2) facilitating the learning of pose variations, and 3) transferring pose information to other object identities. Based on these properties, our method enables the generation of 3D deformable objects with diversity in both identities and poses, using variations of a single object. It does not require explicit shape parameterization such as skeletons or joints, point-level or shape-level correspondence supervision, or variations of the target object for pose transfer.To achieve pose disentanglement, compactness for generative models, and transferability, we first design the pose extractor to represent the pose as a keypoint-based hybrid representation and the pose applier to learn an implicit deformation field. To better distill pose information from the object's geometry, we propose the implicit pose applier to output an intrinsic mesh property, the face Jacobian. Once the extracted pose information is transferred to the target object, the pose applier is fine-tuned in a self-supervised manner to better describe the target object's shapes with pose variations. The extracted poses are also used to train a cascaded diffusion model to enable the generation of novel poses.Our experiments with the DeformThings4D and Human datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in pose transfer and the ability to generate diverse deformed shapes with various objects and poses.

paragraphs: Transferring a pose between deformable objects requires distinguishing how an object is arranged from what makes it that particular object. This paper learns representations intended to separate pose from identity, capture pose variation, and transfer that information to other identities. It also uses the learned representation to generate objects with varied identities and poses.

A pose extractor produces a compact hybrid representation based on keypoints, while a pose applier learns an implicit deformation field. The applier outputs a mesh property called the face Jacobian to help isolate pose information from geometry. After transfer, self-supervised fine-tuning adapts the applier to the target object's shapes under different poses.

The method does not require an explicit skeleton or joint parameterization, correspondence supervision between points or shapes, or target-object pose variations for transfer. Extracted poses also train a cascaded diffusion model for generating new poses. Experiments on DeformThings4D and Human report state-of-the-art pose-transfer performance and diverse generated deformations. The approach connects transferable pose representations with both adaptation to new identities and generative modeling.
summary.tldr: The method learns transferable 3D pose representations without skeletons or correspondence supervision and uses them to generate diverse deformations.

title: Neural Pose Representation Learning for Generating and Transferring Non-Rigid Object Poses

abstract: Modeling and producing lifelike clothed human images has attracted researchers' attention from different areas for decades, with the complexity from highly articulated and structured content. Rendering algorithms decompose and simulate the imaging process of a camera, while are limited by the accuracy of modeled variables and the efficiency of computation. Generative models can produce impressively vivid human images, however still lacking in controllability and editability. This paper studies photorealism enhancement of rendered images, leveraging generative power from diffusion models on the controlled basis of rendering. We introduce a novel framework to translate rendered images into their realistic counterparts, which consists of two stages: Domain Knowledge Injection (DKI) and Realistic Image Generation (RIG). In DKI, we adopt positive (real) domain finetuning and negative (rendered) domain embedding to inject knowledge into a pretrained Text-to-image (T2I) diffusion model. In RIG, we generate the realistic image corresponding to the input rendered image, with a Texture-preserving Attention Control (TAC) to preserve fine-grained clothing textures, exploiting the decoupled features encoded in the UNet structure. Additionally, we introduce SynFashion dataset, featuring high-quality digital clothing images with diverse textures. Extensive experimental results demonstrate the superiority and effectiveness of our method in rendered-to-real image translation.

paragraphs: Rendered images offer control over the appearance and arrangement of clothed people, but achieving photographic realism is difficult. Generative models can produce vivid images while offering less direct control over their contents. FashionR2R combines these strengths by using a diffusion model to enhance a rendered image while preserving its clothing detail.

The framework has two stages. Domain Knowledge Injection teaches a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model about the distinction between real and rendered imagery through real-domain fine-tuning and a rendered-domain embedding. Realistic Image Generation then produces a realistic counterpart of the input. Within this second stage, Texture-preserving Attention Control uses separated features in the UNet architecture to retain fine clothing textures.

The authors also introduce SynFashion, a dataset of high-quality digital clothing images with varied textures. Experiments report superior and effective rendered-to-real translation. The method's defining concern is correspondence: the output should enhance the realism of the supplied rendering while keeping its fine-grained garment appearance. This connects generative image enhancement to the control already provided by rendering.
summary.tldr: FashionR2R enhances rendered clothing images with diffusion models while using attention control to preserve fine garment textures.

title: FashionR2R: Texture-preserving Rendered-to-Real Image Translation with Diffusion Models

abstract: Decision Transformers have recently emerged as a new and compelling paradigm for offline Reinforcement Learning (RL), completing a trajectory in an autoregressive way. While improvements have been made to overcome initial shortcomings, online finetuning of decision transformers has been surprisingly under-explored. The widely adopted state-of-the-art Online Decision Transformer (ODT) still struggles when pretrained with low-reward offline data. In this paper, we theoretically analyze the online-finetuning of the decision transformer, showing that the commonly used Return-To-Go (RTG) that's far from the expected return hampers the online fine-tuning process. This problem, however, is well-addressed by the value function and advantage of standard RL algorithms. As suggested by our analysis, in our experiments, we hence find that simply adding TD3 gradients to the finetuning process of ODT effectively improves the online finetuning performance of ODT, especially if ODT is pretrained with low-reward offline data. These findings provide new directions to further improve decision transformers.

paragraphs: Decision Transformers learn from recorded trajectories by predicting their continuation. After this offline training, online fine-tuning should let them improve through further interaction. The paper investigates why the Online Decision Transformer struggles with this transition when its initial training data contains low rewards.

The theoretical analysis identifies a problem with return-to-go conditioning: a requested return far from the expected return can hamper online fine-tuning. Standard reinforcement learning provides value functions and advantages that address this issue. The analysis therefore motivates bringing reinforcement learning updates into the fine-tuning process rather than relying entirely on the existing trajectory-completion objective.

In experiments, simply adding TD3 gradients improves Online Decision Transformer fine-tuning, especially after pretraining on low-reward data. The result connects a specific conditioning mismatch to a practical modification of training. It suggests that value-based learning signals can help a pretrained sequence model improve when its offline experience offers a weak starting point. The paper presents this combination as a direction for further Decision Transformer development, supported by its theoretical analysis and reported experiments.
summary.tldr: Adding TD3 gradients improves online Decision Transformer fine-tuning, particularly when low-reward pretraining makes return-to-go conditioning problematic.

title: Reinforcement Learning Gradients as Vitamin for Online Finetuning Decision Transformers

abstract: Boosting is an extremely successful idea, allowing one to combine multiple low accuracy classifiers into a much more accurate voting classifier. In this work, we present a new and surprisingly simple Boosting algorithm that obtains a provably optimal sample complexity. Sample optimal Boosting algorithms have only recently been developed, and our new algorithm has the fastest runtime among all such algorithms and is the simplest to describe: Partition your training data into 5 disjoint pieces of equal size, run AdaBoost on each, and combine the resulting classifiers via a majority vote. In addition to this theoretical contribution, we also perform the first empirical comparison of the proposed sample optimal Boosting algorithms. Our pilot empirical study suggests that our new algorithm might outperform previous algorithms on large data sets.

paragraphs: Boosting combines relatively inaccurate classifiers into a more accurate voting predictor. This paper focuses on achieving that improvement with provably optimal sample complexity: using training examples as efficiently as the theoretical problem permits. Algorithms with this guarantee had only recently become available, motivating a simpler and faster way to obtain it.

The proposed procedure is straightforward. Split the training data into five equally sized, disjoint subsets, run AdaBoost separately on each subset, and combine the five resulting classifiers by majority vote. The authors prove that this construction achieves optimal sample complexity. They also establish the fastest runtime among the sample-optimal boosting algorithms considered, pairing the statistical guarantee with a computational advantage.

The paper additionally presents the first empirical comparison of the proposed sample-optimal boosting algorithms. Its pilot study suggests that the new method might outperform earlier algorithms on large datasets. This practical conclusion is deliberately tentative: the strongest claims concern the proved sample complexity and runtime, while the observed performance advantage remains a finding from an initial empirical study.
summary.tldr: A majority vote over five separately trained AdaBoost classifiers achieves provably optimal sample complexity with a simple, fast procedure.

title: The Many Faces of Optimal Weak-to-Strong Learning

abstract: We study the problem of differentially private stochastic convex optimization (DP-SCO) with heavy-tailed gradients, where we assume a $k^{\text{th}}$-moment bound on the Lipschitz constants of sample functions, rather than a uniform bound. We propose a new reduction-based approach that enables us to obtain the first optimal rates (up to logarithmic factors) in the heavy-tailed setting, achieving error $G_2 \cdot \frac 1 {\sqrt n} + G_k \cdot (\frac{\sqrt d}{n\epsilon})^{1 - \frac 1 k}$ under $(\epsilon, \delta)$-approximate differential privacy, up to a mild $\textup{polylog}(\frac{1}{\delta})$ factor, where $G_2^2$ and $G_k^k$ are the $2^{\text{nd}}$ and $k^{\text{th}}$ moment bounds on sample Lipschitz constants, nearly-matching a lower bound of [LR23].We then give a suite of private algorithms for DP-SCO with heavy-tailed gradients improving our basic result under additional assumptions, including an optimal algorithm under a known-Lipschitz constant assumption, a near-linear time algorithm for smooth functions, and an optimal linear time algorithm for smooth generalized linear models.

paragraphs: This paper studies stochastic convex optimization under differential privacy when gradients can have heavy tails. Instead of requiring every sample function to have a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, it assumes a bounded kth moment of those constants. This permits occasional large values while retaining statistical control over their distribution.

A new reduction-based approach achieves rates that are optimal up to logarithmic factors under approximate differential privacy. The error combines a statistical term, G2 divided by sqrt(n), with a privacy-related term, Gk times (sqrt(d)/(n epsilon)) raised to 1 minus 1/k. Here the moment bounds, sample count, dimension, and privacy parameter determine the trade-off.

The bound nearly matches an existing lower bound, with an additional mild polylogarithmic dependence on the approximate-privacy parameter delta. The authors also give stronger algorithmic results under additional assumptions: optimality with a known Lipschitz constant, near-linear runtime for smooth functions, and optimal linear-time performance for smooth generalized linear models. These refinements depend on their respective assumptions.
summary.tldr: A reduction-based approach achieves nearly optimal private convex-optimization error under moment bounds that allow heavy-tailed gradients.

title: Private Stochastic Convex Optimization with Heavy Tails: Near-Optimality from Simple Reductions

abstract: There has been significant recent interest in graph-based nearest neighbor search methods, many of which are centered on the construction of (approximately) "navigable" graphs over high-dimensional point sets. A graph is navigable if we can successfully move from any starting node to any target node using a greedy routing strategy where we always move to the neighbor that is closest to the destination according to the given distance function. The complete graph is obviously navigable for any point set, but the important question for applications is if sparser graphs can be constructed. While this question is fairly well understood in low-dimensions, we establish some of the first upper and lower bounds for high-dimensional point sets. First, we give a simple and efficient way to construct a navigable graph with average degree $O(\sqrt{n \log n })$ for any set of $n$ points, in any dimension, for any distance function. We compliment this result with a nearly matching lower bound: even under the Euclidean metric in $O(\log n)$ dimensions, a random point set has no navigable graph with average degree $O(n^{\alpha})$ for any $\alpha < 1/2$. Our lower bound relies on sharp anti-concentration bounds for binomial random variables, which we use to show that the {near-neighborhoods} of a set of random points do not overlap significantly, forcing any navigable graph to have many edges.

paragraphs: A navigable graph lets a search reach any target node from any starting node by repeatedly choosing the neighbor closest to the destination. Connecting every pair of points makes this easy, but creates many edges. This paper studies how sparse such graphs can be for high-dimensional point sets.

The authors give an efficient construction whose average degree is O(sqrt(n log n)) for n points. It applies in any dimension and with any distance function. The guarantee therefore provides a broadly applicable way to construct a graph that supports this greedy routing rule while using fewer connections than a complete graph.

A nearly matching lower bound shows that some high-dimensional point sets require many edges. Even for Euclidean distance in O(log n) dimensions, a random point set admits no navigable graph with average degree O(n^alpha) for alpha below one-half. The proof shows that nearby regions around random points overlap too little to share enough routing connections, establishing a structural limit on sparsity.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs sparse navigable graphs for arbitrary point sets and proves a nearly matching high-dimensional sparsity limit.

title: Navigable Graphs for High-Dimensional Nearest Neighbor Search: Constructions and Limits

abstract: In the era of big data, graphs have emerged as a natural representation of intricate relationships. However, graph sizes often become unwieldy, leading to storage, computation, and analysis challenges. A crucial demand arises for methods that can effectively downsize large graphs while retaining vital insights. Graph coarsening seeks to simplify large graphs while maintaining the basic statistics of the graphs, such as spectral properties and $\epsilon$-similarity in the coarsened graph. This ensures that downstream processes are more efficient and effective. Most published methods are suitable for homophilic datasets, limiting their universal use. We propose **U**niversal **G**raph **C**oarsening (UGC), a framework equally suitable for homophilic and heterophilic datasets. UGC integrates node attributes and adjacency information, leveraging the dataset's heterophily factor. Results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that UGC preserves spectral similarity while coarsening. In comparison to existing methods, UGC is 4x to 15x faster, has lower eigen-error, and yields superior performance on downstream processing tasks even at 70% coarsening ratios.

paragraphs: Large graphs can become expensive to store, process, and analyze. Graph coarsening reduces their size while trying to preserve important structural properties, including spectral information. The paper identifies a coverage problem in existing methods: most are suited to homophilic datasets, limiting their usefulness across different patterns of relationships.

Universal Graph Coarsening is designed for both homophilic and heterophilic datasets. It combines node attributes with adjacency information and incorporates the dataset's heterophily factor. This brings information about the nodes and the pattern of their connections into the same coarsening framework, allowing the approach to address both kinds of dataset.

On benchmark datasets, UGC preserves spectral similarity and has lower eigen-error than existing methods. It is also reported to be four to fifteen times faster and to deliver better downstream performance even at 70% coarsening ratios. These findings assess compression through several connected outcomes: computational cost, retained graph structure, and the usefulness of the smaller graph for subsequent tasks.
summary.tldr: UGC combines node attributes and connectivity to coarsen homophilic and heterophilic graphs while preserving useful structure and improving processing speed.

title: UGC: Universal Graph Coarsening

abstract: Training agents that are robust to environmental changes remains a significant challenge in deep reinforcement learning (RL). Unsupervised environment design (UED) has recently emerged to address this issue by generating a set of training environments tailored to the agent's capabilities. While prior works demonstrate that UED has the potential to learn a robust policy, their performance is constrained by the capabilities of the environment generation. To this end, we propose a novel UED algorithm, adversarial environment design via regret-guided diffusion models (ADD). The proposed method guides the diffusion-based environment generator with the regret of the agent to produce environments that the agent finds challenging but conducive to further improvement. By exploiting the representation power of diffusion models, ADD can directly generate adversarial environments while maintaining the diversity of training environments, enabling the agent to effectively learn a robust policy. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method successfully generates an instructive curriculum of environments, outperforming UED baselines in zero-shot generalization across novel, out-of-distribution environments.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning agents can struggle when their surroundings change. Unsupervised environment design addresses this by generating training environments suited to an agent’s current abilities. The paper identifies the environment generator as an important bottleneck: even a useful training strategy depends on being able to produce varied situations that help the agent improve.

The proposed method, ADD, uses a diffusion model to generate environments and guides that generator with the agent’s regret. This guidance aims to produce situations that are challenging while still offering opportunities for improvement. The diffusion model supplies the expressive capacity to generate adversarial environments while preserving diversity across the training experience.

In the reported experiments, ADD produces a useful curriculum and outperforms other environment-design methods when agents face unfamiliar environments without further training. These results support the idea that choosing training challenges and maintaining their variety can work together. The finding concerns the tested out-of-distribution environments; it demonstrates improved generalization there rather than establishing robustness to every possible environmental change.
summary.tldr: ADD uses regret-guided diffusion to generate diverse training challenges and improves agents’ generalization to unfamiliar environments in experiments.

title: Adversarial Environment Design via Regret-Guided Diffusion Models

abstract: In many real-world decision problems there is partially observed, hidden or latent information that remains fixed throughout an interaction. Such decision problems can be modeled as Latent Markov Decision Processes (LMDPs), where a latent variable is selected at the beginning of an interaction and is not disclosed to the agent initially. In last decade, there has been significant progress in designing learning algorithms for solving LMDPs under different structural assumptions. However, for general LMDPs, there is no known learning algorithm that provably matches the existing lower bound. We effectively resolve this open question, introducing the first sample-efficient algorithm for LMDPs without *any additional structural assumptions*. Our result builds off a new perspective on the role off-policy evaluation guarantees and coverage coefficient in LMDPs, a perspective, which has been overlooked in the context of exploration in partially observed environments. Specifically, we establish a novel off-policy evaluation lemma and introduce a new coverage coefficient for LMDPs. Then, we show how these can be used to derive near-optimal guarantees of an optimistic exploration algorithm. These results, we believe, can be valuable for a wide range of interactive learning problems beyond the LMDP class, and especially, for partially observed environments.

paragraphs: Some sequential decision problems contain hidden information that is chosen at the start and stays fixed throughout the interaction. Latent Markov Decision Processes model this situation. Earlier learning algorithms achieved guarantees under various structural assumptions, but a general algorithm matching the known sample-complexity lower bound had remained unavailable.

This paper introduces a sample-efficient algorithm for general latent MDPs without additional structural assumptions. The analysis develops a new off-policy evaluation lemma and a new coverage coefficient. These tools connect what can be inferred about policies from collected experience with the exploration needed when part of the environment is hidden.

Using those tools, the authors establish near-optimal guarantees for an optimistic exploration algorithm, effectively resolving the stated gap with existing lower bounds. The significance is a guarantee on the amount of interaction needed to learn in the general latent-MDP setting. The authors also suggest that this analytical perspective may help with other interactive learning problems, particularly partially observed environments, while presenting that broader relevance as a possibility.
summary.tldr: New off-policy evaluation and coverage tools yield near-optimal exploration guarantees for latent MDPs without additional structural assumptions.

title: RL in Latent MDPs is Tractable: Online Guarantees via Off-Policy Evaluation

abstract: Protein representation learning is indispensable for various downstream applications of artificial intelligence for bio-medicine research, such as drug design and function prediction. However, achieving effective representation learning for proteins poses challenges due to the diversity of data modalities involved, including sequence, structure, and function annotations. Despite the impressive capabilities of large language models in biomedical text modelling, there remains a pressing need for a framework that seamlessly integrates these diverse modalities, particularly focusing on the three critical aspects of protein information: sequence, structure, and function. Moreover, addressing the inherent data scale differences among these modalities is essential. To tackle these challenges, we introduce ProtGO, a unified model that harnesses a teacher network equipped with a customized graph neural network (GNN) and a Gene Ontology (GO) encoder to learn hybrid embeddings. Notably, our approach eliminates the need for additional functions as input for the student network, which shares the same GNN module. Importantly, we utilize a domain adaptation method to facilitate distribution approximation for guiding the training of the teacher-student framework. This approach leverages distributions learned from latent representations to avoid the alignment of individual samples. Benchmark experiments highlight that ProtGO significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, clearly demonstrating the advantages of the proposed unified framework.
