paragraphs: Protein information appears in several forms, including sequence, structure, and functional annotations. Learning a useful representation requires integrating these sources despite differences in their availability and scale. ProtGO addresses this problem through a unified representation-learning framework intended to support downstream biomedical applications.

The framework uses a teacher network combining a customized graph neural network with a Gene Ontology encoder to learn hybrid representations. A student network shares the same graph-neural-network module but does not require additional function information as input. This arrangement lets functional information guide learning while supporting a student whose input requirements do not include those annotations.

To train the teacher and student, the authors use domain adaptation to approximate distributions in the learned representation space. This avoids requiring alignment of individual samples, addressing the integration problem at the distribution level. Benchmark experiments show significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. The stated findings support combining protein modalities through function-guided teacher-student learning, with distribution matching providing the link between the representations used during training.
summary.tldr: ProtGO uses function-guided teacher-student learning and distribution matching to integrate protein information without requiring function inputs for the student.

title: ProtGO: Function-Guided Protein Modeling for Unified Representation Learning

abstract: Current LLM alignment techniques use pairwise human preferences at a sample level, and as such, they do not imply an alignment on the distributional level. We propose in this paper Alignment via Optimal Transport (AOT), a novel method for distributional preference alignment of LLMs. AOT aligns LLMs on unpaired preference data by making the reward distribution of the positive samples stochastically dominant in the first order on the distribution of negative samples. We introduce a convex relaxation of this first-order stochastic dominance and cast it as an optimal transport problem with a smooth and convex cost. Thanks to the one-dimensional nature of the resulting optimal transport problem and the convexity of the cost, it has a closed-form solution via sorting on empirical measures. We fine-tune LLMs with this AOT objective, which enables alignment by penalizing the violation of the stochastic dominance of the reward distribution of the positive samples on the reward distribution of the negative samples. We analyze the sample complexity of AOT by considering the dual of the OT problem and show that it converges at the parametric rate. Empirically, we show on a diverse set of alignment datasets and LLMs that AOT leads to state-of-the-art models in the 7B family of models when evaluated with Open LLM Benchmarks and AlpacaEval. Code for $\mathsf{AOT}$ is available in the Hugging Face TRL library \url{https://ibm.biz/AOT_TRL}.

paragraphs: Learning from individual preference pairs does not by itself establish that preferred responses have better rewards across their full distribution. Alignment via Optimal Transport, or AOT, targets that broader relationship. It works with unpaired positive and negative preference samples, seeking first-order stochastic dominance of the positive reward distribution over the negative one.

The authors introduce a convex relaxation of this dominance requirement and express it as an optimal transport problem with a smooth, convex cost. Because the transport problem is one-dimensional, its empirical solution can be obtained by sorting. The resulting fine-tuning objective penalizes violations of the desired distributional ordering, giving a practical training procedure for the broader alignment target.

The paper also analyzes sample complexity through the transport problem's dual formulation and establishes convergence at the parametric rate. Across multiple alignment datasets and language models, the authors report state-of-the-art results within the 7B model family on Open LLM Benchmarks and AlpacaEval. These findings support distribution-level preference objectives as a useful approach to language-model fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: AOT fine-tunes language models with an efficiently computed transport objective that penalizes undesirable ordering of positive and negative reward distributions.

title: Distributional Preference Alignment of LLMs via Optimal Transport

abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have recently achieved rapid progress, exhibiting great perception and reasoning abilities concerning visual information. However, when faced with prompts in different sizes of solution spaces, LVLMs fail to always give consistent answers regarding the same knowledge point. This inconsistency of answers between different solution spaces is prevalent in LVLMs and erodes trust. To this end, we provide a multi-modal benchmark ConBench, to intuitively analyze how LVLMs perform when the solution space of a prompt revolves around a knowledge point. Based on the ConBench tool, we are the first to reveal the tapestry and get the following findings: (1) In the discriminate realm, the larger the solution space of the prompt, the lower the accuracy of the answers. (2) Establish the relationship between the discriminative and generative realms: the accuracy of the discriminative question type exhibits a strong positive correlation with its Consistency with the caption. (3) Compared to open-source models, closed-source models exhibit a pronounced bias advantage in terms of Consistency. Eventually, we ameliorate the consistency of LVLMs by trigger-based diagnostic refinement, indirectly improving the performance of their caption. We hope this paper will accelerate the research community in better evaluating their models and encourage future advancements in the consistency domain.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can give conflicting answers about the same visual fact when the prompt changes the range of possible answers. This paper introduces ConBench to examine that inconsistency systematically. The benchmark varies a prompt’s solution space around a common knowledge point, testing whether different ways of asking remain compatible.

The authors report that discriminative question accuracy falls as the solution space grows. They also find a strong positive correlation between discriminative accuracy and agreement with the model’s caption. This connects answers that distinguish among possibilities with freely generated descriptions. In the evaluated comparisons, closed-source models show a pronounced consistency advantage that the authors characterize in terms of bias.

The paper then applies trigger-based diagnostic refinement to improve consistency, reporting an indirect improvement in caption performance as well. These findings make agreement across prompt forms an additional dimension of model evaluation. A model’s ability to answer one question correctly does not, by itself, describe how consistently it expresses the same visual knowledge across different questions and captions.
summary.tldr: ConBench reveals inconsistencies across vision-language prompt formats, and diagnostic refinement improves agreement and caption performance.

title: Unveiling the Tapestry of Consistency in Large Vision-Language Models

abstract: The advancement of Machine Learning has enabled the widespread deployment of Machine Learning as a Service (MLaaS) applications. However, the untrustworthy nature of third-party ML services poses backdoor threats. Existing defenses in MLaaS are limited by their reliance on training samples or white-box model analysis, highlighting the need for a black-box backdoor purification method. In our paper, we attempt to use diffusion models for purification by introducing noise in a forward diffusion process to destroy backdoors and recover clean samples through a reverse generative process. However, since a higher noise also destroys the semantics of the original samples, it still results in a low restoration performance. To investigate the effectiveness of noise in eliminating different types of backdoors, we conducted a preliminary study, which demonstrates that backdoors with low visibility can be easily destroyed by lightweight noise and those with high visibility need to be destroyed by high noise but can be easily detected. Based on the study, we propose SampDetox, which strategically combines lightweight and high noise. SampDetox applies weak noise to eliminate low-visibility backdoors and compares the structural similarity between the recovered and original samples to localize high-visibility backdoors. Intensive noise is then applied to these localized areas, destroying the high-visibility backdoors while preserving global semantic information. As a result, detoxified samples can be used for inference, even by poisoned models. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of SampDetox in defending against various state-of-the-art backdoor attacks.

paragraphs: A third-party machine learning service may contain a backdoor, while its users lack access to training data or model internals. SampDetox tackles this black-box setting by purifying inputs before inference. Diffusion-based purification adds noise to disrupt a backdoor and then reconstructs the sample, but excessive noise can also destroy the content needed for a correct prediction.

A preliminary study finds that low-visibility backdoors are vulnerable to weak noise, whereas high-visibility backdoors require stronger noise but are easier to detect. SampDetox uses this distinction in stages. It first applies weak noise, then compares the reconstructed sample with the original using structural similarity to locate conspicuous backdoor regions. Stronger noise is concentrated on those regions.

This localized treatment aims to remove visible triggers while preserving the sample's overall semantic content. The purified inputs can then be submitted even to a poisoned model. Experiments report effective defense against several state-of-the-art backdoor attacks, supporting the strategy of matching perturbation strength and location to the backdoor characteristics observed in the study.
summary.tldr: SampDetox purifies inputs with weak global noise and stronger localized noise to defend against backdoors without accessing model internals.

title: SampDetox: Black-box Backdoor Defense via Perturbation-based Sample Detoxification

abstract: LLM agents have demonstrated remarkable performance across various applications, primarily due to their advanced capabilities in reasoning, utilizing external knowledge and tools, calling APIs, and executing actions to interact with environments. Current agents typically utilize a memory module or a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanism, retrieving past knowledge and instances with similar embeddings from knowledge bases to inform task planning and execution. However, the reliance on unverified knowledge bases raises significant concerns about their safety and trustworthiness. To uncover such vulnerabilities, we propose a novel red teaming approach AgentPoison, the first backdoor attack targeting generic and RAG-based LLM agents by poisoning their long-term memory orRAG knowledge base. In particular, we form the trigger generation process as a constrained optimization to optimize backdoor triggers by mapping the triggered instances to a unique embedding space, so as to ensure that whenever a user instruction contains the optimized backdoor trigger, the malicious demonstrations are retrieved from the poisoned memory or knowledge base with high probability. In the meantime, benign instructions without the trigger will still maintain normal performance. Unlike conventional backdoor attacks, AgentPoison requires no additional model training or fine-tuning, and the optimized backdoor trigger exhibits superior transferability, resilience, and stealthiness. Extensive experiments demonstrate AgentPoison's effectiveness in attackingthree types of real-world LLM agents: RAG-based autonomous driving agent, knowledge-intensive QA agent, and healthcare EHRAgent. We inject the poisoning instances into the RAG knowledge base and long-term memories of these agents, respectively, demonstrating the generalization of AgentPoison. On each agent, AgentPoison achieves an average attack success rate of $\ge$ 80% with minimalimpact on benign performance ($\le$ 1%) with a poison rate < 0.1%. The code and data is available at https://github.com/BillChan226/AgentPoison.

However, the reliance on unverified knowledge bases raises significant concerns about their safety and trustworthiness. To uncover such vulnerabilities, we propose a novel red teaming approach AgentPoison, the first backdoor attack targeting generic and RAG-based LLM agents by poisoning their long-term memory orRAG knowledge base. In particular, we form the trigger generation process as a constrained optimization to optimize backdoor triggers by mapping the triggered instances to a unique embedding space, so as to ensure that whenever a user instruction contains the optimized backdoor trigger, the malicious demonstrations are retrieved from the poisoned memory or knowledge base with high probability. In the meantime, benign instructions without the trigger will still maintain normal performance. Unlike conventional backdoor attacks, AgentPoison requires no additional model training or fine-tuning, and the optimized backdoor trigger exhibits superior transferability, resilience, and stealthiness. Extensive experiments demonstrate AgentPoison's effectiveness in attackingthree types of real-world LLM agents: RAG-based autonomous driving agent, knowledge-intensive QA agent, and healthcare EHRAgent. We inject the poisoning instances into the RAG knowledge base and long-term memories of these agents, respectively, demonstrating the generalization of AgentPoison. On each agent, AgentPoison achieves an average attack success rate of $\ge$ 80% with minimalimpact on benign performance ($\le$ 1%) with a poison rate < 0.1%. The code and data is available at https://github.com/BillChan226/AgentPoison.

paragraphs: Language-model agents often retrieve stored experiences or external knowledge before planning and acting. AgentPoison examines how this dependence can become a vulnerability when the retrieved material is unverified. Its attack targets the agent's long-term memory or retrieval knowledge base, rather than requiring changes to the underlying language model.

The method optimizes a backdoor trigger so that instructions containing it are likely to retrieve malicious demonstrations. Instructions without the trigger are intended to retain normal behavior. This makes the retrieval process central to the attack: a small amount of poisoned material can influence which examples the agent uses to guide its actions, without additional model training or fine-tuning.

Experiments cover autonomous driving, knowledge-intensive question answering, and a healthcare agent. For each agent, the authors report average attack success of at least 80%, benign-performance impact of at most 1%, and a poisoning rate below 0.1%. These results demonstrate a targeted retrieval vulnerability across the tested agents, including cases where ordinary performance remains largely unchanged.
summary.tldr: AgentPoison shows that small amounts of poisoned retrieval content can trigger harmful agent behavior while leaving ordinary performance largely intact.

title: AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases

abstract: We propose a novel approach to sequential Bayesian inference based on variational Bayes (VB). The key insight is that, in the online setting, we do not need to add the KL term to regularize to the prior (which comes from the posterior at the previous timestep); instead we can optimize just the expected log-likelihood, performing a single step of natural gradient descent starting at the prior predictive. We prove this method recovers exact Bayesian inference if the model is conjugate. We also show how to compute an efficient deterministic approximation to the VB objective, as well as our simplified objective, when the variational distribution is Gaussian or a sub-family, including the case of a diagonal plus low-rankprecision matrix.We show empirically that ourmethod outperforms other online VB methods in the non-conjugate setting, such as online learning for neural networks, especially when controlling for computational costs.

We prove this method recovers exact Bayesian inference if the model is conjugate. paragraphs: BONG proposes a simpler way to update Bayesian beliefs as observations arrive sequentially. In this setting, the posterior from the previous timestep supplies the next prior. Conventional variational Bayes includes a term that penalizes departure from that prior, alongside a term measuring how well the model explains the new data.

The paper’s key move is to omit the explicit prior-regularization term and instead take one natural-gradient step on the expected log-likelihood, starting from the prior predictive distribution. This makes the starting point and update geometry central to the procedure. The authors prove that this update recovers exact Bayesian inference for conjugate models, where the prior and likelihood have compatible mathematical forms.

For Gaussian variational distributions and related restricted families, the paper also develops efficient deterministic approximations to both objectives. These include distributions represented with diagonal-plus-low-rank precision matrices. In non-conjugate experiments, including online neural-network learning, BONG outperforms other online variational methods, especially when computational costs are taken into account.
summary.tldr: BONG simplifies online Bayesian updates with a single natural-gradient step that is exact for conjugate models and empirically efficient beyond them.

title: Bayesian Online Natural Gradient (BONG)

abstract: We study adversarially robust transfer learning, wherein, given labeled data on multiple (source) tasks, the goal is to train a model with small robust error on a previously unseen (target) task.In particular, we consider a multi-task representation learning (MTRL) setting, i.e., we assume that the source and target tasks admit a simple (linear) predictor on top of a shared representation (e.g., the final hidden layer of a deep neural network).In this general setting, we provide rates on~the excess adversarial (transfer) risk for Lipschitz losses and smooth nonnegative losses.These rates show that learning a representation using adversarial training on diverse tasks helps protect against inference-time attacks in data-scarce environments.Additionally, we provide novel rates for the single-task setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies how learning from several labeled tasks can help a model resist adversarial attacks on a new task. The goal is transfer with low robust error: predictions should remain reliable under attacks at inference time, even when the target task has little training data. The question is therefore about transferring protection as well as predictive ability.

The analysis assumes that source and target tasks share a useful representation, with each task requiring only a linear predictor on top. Under this shared structure, the authors derive bounds on excess adversarial transfer risk for two classes of losses: Lipschitz losses and smooth nonnegative losses. These bounds describe the error associated with learning a robust predictor rather than having an ideal one available.

The resulting rates support adversarially training representations across diverse tasks as a way to improve protection in data-scarce settings. This is a theoretical conclusion within the stated representation and loss assumptions. The paper also establishes new rates for learning a single task, connecting its transfer analysis to the simpler setting without multiple source tasks.
summary.tldr: Under shared-representation assumptions, theoretical bounds show how adversarial training across diverse tasks can improve robustness on a new task with limited data.

title: Adversarially Robust Multi-task Representation Learning

abstract: In recent years, significant progress has been made in multi-objective reinforcement learning (RL) research, which aims to balance multiple objectives by incorporating preferences for each objective. In most existing studies, specific preferences must be provided during deployment to indicate the desired policies explicitly. However, designing these preferences depends heavily on human prior knowledge, which is typically obtained through extensive observation of high-performing demonstrations with expected behaviors. In this work, we propose a simple yet effective offline adaptation framework for multi-objective RL problems without assuming handcrafted target preferences, but only given several demonstrations to implicitly indicate the preferences of expected policies. Additionally, we demonstrate that our framework can naturally be extended to meet constraints on safety-critical objectives by utilizing safe demonstrations, even when the safety thresholds are unknown. Empirical results on offline multi-objective and safe tasks demonstrate the capability of our framework to infer policies that align with real preferences while meeting the constraints implied by the provided demonstrations.

paragraphs: Multi-objective reinforcement learning must balance several goals, often by requiring a user to specify preferences at deployment. Choosing those preferences can be difficult: people may recognize desirable behavior in demonstrations without knowing how to express the corresponding trade-off explicitly. This paper proposes an offline adaptation framework that uses several demonstrations to indicate the intended behavior.

The framework does not assume handcrafted target preferences. Instead, the demonstrations implicitly communicate the preferences of the desired policy. This changes the information users must provide, replacing an explicit specification of competing objectives with examples of what they want the policy to do.

The authors also extend the approach to safety-critical objectives by using safe demonstrations, even when safety thresholds are unknown. Empirical evaluations on offline multi-objective and safe tasks show policies that align with the intended preferences while satisfying constraints implied by the demonstrations. The safety result is tied to this demonstrated information and the evaluated tasks; it is presented as an empirical capability of the framework.
summary.tldr: This offline reinforcement learning framework uses demonstrations to infer objective preferences and accommodate implied safety constraints without explicit target weights or known thresholds.

title: An Offline Adaptation Framework for Constrained Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Various forms of sparse attention have been explored to mitigate the quadratic computational and memory cost of the attention mechanism in transformers. We study sparse transformers not through a lens of efficiency but rather in terms of learnability and generalization. Empirically studying a range of attention mechanisms, we find that input-dependent sparse attention models appear to converge faster and generalize better than standard attention models, while input-agnostic sparse attention models show no such benefits -- a phenomenon that is robust across architectural and optimization hyperparameter choices. This can be interpreted as demonstrating that concentrating a model's "semantic focus" with respect to the tokens currently being considered (in the form of input-dependent sparse attention) accelerates learning. We develop a theoretical characterization of the conditions that explain this behavior. We establish a connection between the stability of the standard softmax and the loss function's Lipschitz properties, then show how sparsity affects the stability of the softmax and the subsequent convergence and generalization guarantees resulting from the attention mechanism. This allows us to theoretically establish that input-agnostic sparse attention does not provide any benefits. We also characterize conditions when semantic focus (input-dependent sparse attention) can provide improved guarantees, and we validate that these conditions are in fact met in our empirical evaluations.

paragraphs: Sparse attention is often studied as a way to reduce transformer computation. This paper instead asks how sparsity affects learning and generalization. Across the studied mechanisms, attention that selects connections based on the current input appears to learn faster and generalize better, while input-independent sparsity shows no comparable benefit.

The authors interpret the useful form as semantic focus: concentrating attention according to the tokens being processed. They develop theory linking softmax stability to how sensitively the loss changes, then analyze how sparsity influences convergence and generalization guarantees. This separates the effects of merely removing attention connections from those of choosing connections using input information.

Within the theoretical characterization, input-independent sparsity provides no improvement, whereas input-dependent sparsity can improve guarantees under specified conditions. The experiments satisfy those conditions, and the observed pattern persists across architectural and optimization choices. The result is a conditional explanation of why some sparse attention designs help learning, beyond their potential savings in computation and memory.
summary.tldr: Input-dependent sparse attention can improve transformer learning and generalization under characterized conditions, unlike sparsity chosen independently of the input.

title: Transformers Learn Faster with Semantic Focus

abstract: Generating music with coherent structure, harmonious instrumental and vocal elements remains a significant challenge in song generation. Existing language models and diffusion-based methods often struggle to balance global coherence with local fidelity, resulting in outputs that lack musicality or suffer from incoherent progression and mismatched lyrics. This paper introduces SongBloom, a novel framework for full-length song generation that leverages an interleaved paradigm of autoregressive sketching and diffusion-based refinement. SongBloom employs an autoregressive diffusion model that combines the high fidelity of diffusion models with the scalability of language models. Specifically, it gradually extends a musical sketch from short to long and refines the details from coarse to fine-grained. The interleaved generation paradigm effectively integrates prior semantic and acoustic context to guide the generation process. Experimental results demonstrate that SongBloom outperforms existing methods across both subjective and objective metrics and achieves performance comparable to the state-of-the-art commercial music generation platforms. Audio samples are available on our demo page: https://cypress-yang.github.io/SongBloom_demo.

paragraphs: Generating a full song requires both coherent progression over time and convincing detail in vocals and instruments. Existing approaches can struggle to satisfy both, producing weak musical structure, inconsistent progression, or lyrics that do not fit. SongBloom addresses this tension by combining autoregressive generation with diffusion-based refinement in an interleaved process.

The system gradually extends a musical sketch from shorter to longer duration while refining its details from coarse to fine. Its autoregressive diffusion model combines the scalability associated with language models and the fidelity associated with diffusion models. Earlier semantic and acoustic context helps guide continued generation, connecting the developing song's structure with the details being produced.

Experiments show improvements over existing methods on both subjective and objective measures, with performance reported as comparable to leading commercial music-generation platforms. These findings support interleaving extension and refinement as a useful way to coordinate global musical development with local sound quality. The contribution centers on how the generation process is organized to keep these demands connected throughout a full-length song.
summary.tldr: SongBloom interleaves autoregressive musical sketching with diffusion refinement to improve full-song coherence and sound quality.

title: SongBloom: Coherent Song Generation via Interleaved Autoregressive Sketching and Diffusion Refinement

abstract: This work examines risk bounds for nonparametric distributional regression estimators. For convex-constrained distributional regression, general upper bounds are established for the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and the worst-case mean squared error (MSE) across the domain. These theoretical results are applied to isotonic and trend filtering distributional regression, yielding convergence rates consistent with those for mean estimation. Furthermore, a general upper bound is derived for distributional regression under non-convex constraints, with a specific application to neural network-based estimators. Comprehensive experiments on both simulated and real data validate the theoretical contributions, demonstrating their practical effectiveness.

paragraphs: Distributional regression estimates a predictive distribution rather than only a single mean value. This paper studies how accurately nonparametric methods can perform that task. Its main contribution is a set of upper bounds on estimation risk, providing theoretical control over errors for different families of constrained distributional estimators.

For convex constraints, the authors establish general bounds using the continuous ranked probability score and worst-case mean squared error across the domain. They then apply these results to isotonic and trend-filtering distributional regression. The resulting convergence rates are consistent with those for mean estimation, connecting the statistical behavior of these distribution-estimation methods with that of their mean-estimation counterparts.

The analysis also extends to non-convex constraints through another general upper bound, with neural-network estimators as a specific application. Experiments on simulated and real data support the theoretical contributions and their practical effectiveness. Together, the results provide a framework for understanding estimation error across several distributional regression approaches, while retaining the distinction between their constraint structures.
summary.tldr: The paper derives risk bounds for constrained distributional regression, including isotonic, trend-filtering, and neural-network estimators.

title: Risk Bounds For Distributional Regression

abstract: Disaggregated evaluation across subgroups is critical for assessing the fairness of machine learning models, but its uncritical use can mislead practitioners. We show that equal performance across subgroups is an unreliable measure of fairness when data are representative of the relevant populations but reflective of real-world disparities. Furthermore, when data are not representative due to selection bias, both disaggregated evaluation and alternative approaches based on conditional independence testing may be invalid without explicit assumptions regarding the bias mechanism. We use causal graphical models to characterize fairness properties and metric stability across subgroups under different data generating processes. Our framework suggests complementing disaggregated evaluations with explicit causal assumptions and analysis to control for confounding and distribution shift, including conditional independence testing and weighted performance estimation. These findings have broad implications for how practitioners design and interpret model assessments given the ubiquity of disaggregated evaluation.

We show that equal performance across subgroups is an unreliable measure of fairness when data are representative of the relevant populations but reflective of real-world disparities. We use causal graphical models to characterize fairness properties and metric stability across subgroups under different data generating processes. paragraphs: Evaluating a model separately across population subgroups is important for examining fairness, but equal scores do not automatically imply fair behavior. This paper shows why interpreting those scores requires understanding how the data were generated. Even representative data can reflect existing social disparities that make performance equality an unreliable fairness criterion.

Selection bias creates a further challenge when the observed data do not represent the relevant population. In that situation, both subgroup evaluation and alternatives based on conditional independence testing may be invalid unless the analysis makes explicit assumptions about the selection process. Changing the statistical test alone does not resolve uncertainty about how people or observations entered the dataset.

The authors use causal graphical models to characterize fairness properties and the stability of subgroup metrics under different data-generating processes. Their framework suggests combining disaggregated evaluation with explicit causal reasoning about confounding and distribution shift, potentially using conditional independence tests and weighted performance estimates. The practical implication is to treat subgroup metrics as evidence requiring interpretation within a causal account of the data, rather than as a self-sufficient verdict on fairness.
summary.tldr: Subgroup performance comparisons can mislead fairness assessments unless their interpretation accounts for real-world disparities, selection bias, and causal assumptions.

title: Understanding challenges to the interpretation of disaggregated evaluations of algorithmic fairness

abstract: Surrogate models are widely used to approximate complex systems across science and engineering to reduce computational costs. Despite their widespread adoption, the field lacks standardisation across key stages of the modelling pipeline, including data sampling, model selection, evaluation, and downstream analysis. This fragmentation limits reproducibility and cross-domain utility – a challengefurther exacerbated by the rapid proliferation of AI-driven surrogate models. We argue for the urgent need to establish a structured reporting standard, the Surrogate Model Reporting Standard (SMRS), that systematically captures essential design and evaluation choices while remaining agnostic to implementation specifics. By promoting a standardised yet flexible framework, we aim to improve the reliabilityof surrogate modelling, foster interdisciplinary knowledge transfer, and, as a result, accelerate scientific progress in the AI era.

paragraphs: Surrogate models approximate complex systems so that scientific and engineering work can proceed at lower computational cost. The paper identifies a reporting problem across this field: choices about data sampling, model selection, evaluation, and downstream analysis are not consistently documented. That fragmentation makes results harder to reproduce and knowledge harder to transfer between domains.

The authors advocate a Surrogate Model Reporting Standard, or SMRS, to capture essential design and evaluation decisions in a structured way. The proposed direction remains independent of implementation details, so different modeling approaches can share a reporting framework. Its purpose is to make consequential choices visible without prescribing one technical method for building every surrogate.

The growth of AI-driven surrogate modeling makes this coordination increasingly pressing in the authors' argument. A standardized but flexible reporting approach is intended to improve reliability and interdisciplinary reuse, ultimately supporting scientific progress. These are the aims of a proposed reporting standard. The contribution is an argument for organizing and communicating modeling evidence more consistently across a fragmented field.
summary.tldr: SMRS advocates flexible, standardized reporting of surrogate-model design and evaluation choices to improve reproducibility and cross-domain reuse.

title: SMRS: advocating a unified reporting standard for surrogate models in the artificial intelligence era.

abstract: Incomplete multi-view data, where certain views are entirely missing for some samples, poses significant challenges for traditional multi-view clustering methods. Existing deep incomplete multi-view clustering approaches often rely on static fusion strategies or two-stage pipelines, leading to suboptimal fusion results and error propagation issues. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel incomplete multi-view clustering framework based on Hierarchical Semantic Alignment and Cooperative Completion (HSACC). HSACC achieves robust cross-view fusion through a dual-level semantic space design. In the low-level semantic space, consistency alignment is ensured by maximizing mutual information across views. In the high-level semantic space, adaptive view weights are dynamically assigned based on the distributional affinity between individual views and an initial fused representation, followed by weighted fusion to generate a unified global representation. Additionally, HSACC implicitly recovers missing views by projecting aligned latent representations into high-dimensional semantic spaces and jointly optimizes reconstruction and clustering objectives, enabling cooperative learning of completion and clustering. Experimental results demonstrate that HSACC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on five benchmark datasets. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the hierarchical alignment and dynamic weighting mechanisms, while parameter analysis confirms the model's robustness to hyperparameter variations. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/XiaojianDing/2025-NeurIPS-HSACC}.

Its design combines hierarchical alignment, adaptive fusion, and joint learning of completion and clustering.

At a higher level, it compares each view’s distribution with an initial fused representation and assigns adaptive weights before combining the views. Missing views are implicitly recovered by projecting aligned latent representations into higher-dimensional semantic spaces.

On five benchmark datasets, HSACC significantly outperforms state-of-the-art comparison methods. Ablations support the contributions of hierarchical alignment and dynamic weighting, while parameter analysis finds robustness to hyperparameter changes. These results support the coordinated design: aligning views, adjusting their influence, and learning completion jointly all contribute to the reported clustering improvements.
summary.tldr: HSACC jointly aligns, weights, and completes incomplete views to improve clustering, outperforming comparison methods on five benchmark datasets.

title: Incomplete Multi-view Clustering via Hierarchical Semantic Alignment and Cooperative Completion

abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) like OpenAI-o1 have shown impressive capabilities in natural language reasoning. However, these models frequently demonstrate inefficiencies or inaccuracies when tackling complex mathematical operations. While integrating computational tools such as Code Interpreters (CIs) offers a promising solution, it introduces a critical challenge: a conflict between the model's internal, probabilistic reasoning and the external, deterministic knowledge provided by the CI, which often leads models to unproductive deliberation. To overcome this, we introduce CoRT (Code-Optimized Reasoning Training), a post-training framework designed to teach LRMs to effectively utilize CIs. We propose **Hint-Engineering**, a new data synthesis strategy that strategically injects diverse hints at optimal points within reasoning paths. This approach generates high-quality, code-integrated reasoning data specifically tailored to optimize LRM-CI interaction. Using this method, we have synthesized 30 high-quality samples to post-train models ranging from 1.5B to 32B parameters through supervised fine-tuning. CoRT further refines the multi-round interleaving of external CI usage and internal thinking by employing rejection sampling and reinforcement learning. Our experimental evaluations demonstrate CoRT's effectiveness, yielding absolute improvements of 4\% and 8\% on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, respectively, across five challenging mathematical reasoning datasets. Moreover, CoRT significantly enhances efficiency, reducing token usage by approximately 30\% for the 32B model and 50\% for the 1.5B model compared to pure natural language reasoning baselines. The models and code are available at: [this url](https://github.com/ChengpengLi1003/CoRT).

The paper identifies friction between the model's probabilistic internal reasoning and the interpreter's deterministic results, which can lead to unproductive deliberation. CoRT is a post-training framework designed to teach models how to coordinate these two forms of computation.

Its Hint-Engineering strategy inserts varied hints at selected points in reasoning paths to create examples that integrate code use with thinking. title: Teaching Language Models to Reason with Tools

abstract: Vision-language models heavily rely on visual representations, yet ensuring its efficiency remains a critical challenge. Most existing approaches focus on reducing visual tokens either at the visual encoder phase or during the LLM decoder stage. Inspired by human visual cognition, where an initial global glance precedes focused attention on semantically salient regions, we introduce Glance2Gaze, a cognitively inspired framework that mimics the human two-stage attention process. The framework consists of two key components: the Glance Fusion module, which integrates multi-layer vision transformer features with text-aware attention to generate a semantically enriched global representation, and the Gaze Compression module, which utilizes a novel query-guided mechanism to selectively compress visual tokens based on their semantic relevance. Experimental results on widely adopted benchmarks demonstrate that Glance2Gaze outperforms existing methods, achieving superior performance with equal or lower computational cost. Furthermore, it generalizes well to high-resolution and video scenarios, showcasing robust and scalable efficiency improvements in VLMs.

abstract: Our objective is to develop compact video representations that are sensitive to visual change over time. To measure such time-sensitivity, we introduce a new task: chiral action recognition, where one needs to distinguish between a pair of temporally opposite actions, such as “opening vs. closing a door", “approaching vs. moving away from something", “folding vs. unfolding paper", etc. Such actions (i) occur frequently in everyday life, (ii) require understanding of simple visual change over time (in object state, size, spatial position, count . . . ), and (iii) are known to be poorly represented by many video embeddings. Our goal is to build time aware video representations which offer linear separability between these chiral pairs. To that end, we propose a self-supervised adaptation recipe to inject time-sensitivity into a sequence of frozen image features. Our model is based on an auto-encoder with a latent space with inductive bias inspired by perceptual straightening. We show that this results in a compact but time-sensitive video representation for the proposed task across three datasets: Something-Something, EPIC-Kitchens, and Charade. Our method (i) outperforms much larger video models pre-trained on large-scale video datasets, and (ii) leads to an improvement in classification performance on standard benchmarks when combined with these existing models.

The objective is a compact representation in which opposite actions can be separated by a linear classifier, making temporal direction accessible through a simple decision boundary.

Combining it with existing models also improves classification on standard benchmarks. Together, these findings suggest that the learned temporal information complements capabilities already present in those models.
summary.tldr: A self-supervised adaptation method produces compact video representations that distinguish temporally opposite actions and complement existing video models.

title: Chirality in Action: Time-Aware Video Representation Learning by Latent Straightening

abstract: Theoretical works on supervised transfer learning (STL)---where the learner has access to labeled samples from both source and target distributions---have for the most part focused on statistical aspects of the problem, while efficient optimization has received less attention. We consider the problem of designing an SGD procedure for STL that alternates sampling between source and target data, while maintaining statistical transfer guarantees without prior knowledge of the quality of the source data. A main algorithmic difficulty is in understanding how to design such an adaptive sub-sampling mechanism at each SGD step, to automatically gain from the source when it is informative, or bias towards the target and avoid negative transfer when the source is less informative. We show that, such a mixed-sample SGD procedure is feasible for general prediction tasks with convex losses, rooted in tracking an abstract sequence of constrained convex programs that serve to maintain the desired transfer guarantees. We instantiate these results in the concrete setting of linear regression with square loss, and show that the procedure converges, with $1/\sqrt{T}$ rate, to a solution whose statistical performance on the target is adaptive to the a priori unknown quality of the source. Experiments with synthetic and real datasets support the theory.

paragraphs: Supervised transfer learning uses labeled data from a source distribution to help predictions on a target distribution. The source can be useful, but poorly matched source data can also hurt target performance. This paper studies how stochastic gradient descent can adaptively choose between source and target samples without knowing beforehand how helpful the source will be.

The proposed mixed-sample procedure changes its sampling behavior at individual optimization steps. Its theoretical foundation is an abstract sequence of constrained convex programs that preserves the desired statistical transfer guarantees. The authors establish that such a procedure is feasible for general prediction problems with convex losses, connecting efficient optimization to adaptation based on source quality.

For linear regression with squared loss, they provide a concrete instance that converges at a rate of 1/√T. The resulting solution's target statistical performance adapts to the initially unknown usefulness of the source data. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the theory. The contribution is an end-to-end account of how to optimize while gaining from informative source data and avoiding negative transfer from less informative data.
summary.tldr: Mixed-sample SGD adaptively draws source or target data while preserving transfer guarantees without prior knowledge of source quality.

title: Mixed-Sample SGD: an End-to-end Analysis of Supervised Transfer Learning

abstract: We present $\textbf{FlowRL}$, a novel framework for online reinforcement learning that integrates flow-based policy representation with Wasserstein-2-regularized optimization. We argue that in addition to training signals, enhancing the expressiveness of the policy class is crucial for the performance gains in RL. Flow-based generative models offer such potential, excelling at capturing complex, multimodal action distributions. However, their direct application in online RL is challenging due to a fundamental objective mismatch: standard flow training optimizes for static data imitation, while RL requires value-based policy optimization through a dynamic buffer, leading to difficult optimization landscapes. FlowRL first models policies via a state-dependent velocity field, generating actions through deterministic ODE integration from noise. We derive a constrained policy search objective that jointly maximizes Q through the flow polciy while bounding the Wasserstein-2 distance to a behavior-optimal policy implicitly derived from the replay buffer. This formulation effectively aligns the flow optimization with the RL objective, enabling efficient and value-aware policy learning despite the complexity of the policy class. Empirical evaluations on DMControl and Humanoidbench demonstrate that FlowRL achieves competitive performance in online reinforcement learning benchmarks.

paragraphs: A reinforcement-learning policy may need to represent several very different useful actions in the same situation. Flow-based generative models can express such complex action distributions, but their usual training objective imitates a fixed dataset. Online reinforcement learning instead needs to improve actions according to estimated value while its experience buffer keeps changing.

FlowRL addresses this mismatch by representing a policy as a state-dependent velocity field. Starting from noise, it generates an action through deterministic integration of an ordinary differential equation. Its policy-search objective raises estimated action value while constraining the Wasserstein-2 distance from a behavior-optimal policy implicitly obtained from the replay buffer. The distance constraint links improvement to the available experience.

This formulation connects the expressive flow model directly to the reinforcement-learning objective, rather than relying only on imitation-oriented training. Evaluations on DMControl and Humanoidbench show competitive online learning performance. The findings support flow-based policies as a practical option when paired with an optimization objective designed for value improvement and a changing experience distribution.
summary.tldr: FlowRL combines expressive flow-based action generation with constrained value optimization for competitive online reinforcement learning.

title: Flow-Based Policy for Online Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We introduce a comprehensive framework for modeling single cell transcriptomic responses to perturbations, aimed at standardizing benchmarking in this rapidly evolving field. Our approach includes a modular and user-friendly model development and evaluation platform, a collection of diverse perturbational datasets, and a set of metrics designed to fairly compare models and dissect their performance. Through extensive evaluation of both published and baseline models across diverse datasets, we highlight the limitations of widely used models, such as mode collapse. We also demonstrate the importance of rank metrics which complement traditional model fit measures, such as RMSE, for validating model effectiveness. Notably, our results show that while no single model architecture clearly outperforms others, simpler architectures are generally competitive and scale well with larger datasets. Overall, this benchmarking exercise sets new standards for model evaluation, supports robust model development, and furthers the use of these models to simulate genetic and chemical screens for therapeutic discovery.

paragraphs: Models of cellular perturbations aim to predict how single-cell gene-expression profiles respond to changes. PerturBench provides a common framework for developing and comparing these models. It combines a modular evaluation platform, varied perturbation datasets, and metrics intended to reveal different aspects of predictive performance.

The evaluation identifies limitations in widely used models, including mode collapse, where predictions fail to preserve the diversity of responses. It also shows why rank-based metrics matter alongside fit measures such as root mean square error. Evaluating how predictions are ordered supplies complementary evidence about model effectiveness that an overall numerical fit score does not provide alone.

Across the tested datasets and models, no architecture clearly dominates. Simpler architectures are generally competitive and scale well as datasets become larger. These results make evaluation design and straightforward baselines central to assessing progress. The framework is intended to support more reliable model development and the eventual use of predicted cellular responses to simulate genetic and chemical screens for therapeutic discovery.
summary.tldr: PerturBench standardizes cellular-perturbation evaluation and finds competitive simple models, important metric differences, and failures such as mode collapse.

title: PerturBench: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Cellular Perturbation Analysis

abstract: While large transformer models excel in predictive performance, their lack of interpretability restricts their usefulness in high-stakes domains. To remedy this, we propose the Generalized Induction-Head Model (GIM), an interpretable model for next-token prediction inspired by the observation of “induction heads” in LLMs. GIM is a retrieval-based module that identifies similar sequences in the input context by combining exact n-gram matching and fuzzy matching based on a neural similarity metric. We evaluate GIM in two settings: language modeling and fMRI response prediction. In language modeling, GIM improves next-token prediction by up to 25%p over interpretable baselines, significantly narrowing the gap with black-box LLMs. In an fMRI setting, GIM improves neural response prediction by 20% and offers insights into the language selectivity of the brain. GIM represents a significant step toward uniting interpretability and performance across domains. The code is available at https://github.com/ejkim47/generalized-induction-head.

paragraphs: Accurate predictions are harder to trust in high-stakes settings when the model's reasoning is opaque. This paper proposes the Generalized Induction-Head Model, or GIM, as an interpretable approach to next-token prediction. It takes inspiration from induction heads observed in language models and builds prediction around retrieving similar sequences from the available context.

GIM combines two ways of finding those sequences. Exact matching recognizes repeated groups of tokens, while a learned neural similarity measure supports fuzzy matches when sequences are related without being identical. This combination broadens the material the retrieval module can use while keeping similar contextual sequences central to the prediction process.

The authors evaluate GIM in language modeling and prediction of fMRI responses. For language modeling, they report improvements of up to 25 percentage points over interpretable baselines, narrowing the gap with black-box language models. In the fMRI setting, they report a 20% improvement in response prediction and insights into the brain's language selectivity. These results support retrieval-based modeling as a route toward combining predictive performance with interpretability across the two settings.
summary.tldr: GIM combines exact and learned sequence matching to improve interpretable language prediction and fMRI response prediction.

title: Interpretable Next-token Prediction via the Generalized Induction Head

abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have emerged as foundational tools for real-world AI applications. Despite their remarkable capabilities, current LVLMs process entire images at the token level, leading to significant inefficiencies compared to human cognition, which selectively focuses on high-level vision concepts. This token-level redundancy becomes increasingly problematic for high-resolution images and long video sequences, resulting in large computational costs and limited scalability in practical applications. To address this limitation, we introduce the concept of a vision concept model, a novel paradigm that enables LVLMs to dynamically extract the most relevant vision concepts from complex inputs, based on task-specific instructions. To optimize this vision concept modeling process, we propose VCM, a self-supervised framework that leverages vision-language correlations across diverse instances. VCM is designed to learn meaningful vision concepts without the need for expensive concept-level annotations. At its core, it employs a forward-backward optimization algorithm that supports LVLMs to adjust concept granularity and spatial alignment dynamically. Experiments demonstrate that VCM remarkably reduces computational costs (e.g., achieving up to 85\% fewer FLOPs for LLaVA-1.5-7B), while maintaining strong performance across a series of vision-language tasks. The codebase is available at https://github.com/RainBowLuoCS/VCM.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can spend substantial computation processing image tokens that are redundant for a particular task. This becomes especially costly with high-resolution images and long videos. VCM introduces vision concept modeling, in which the model extracts relevant visual concepts according to the instruction it receives.

The framework learns from correlations between vision and language across different instances, without requiring expensive annotations of individual concepts. A forward-backward optimization algorithm lets the model adjust both the granularity of its concepts and their spatial alignment. The intended effect is an adaptive representation whose detail and organization reflect the task being requested.

Experiments report substantial computational savings while maintaining strong performance across several vision-language tasks. For LLaVA-1.5-7B, the reduction reaches up to 85% fewer floating-point operations. The findings support instruction-dependent concept extraction as a way to reduce visual processing costs. The contribution combines compression with learned semantic organization, so the model can vary which visual information it emphasizes instead of processing every input with the same token-level workload.
summary.tldr: VCM learns instruction-relevant visual concepts, reducing computation by up to 85% for LLaVA-1.5-7B while maintaining strong task performance.

title: VCM: Vision Concept Modeling with Adaptive Vision Token Compression via Instruction Fine-Tuning

abstract: Due to the difficulty in collecting all unexpected abnormal patterns, One-Class Classification (OCC) has become the most popular approach to anomaly detection (AD). Reconstruction-based AD method relies on the discrepancy between inputs and reconstructed results to identify unobserved anomalies. However, recent methods trained only on normal samples may generalize to certain abnormal inputs, leading to well-reconstructed anomalies and degraded performance. To address this, we constrain reconstructions to remain on the normal manifold using a novel AD framework based on contraction mapping. This mapping guarantees that any input converges to a fixed point through iterations of this mapping. Based on this property, training the contraction mapping using only normal data ensures that its fixed point lies within the normal manifold. As a result, abnormal inputs are iteratively transformed toward the normal manifold, increasing the reconstruction error. In addition, the inherent invertibility of contraction mapping enables flow-based density estimation, where a prior distribution learned from the previous reconstruction is used to estimate the input likelihood for anomaly detection, further improving the performance. Using both mechanisms, we propose a bidirectional structure with forward reconstruction and backward density estimation. Extensive experiments on tabular data, natural image, and industrial image data demonstrate the effectiveness of our method. The code is available at URD.

The paper proposes a framework that directs reconstructions toward the normal-data manifold, the region representing normal samples, so abnormal inputs become less faithfully reconstructed.

The approach uses a contraction mapping whose repeated application converges to a fixed point. The authors use normal-only training to place that fixed point within the normal manifold. summary.tldr: The framework combines contraction-guided reconstruction and density estimation to detect anomalies using training data containing only normal examples.

title: Unifying Reconstruction and Density Estimation via Invertible Contraction Mapping in One-Class Classification

abstract: Hybrid Optical Neural Networks (ONNs, typically consisting of an optical frontend and a digital backend) offer an energy-efficient alternative to fully digital deep networks for real-time, power-constrained systems. However, their adoption is limited by two main challenges: the accuracy gap compared to large-scale networks during training, and discrepancies between simulated and fabricated systems that further degrade accuracy. While previous work has proposed end-to-end optimizations for specific datasets (e.g., MNIST) and optical systems, these approaches typically lack generalization across tasks and hardware designs. To address these limitations, we propose a task-agnostic and hardware-agnostic pipeline that supports image classification and segmentation across diverse optical systems. To assist optical system design before training, we design the metasurface layout based on fabrication constraints. For training, we introduce Neural Tangent Knowledge Distillation (NTKD), which aligns optical models with electronic teacher networks, thereby narrowing the accuracy gap. After fabrication, NTKD also guides fine-tuning of the digital backend to compensate for implementation errors. Experiments on multiple datasets (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR, Carvana Masking) and hardware configurations show that our pipeline consistently improves ONN performance and enables practical deployment in both pre-fabrication simulations and physical implementations.

Results cover both simulations before fabrication and physical implementations. The practical contribution is a connected workflow that transfers teacher knowledge while addressing the mismatch between an optical design and its realized behavior.
summary.tldr: Neural Tangent Knowledge Distillation improves optical networks during training and guides digital correction after hardware fabrication.

title: Neural Tangent Knowledge Distillation for Optical Convolutional Networks

abstract: The famous theorem of Fritz John states that any convex body has a unique maximal volume inscribed ellipsoid, known as the John Ellipsoid. Computing the John Ellipsoid is a fundamental problem in convex optimization. In this paper, we focus on approximating the John Ellipsoid inscribed in a convex and centrally symmetric polytope defined by $P := \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^d : -\mathbf{1}_n \leq A x \leq \mathbf{1}_n \},$ where $ A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ is a rank-$d$ matrix and $ \mathbf{1}_n \in \mathbb{R}^n $ is the all-ones vector. We develop two efficient algorithms for approximating the John Ellipsoid. The first is a sketching-based algorithm that runs in nearly input-sparsity time $ \widetilde{O}(\mathrm{nnz}(A) + d^\omega) $, where $ \mathrm{nnz}(A) $ denotes the number of nonzero entries in the matrix $A$ and $ \omega \approx 2.37$ is the current matrix multiplication exponent. The second is a treewidth-based algorithm that runs in time $ \widetilde{O}(n \tau^2)$, where $\tau$ is the treewidth of the dual graph of the matrix $A$. Our algorithms significantly improve upon the state-of-the-art running time of $ \widetilde{O}(n d^2) $ achieved by [Cohen, Cousins, Lee, and Yang, COLT 2019].

paragraphs: The John ellipsoid is the largest-volume ellipsoid that fits inside a convex body. This paper develops faster ways to approximate it for a particular class of bodies: centrally symmetric polytopes described by linear inequalities of the form −1 ≤ Ax ≤ 1. The matrix A has n rows, d columns, and full column rank, defining the setting for the algorithms.

The first algorithm uses sketching and has running time approximately proportional to the number of nonzero entries in A plus d raised to the matrix multiplication exponent, with logarithmic factors suppressed. This connects much of the computation to the amount of matrix data actually present. The second algorithm uses the treewidth of A’s dual graph and runs in roughly n times the square of that treewidth, again suppressing logarithmic factors.

The previous stated running time scales as n times d squared. The new bounds therefore expose benefits from sparsity and graph structure in this optimization problem. Both algorithms approximate the ellipsoid, and their guarantees concern the specified symmetric polytopes rather than arbitrary convex-body representations.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms accelerate John ellipsoid approximation by exploiting matrix sparsity or the treewidth of an associated graph.

title: Faster Algorithms for Structured John Ellipsoid Computation

abstract: This paper investigates nonparametric quantile regression using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and sparse recurrent neural networks (SRNNs) to approximate the conditional quantile function, which is assumed to follow a compositional hierarchical interaction model. We show that RNN- and SRNN-based estimators with rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation and appropriately designed architectures achieve the optimal nonparametric convergence rate, up to a logarithmic factor, under stationary, exponentially $\boldsymbol{\beta}$-mixing processes. To establish this result, we derive sharp approximation error bounds for functions in the hierarchical interaction model using RNNs and SRNNs, exploiting their close connection to sparse feedforward neural networks (SFNNs). Numerical experiments and an empirical study on the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJIA) further support our theoretical findings.

paragraphs: This paper studies recurrent networks for estimating conditional quantiles, which describe different positions within an outcome distribution given the available information. It considers both ordinary and sparse recurrent neural networks with ReLU activations. The central question is how accurately these models can estimate a structured quantile function from dependent observations.

The theoretical result relies on specific assumptions. The conditional quantile function follows a compositional hierarchical interaction model, and the observations come from a stationary process with exponentially decaying beta-mixing dependence. Under these conditions and appropriately chosen architectures, the estimators achieve the optimal nonparametric convergence rate up to a logarithmic factor.

To establish that rate, the authors derive sharp bounds on how well the recurrent architectures approximate functions in the assumed class. Their analysis uses connections to sparse feedforward networks. Numerical experiments and a study of the Dow Jones Industrial Average support the theoretical findings. The contribution is a conditional statistical guarantee linking recurrent architecture design, function structure, and dependence in sequential data.
summary.tldr: Properly designed ReLU recurrent networks attain near-optimal quantile-estimation rates under stated structural and time-dependence assumptions.

title: Nonparametric Quantile Regression with ReLU-Activated Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Spiking Transformers have recently emerged as promising architectures for combining the efficiency of spiking neural networks with the representational power of self-attention. However, the lack of standardized implementations, evaluation pipelines, and consistent design choices has hindered fair comparison and principled analysis. In this paper, we introduce \textbf{STEP}, a unified benchmark framework for Spiking Transformers that supports a wide range of tasks, including classification, segmentation, and detection across static, event-based, and sequential datasets. STEP provides modular support for diverse components such as spiking neurons, input encodings, surrogate gradients, and multiple backends (e.g., SpikingJelly, BrainCog). Using STEP, we reproduce and evaluate several representative models, and conduct systematic ablation studies on attention design, neuron types, encoding schemes, and temporal modeling capabilities. We also propose a unified analytical model for energy estimation, accounting for spike sparsity, bitwidth, and memory access, and show that quantized ANNs may offer comparable or better energy efficiency. Our results suggest that current Spiking Transformers rely heavily on convolutional frontends and lack strong temporal modeling, underscoring the need for spike-native architectural innovations. The full code is available at: https://github.com/Fancyssc/STEP.

paragraphs: Spiking Transformers aim to combine efficient spike-based computation with self-attention's representational power. Comparing these models is difficult when implementations, evaluation procedures, and design choices differ. STEP provides a shared framework intended to make those comparisons fairer and the resulting findings easier to reproduce.

The platform supports classification, segmentation, and detection on static, event-based, and sequential data. Its modular components include neuron types, input encodings, surrogate gradients, and multiple software backends. The authors reproduce representative models and systematically vary attention designs, neurons, encodings, and temporal modeling components to examine what contributes to performance.

STEP also introduces an analytical energy model that accounts for spike sparsity, numerical bitwidth, and memory access. Under this analysis, quantized conventional neural networks may match or exceed spiking models' energy efficiency. The experiments further suggest that current Spiking Transformers depend heavily on convolutional frontends and have weak temporal modeling. These findings motivate architectures designed more directly around spike-based computation, while qualifying broad assumptions about existing models' efficiency.
summary.tldr: STEP standardizes Spiking Transformer evaluation and finds that current designs may offer limited temporal modeling and no clear energy advantage over quantized networks.

title: STEP: A Unified Spiking Transformer Evaluation Platform for Fair and Reproducible Benchmarking

abstract: We tackle the challenge of LiDAR-based place recognition, which traditionally depends on costly and time-consuming prior 3D maps. To overcome this, we first construct LiRSI-XA dataset, which encompasses approximately $110,000$ remote sensing submaps and $13,000$ LiDAR point cloud submaps captured in urban scenes, and propose a novel method, L2RSI, for cross-view LiDAR place recognition using high-resolution Remote Sensing Imagery. This approach enables large-scale localization capabilities at a reduced cost by leveraging readily available overhead images as map proxies. L2RSI addresses the dual challenges of cross-view and cross-modal place recognition by learning feature alignment between point cloud submaps and remote sensing submaps in the semantic domain. Additionally, we introduce a novel probability propagation method based on particle estimation to refine position predictions, effectively leveraging temporal and spatial information. This approach enables large-scale retrieval and cross-scene generalization without fine-tuning. Extensive experiments on LiRSI-XA demonstrate that, within a $100km^2$ retrieval range, L2RSI accurately localizes $83.27\%$ of point cloud submaps within a $30m$ radius for top-$1$ retrieved location. Our project page is publicly available at https://shizw695.github.io/L2RSI/.

paragraphs: LiDAR-based place recognition typically compares a current point cloud with a previously collected three-dimensional map. Building that map can be costly and slow. L2RSI instead uses high-resolution overhead imagery as a map proxy, aiming to locate LiDAR observations across large urban areas with less prior mapping effort.

The challenge is to match information that differs in both viewing direction and sensing modality. L2RSI learns to align point-cloud submaps and remote-sensing submaps through semantic features. It then refines location predictions using a particle-estimation-based probability propagation method that incorporates spatial and temporal information. The authors also introduce LiRSI-XA, containing approximately 110,000 remote-sensing submaps and 13,000 LiDAR point-cloud submaps.

On this dataset, the top-ranked retrieved location falls within 30 meters of the correct position for 83.27% of point-cloud submaps across a 100-square-kilometer search area. The authors also report cross-scene generalization without fine-tuning. These findings support overhead imagery as a practical reference for large-area LiDAR localization, with semantic alignment bridging the sensing differences and probability propagation refining predictions across space and time.
summary.tldr: L2RSI locates urban LiDAR scans using overhead imagery, combining semantic alignment with spatial and temporal prediction refinement.

title: L2RSI: Cross-view LiDAR-based Place Recognition for Large-scale Urban Scenes via Remote Sensing Imagery

abstract: The task of a neural associative memory is to retrieve a set of previously memorized patterns from their noisy versions by using a network of neurons. Hence, an ideal network should be able to 1) gradually learn a set of patterns, 2) retrieve the correct pattern from noisy queries and 3) maximize the number of memorized patterns while maintaining the reliability in responding to queries. We show that by considering the inherent redundancy in the memorized patterns, one can obtain all the mentioned properties at once. This is in sharp contrast with the previous work that could only improve one or two aspects at the expense of the third. More specifically, we devise an iterative algorithm that learns the redundancy among the patterns. The resulting network has a retrieval capacity that is exponential in the size of the network. Lastly, by considering the local structures of the network, the asymptotic error correction performance can be made linear in the size of the network.

paragraphs: A neural associative memory should recover a stored pattern when presented with a corrupted version. It also needs to learn patterns gradually and store many of them without losing retrieval reliability. This paper studies how these three objectives can be achieved together by exploiting redundancy already present in the patterns.

The authors develop an iterative learning algorithm that discovers that redundancy. In their construction, the resulting network has retrieval capacity exponential in network size. The role of redundancy is central: the stated capacity result arises from using structure in the memorized patterns, rather than treating every possible collection of patterns as equally suitable.

The paper also uses local network structure to obtain asymptotic error-correction performance that can scale linearly with network size. Together, these results address storage, incremental learning, and recovery from noise within one framework. The contribution is a way to use shared structure among patterns to avoid the tradeoffs that the authors identify in earlier approaches.
summary.tldr: Learning redundancy among stored patterns enables associative memories with exponential retrieval capacity and potentially linear-scaling error correction.

title: Iterative Learning and Denoising in Convolutional Neural Associative Memories

abstract: We extend kernelized matrix factorization with a fully Bayesian treatment and with an ability to work with multiple side information sources expressed as different kernels. Kernel functions have been introduced to matrix factorization to integrate side information about the rows and columns (e.g., objects and users in recommender systems), which is necessary for making out-of-matrix (i.e., cold start) predictions. We discuss specifically bipartite graph inference, where the output matrix is binary, but extensions to more general matrices are straightforward. We extend the state of the art in two key aspects: (i) A fully conjugate probabilistic formulation of the kernelized matrix factorization problem enables an efficient variational approximation, whereas fully Bayesian treatments are not computationally feasible in the earlier approaches. (ii) Multiple side information sources are included, treated as different kernels in multiple kernel learning that additionally reveals which side information sources are informative. Our method outperforms alternatives in predicting drug-protein interactions on two data sets. We then show that our framework can also be used for solving multilabel learning problems by considering samples and labels as the two domains where matrix factorization operates on. Our algorithm obtains the lowest Hamming loss values on 10 out of 14 multilabel classification data sets compared to five state-of-the-art multilabel learning algorithms.
