paragraphs: Kernelized matrix factorization uses information about a matrix's rows and columns to support prediction, including cold-start cases outside the observed matrix. This paper extends the approach with a fully Bayesian formulation and multiple sources of side information. Its main setting is binary relationship prediction between two domains, such as drugs and proteins.

A fully conjugate probabilistic construction makes efficient variational approximation possible. Multiple kernels represent different sources of side information, and the learning procedure also indicates which sources are informative. These two extensions connect uncertainty-aware modeling with the practical need to combine heterogeneous information about both sides of a relationship.

The method outperforms alternatives on two drug–protein interaction datasets. The authors also apply it to multilabel learning by treating samples and labels as the two matrix domains. Against five leading multilabel algorithms, it achieves the lowest Hamming loss on 10 of 14 datasets. These findings support the framework across both relationship prediction and multilabel classification.
summary.tldr: A fully Bayesian matrix factorization model combines multiple side-information kernels and performs strongly on drug–protein prediction and multilabel learning.

title: Kernelized Bayesian Matrix Factorization

abstract: Probabilistic inference on a big data scale is becoming increasingly relevant to both the machine learning and statistics communities. Here we introduce the first fully distributed MCMC algorithm based on stochastic gradients. We argue that stochastic gradient MCMC algorithms are particularly suited for distributed inference because individual chains can draw minibatches from their local pool of data for a flexible amount of time before jumping to or syncing with other chains. This greatly reduces communication overhead and allows adaptive load balancing. Our experiments for LDA on Wikipedia and Pubmed show that relative to the state of the art in distributed MCMC we reduce compute time from 27 hours to half an hour in order to reach the same perplexity level.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a fully distributed Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm based on stochastic gradients for large-scale probabilistic inference. The central challenge is to spread sampling work across machines while keeping communication from dominating the computation. The authors argue that stochastic gradient sampling is especially compatible with this goal.

Each chain can draw minibatches from its local data for a flexible period before moving to, or synchronizing with, other chains. This flexibility reduces the need for frequent communication and allows adaptive load balancing. Local work and coordination can therefore be arranged around the distributed computation rather than requiring continuous interaction between chains.

Experiments apply the method to latent Dirichlet allocation on Wikipedia and Pubmed. Relative to the state of the art in distributed MCMC used for comparison, the authors report reducing computation from 27 hours to half an hour to reach the same perplexity. This is an empirical result for the evaluated inference tasks and comparison.
summary.tldr: Distributed stochastic gradient MCMC reduces communication through flexible local sampling, reaching the same perplexity much faster in the reported LDA experiments.

title: Distributed Stochastic Gradient MCMC

abstract: Policy gradient algorithms have shown considerable recent success in solving high-dimensional sequential decision making tasks, particularly in robotics. However, these methods often require extensive experience in a domain to achieve high performance. To make agents more sample-efficient, we developed a multi-task policy gradient method to learn decision making tasks consecutively, transferring knowledge between tasks to accelerate learning. Our approach provides robust theoretical guarantees, and we show empirically that it dramatically accelerates learning on a variety of dynamical systems, including an application to quadrotor control.

paragraphs: Policy gradient methods learn how to choose actions in sequential decision problems, including high-dimensional robotics tasks. Their practical burden is often the amount of experience required to reach strong performance. This paper addresses that sample-efficiency problem by allowing knowledge gained across tasks to contribute to learning.

The authors develop a multi-task policy gradient method for tasks encountered consecutively. As the agent learns one decision-making task after another, the method transfers knowledge between them to accelerate learning. The online organization makes the sequence of tasks part of the learning process, giving earlier experience a role in the broader training procedure.

The approach comes with theoretical guarantees, and experiments show dramatic learning acceleration across a variety of dynamical systems, including quadrotor control. These findings support knowledge transfer as a way to reduce the experience burden of policy gradient learning in the evaluated settings. The contribution combines sequential multi-task learning with policy optimization, linking a familiar control-learning method to a mechanism for reusing knowledge.
summary.tldr: An online multi-task policy gradient method transfers knowledge across consecutive tasks and substantially accelerates learning in the reported dynamical-system experiments.

title: Online Multi-Task Learning for Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: We study the problem of clustering sensitive data while preserving the privacy of individuals represented in the dataset, which has broad applications in practical machine learning and data analysis tasks. Although the problem has been widely studied in the context of low-dimensional, discrete spaces, much remains unknown concerning private clustering in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{R}^d$. In this work, we give differentially private and efficient algorithms achieving strong guarantees for $k$-means and $k$-median clustering when $d=\Omega(\mathsf{polylog}(n))$. Our algorithm achieves clustering loss at most $\log^3(n)\mathsf{OPT}+\mathsf{poly}(\log n,d,k)$, advancing the state-of-the-art result of $\sqrt{d}\mathsf{OPT}+\mathsf{poly}(\log n,d^d,k^d)$. We also study the case where the data points are $s$-sparse and show that the clustering loss can scale logarithmically with $d$, i.e., $\log^3(n)\mathsf{OPT}+\mathsf{poly}(\log n,\log d,k,s)$. Experiments on both synthetic and real datasets verify the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Clustering sensitive records requires balancing useful groupings with protection for the individuals represented in the data. This paper studies that problem in high-dimensional Euclidean spaces, where private clustering was less understood than in low-dimensional discrete settings. It develops efficient, differentially private algorithms for both k-means and k-median.

For dimensions at least on the order of a polylogarithmic function of the number of records, the algorithms provide improved clustering-loss guarantees. Their bound combines the optimal loss multiplied by log cubed of the dataset size with an additive term polynomial in the logarithm of that size, the dimension, and the number of clusters. The previous bound described in the abstract had a square-root dimension multiplier and an additive term involving dimension-dependent powers.

The authors also consider sparse records, where each point has only a limited number of nonzero coordinates. In that case, the additive bound depends polynomially on log dimension and sparsity. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the method’s effectiveness, complementing the theoretical improvements.
summary.tldr: Efficient private clustering algorithms improve high-dimensional loss guarantees, with further dimension savings for sparse data.

title: Differentially Private Clustering in High-Dimensional Euclidean Spaces

abstract: Recently low displacement rank (LDR) matrices, or so-called structured matrices, have been proposed to compress large-scale neural networks. Empirical results have shown that neural networks with weight matrices of LDR matrices, referred as LDR neural networks, can achieve significant reduction in space and computational complexity while retaining high accuracy. This paper gives theoretical study on LDR neural networks. First, we prove the universal approximation property of LDR neural networks with a mild condition on the displacement operators. We then show that the error bounds of LDR neural networks are as efficient as general neural networks with both single-layer and multiple-layer structure. Finally, we propose back-propagation based training algorithm for general LDR neural networks.

This paper gives theoretical study on LDR neural networks. First, we prove the universal approximation property of LDR neural networks with a mild condition on the displacement operators. paragraphs: Low-displacement-rank matrices provide structured representations of neural-network weights. Prior empirical results cited in the abstract show that these networks can reduce storage and computation substantially while retaining high accuracy. This paper investigates the theoretical capabilities of such networks, addressing what their constrained weight structure still allows them to represent.

The authors prove a universal approximation property under a mild condition on the displacement operators that define the structure. They also show that error bounds for low-displacement-rank networks are as efficient as those for general neural networks, covering both single-layer and multiple-layer structures. These results give mathematical support to the expressive capacity of the compressed models.

The paper additionally proposes a backpropagation-based training algorithm for general low-displacement-rank networks. Together, the results address representation, approximation error, and training. The universal approximation claim remains conditional on the stated operator requirement. Its significance is that structured weight matrices can preserve strong theoretical approximation properties, complementing the earlier empirical motivation for using them to reduce network resource demands.
summary.tldr: Low-displacement-rank networks retain strong approximation guarantees under a mild operator condition, and the paper supplies a general training algorithm.

title: Theoretical Properties for Neural Networks with Weight Matrices of Low Displacement Rank

abstract: This paper develops a Riemannian optimization framework for solving optimization problems on the set of symmetric positive semidefinite stochastic matrices. The paper first reformulates the problem by factorizing the optimization variable as $\mathbf{X}=\mathbf{Y}\mathbf{Y}^T$ and deriving conditions on $p$, i.e., the number of columns of $\mathbf{Y}$, under which the factorization yields a satisfactory solution. The reparameterization of the problem allows its formulation as an optimization over either an embedded or quotient Riemannian manifold whose geometries are investigated. In particular, the paper explicitly derives the tangent space, Riemannian gradients and retraction operator that allow the design of efficient optimization methods on the proposed manifolds. The numerical results reveal that, when the optimal solution has a known low-rank, the resulting algorithms present a clear complexity advantage when compared with state-of-the-art Euclidean and Riemannian approaches for graph clustering applications.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization over matrices that must simultaneously be symmetric, positive semidefinite, and stochastic. These combined requirements create a structured feasible set. The authors develop a Riemannian optimization framework that uses the geometry of that set to formulate and solve the problem.

They replace the matrix variable X with a factorization YYᵀ and derive conditions on the number of columns of Y under which this representation produces a satisfactory solution. The resulting problem can be expressed on either an embedded or a quotient Riemannian manifold. The paper works out tangent spaces, Riemannian gradients, and a retraction operator, providing the ingredients needed to construct optimization algorithms.

Numerical results in graph clustering show a clear complexity advantage over compared Euclidean and Riemannian methods when the optimal solution has a known low rank. That qualification is central to the reported benefit: the factorization exploits the solution's low-rank structure. The contribution combines conditions on the representation with explicit geometric tools and evidence of computational advantages in that setting.
summary.tldr: A matrix-factorization and Riemannian framework offers computational advantages for graph clustering when the optimal solution has a known low rank.

title: Low-Rank Riemannian Optimization on Positive Semidefinite Stochastic Matrices with Applications to Graph Clustering

abstract: This is a theoretical study on the sample complexity of dictionary learning with a general type of reconstruction loss. The goal is to estimate a $m \times d$ matrix $D$ of unit-norm columns when the only available information is a set of training samples. Points $x$ in $\mathbb{R}^m$ are subsequently approximated by the linear combination $Da$ after solving the problem $\min_{a \in \mathbb{R}^d} \Phi(x - Da) + g(a)$; function $g:\mathbb{R}^d \to [0,+\infty)$ is either an indicator function or a sparsity promoting regularizer. Here is considered the case where $ \Phi(x) = \inf_{z \in \mathbb{R}^m} { ||x-z||_2^2 + h(||z||_2)}$ and $h$ is an even and univariate function on the real line. Connections are drawn between $\Phi$ and the Moreau envelope of $h$. A new sample complexity result concerning the $k$-sparse dictionary problem removes the spurious condition on the coherence of $D$ appearing in previous works. Finally, comments are made on the approximation error of certain families of losses. The derived generalization bounds are of order $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log n /n})$ and valid without any further restrictions on the set of dictionaries with unit-norm columns.

Finally, comments are made on the approximation error of certain families of losses. The derived generalization bounds are of order $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log n /n})$ and valid without any further restrictions on the set of dictionaries with unit-norm columns.

paragraphs: Dictionary learning represents a data point as a linear combination of learned dictionary columns. This paper studies how many training samples are needed for such representations to generalize, using dictionaries whose columns have unit norm. Coefficients are selected through a reconstruction objective that also imposes a constraint or encourages sparsity.

The analysis covers a family of reconstruction losses formed by minimizing a squared-distance term plus a radial penalty defined through an even univariate function. The authors connect this construction to Moreau envelopes. This gives a mathematical basis for studying dictionary learning with the specified loss family rather than only one reconstruction loss.

For the k-sparse dictionary problem, a new sample-complexity result removes a coherence condition imposed in earlier work. The derived generalization bounds scale as O(√(log n / n)) and require no additional restrictions on the class of dictionaries with unit-norm columns. The paper also discusses approximation error for certain loss families, connecting the choice of reconstruction loss with the theoretical analysis of learning.
summary.tldr: The paper derives generalization bounds for a family of dictionary-learning losses and removes a previous coherence restriction for sparse dictionaries.

title: The Generalization Error of Dictionary Learning with Moreau Envelopes

abstract: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is one of the most widely used recurrent structures in sequence modeling. It aims to use gates to control information flow (e.g., whether to skip some information or not) in the recurrent computations, although its practical implementation based on soft gates only partially achieves this goal. In this paper, we propose a new way for LSTM training, which pushes the output values of the gates towards 0 or 1. By doing so, we can better control the information flow: the gates are mostly open or closed, instead of in a middle state, which makes the results more interpretable. Empirical studies show that (1) Although it seems that we restrict the model capacity, there is no performance drop: we achieve better or comparable performances due to its better generalization ability; (2) The outputs of gates are not sensitive to their inputs: we can easily compress the LSTM unit in multiple ways, e.g., low-rank approximation and low-precision approximation. The compressed models are even better than the baseline models without compression.
originalAbstract: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is one of the most widely used recurrent structures in sequence modeling. It aims to use gates to control information flow (e.g., whether to skip some information or not) in the recurrent computations, although its practical implementation based on soft gates only partially achieves this goal. In this paper, we propose a new way for LSTM training, which pushes the output values of the gates towards 0 or 1. By doing so, we can better control the information flow: the gates are mostly open or closed, instead of in a middle state, which makes the results more interpretable. Empirical studies show that (1) Although it seems that we restrict the model capacity, there is no performance drop: we achieve better or comparable performances due to its better generalization ability; (2) The outputs of gates are not sensitive to their inputs: we can easily compress the LSTM unit in multiple ways, e.g., low-rank approximation and low-precision approximation. The compressed models are even better than the baseline models without compression.

paragraphs: LSTM networks use gates to regulate information flow during sequence processing. In standard implementations, those gates can remain partially open. This paper proposes training that pushes their outputs toward zero or one, making them mostly closed or open and giving their behavior a clearer interpretation.

The change might appear to reduce the model’s flexibility, but the empirical studies report comparable or better performance with no performance drop. The authors attribute this behavior to better generalization. The result supports the possibility that encouraging more decisive gating can improve how a model uses its capacity, rather than requiring intermediate gate values everywhere.

The experiments also find that gate outputs are relatively insensitive to their inputs, enabling several forms of compression. The paper explores low-rank and low-precision approximations, and the compressed models outperform the uncompressed baselines in the reported studies. The findings therefore connect a training change aimed at information flow with both interpretability and empirical robustness to compression; the gates are encouraged toward binary values rather than claimed to be universally exact binary switches.
summary.tldr: Training LSTM gates toward zero or one yields clearer gating and supports compression while maintaining or improving reported performance.

title: Towards Binary-Valued Gates for Robust LSTM Training

abstract: Many recent successful (deep) reinforcement learning algorithms make use of regularization, generally based on entropy or Kullback-Leibler divergence. We propose a general theory of regularized Markov Decision Processes that generalizes these approaches in two directions: we consider a larger class of regularizers, and we consider the general modified policy iteration approach, encompassing both policy iteration and value iteration. The core building blocks of this theory are a notion of regularized Bellman operator and the Legendre-Fenchel transform, a classical tool of convex optimization. This approach allows for error propagation analyses of general algorithmic schemes of which (possibly variants of) classical algorithms such as Trust Region Policy Optimization, Soft Q-learning, Stochastic Actor Critic or Dynamic Policy Programming are special cases. This also draws connections to proximal convex optimization, especially to Mirror Descent.

Entropy and Kullback–Leibler divergence are common choices, but studying each algorithm separately can obscure their shared structure. This paper develops a general theory of regularized Markov decision processes that brings a wider range of these choices into one framework.

The theory also covers modified policy iteration, an approach broad enough to include both policy iteration and value iteration. Its central tools are a regularized Bellman operator and the Legendre–Fenchel transform from convex optimization. Together, these provide a way to describe regularized updates and analyze how errors propagate through repeated learning steps.

The framework encompasses general algorithmic schemes that include, sometimes through variants, Trust Region Policy Optimization, Soft Q-learning, Stochastic Actor Critic, and Dynamic Policy Programming. It also connects these reinforcement learning methods with proximal optimization, particularly Mirror Descent. The contribution is a common analytical foundation for understanding related algorithms and their error behavior.
summary.tldr: A general theory connects regularized reinforcement learning algorithms and enables analysis of how their errors propagate.

title: A Theory of Regularized Markov Decision Processes

abstract: Configurable Markov Decision Processes (Conf-MDPs) have been recently introduced as an extension of the usual MDP model to account for the possibility of configuring the environment to improve the agent’s performance. Currently, there is still no suitable algorithm to solve the learning problem for real-world Conf-MDPs. In this paper, we fill this gap by proposing a trust-region method, Relative Entropy Model Policy Search (REMPS), able to learn both the policy and the MDP configuration in continuous domains without requiring the knowledge of the true model of the environment. After introducing our approach and providing a finite-sample analysis, we empirically evaluate REMPS on both benchmark and realistic environments by comparing our results with those of the gradient methods.

It does not require knowledge of the environment’s true model. This is central to its intended use: the learner can seek useful changes to the configurable environment without first being given its exact dynamics.

The authors provide a finite-sample analysis and evaluate REMPS in both benchmark and realistic environments, comparing it with gradient methods. The contribution connects the configurable decision-process formulation to an algorithm for continuous settings. Its analysis and evaluations examine joint learning of behavior and environment configuration as a concrete reinforcement-learning problem.
summary.tldr: REMPS jointly learns a policy and environment configuration in continuous domains without requiring the environment’s true model.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Configurable Continuous Environments

abstract: We study the link between generalization and interference in temporal-difference (TD) learning. Interference is defined as the inner product of two different gradients, representing their alignment; this quantity emerges as being of interest from a variety of observations about neural networks, parameter sharing and the dynamics of learning. We find that TD easily leads to low-interference, under-generalizing parameters, while the effect seems reversed in supervised learning. We hypothesize that the cause can be traced back to the interplay between the dynamics of interference and bootstrapping. This is supported empirically by several observations: the negative relationship between the generalization gap and interference in TD, the negative effect of bootstrapping on interference and the local coherence of targets, and the contrast between the propagation rate of information in TD(0) versus TD($\lambda$) and regression tasks such as Monte-Carlo policy evaluation. We hope that these new findings can guide the future discovery of better bootstrapping methods.

It measures interference through the inner product of two gradients, which describes their alignment. That quantity connects individual updates to the behavior of shared parameters and offers a way to examine how learning from different situations interacts.

The authors find that temporal-difference learning readily reaches parameters with low interference and weak generalization. The apparent relationship is reversed in supervised learning. They hypothesize that bootstrapping, in which learning targets depend on existing estimates, interacts with interference dynamics to produce this difference. The proposed causal explanation is presented as a hypothesis supported by empirical observations.

Supporting evidence includes a negative relationship between interference and the generalization gap in TD learning, and adverse effects of bootstrapping on interference and local target coherence. The paper also compares information propagation in TD(0), TD(lambda), and regression tasks such as Monte Carlo policy evaluation. These findings identify update alignment and target construction as connected considerations for developing better bootstrapping methods.
summary.tldr: The paper links weak TD generalization to low gradient interference and presents evidence that bootstrapping contributes to this relationship.

title: Interference and Generalization in Temporal Difference Learning

abstract: Deep neural networks can achieve remarkable generalization performances while interpolating the training data. Rather than the U-curve emblematic of the bias-variance trade-off, their test error often follows a "double descent"—a mark of the beneficial role of overparametrization. In this work, we develop a quantitative theory for this phenomenon in the so-called lazy learning regime of neural networks, by considering the problem of learning a high-dimensional function with random features regression. We obtain a precise asymptotic expression for the bias-variance decomposition of the test error, and show that the bias displays a phase transition at the interpolation threshold, beyond it which it remains constant. We disentangle the variances stemming from the sampling of the dataset, from the additive noise corrupting the labels, and from the initialization of the weights. We demonstrate that the latter two contributions are the crux of the double descent: they lead to the overfitting peak at the interpolation threshold and to the decay of the test error upon overparametrization. We quantify how they are suppressed by ensembling the outputs of $K$ independently initialized estimators. For $K\rightarrow \infty$, the test error is monotonously decreasing and remains constant beyond the interpolation threshold. We further compare the effects of overparametrizing, ensembling and regularizing. Finally, we present numerical experiments on classic deep learning setups to show that our results hold qualitatively in realistic lazy learning scenarios.

paragraphs: Double descent describes test error that rises near the point where a model can interpolate its training data, then falls with further overparameterization. This paper develops a quantitative explanation in the lazy learning regime, using high-dimensional random-features regression to study the phenomenon.

The authors derive an asymptotic bias-variance decomposition and separate variance due to dataset sampling, label noise, and weight initialization. Bias undergoes a transition at the interpolation threshold and stays constant beyond it. The label-noise and initialization contributions produce the peak near interpolation and the subsequent decline, identifying specific sources of the curve rather than attributing it to a single undifferentiated variance term.

The analysis also quantifies how averaging independently initialized estimators suppresses those contributions. In the limit of infinitely many estimators, test error decreases monotonically and becomes constant beyond interpolation. The paper compares ensembling, overparameterization, and regularization, then reports numerical experiments with qualitative agreement in realistic lazy learning scenarios. The theoretical explanation is thus tied to that regime, with experiments supporting its qualitative relevance there.
summary.tldr: A lazy-regime analysis attributes double descent to label-noise and initialization variance and quantifies how ensembling suppresses them.

title: Double Trouble in Double Descent: Bias and Variance(s) in the Lazy Regime

abstract: Online mirror descent (OMD) and dual averaging (DA)—two fundamental algorithms for online convex optimization—are known to have very similar (and sometimes identical) performance guarantees when used with a fixed learning rate. Under dynamic learning rates, however, OMD is provably inferior to DA and suffers a linear regret, even in common settings such as prediction with expert advice. We modify the OMD algorithm through a simple technique that we call stabilization. We give essentially the same abstract regret bound for OMD with stabilization and for DA by modifying the classical OMD convergence analysis in a careful and modular way that allows for straightforward and flexible proofs. Simple corollaries of these bounds show that OMD with stabilization and DA enjoy the same performance guarantees in many applications—even under dynamic learning rates. We also shed light on the similarities between OMD and DA and show simple conditions under which stabilized-OMD and DA generate the same iterates.

Changing the learning rate can break that similarity: ordinary mirror descent can incur regret growing linearly with time, even in familiar problems such as prediction with expert advice.

The paper modifies mirror descent using a technique called stabilization. Through a careful revision of the classical convergence analysis, the authors derive essentially the same abstract regret bound for stabilized mirror descent and dual averaging. The analysis is modular, making it easier to adapt the proof to different applications.

Consequences of these bounds show that the two methods share performance guarantees in many settings even when learning rates vary. The authors also identify simple conditions under which they produce exactly the same iterates, a stronger relationship than merely having comparable bounds. The contribution explains how stabilization can close the dynamic-learning-rate gap while clarifying when the algorithms’ actual update sequences coincide.
summary.tldr: Stabilization lets online mirror descent match dual averaging’s guarantees under changing learning rates, with identical iterates under specified conditions.

title: Online mirror descent and dual averaging: keeping pace in the dynamic case

abstract: Reinforcement learning with function approximation can be unstable and even divergent, especially when combined with off-policy learning and Bellman updates. In deep reinforcement learning, these issues have been dealt with empirically by adapting and regularizing the representation, in particular with auxiliary tasks. This suggests that representation learning may provide a means to guarantee stability. In this paper, we formally show that there are indeed nontrivial state representations under which the canonical SARSA algorithm is stable, even when learning off-policy. We analyze representation learning schemes that are based on the transition matrix of a policy, such as proto-value functions, along three axes: approximation error, stability, and ease of estimation. In the most general case of a defective transition matrix, we show that a Schur basis provides convergence guarantees, but is difficult to estimate from samples. For a fixed reward function, we find that an orthogonal basis of the corresponding Krylov subspace is an even better choice. We conclude by empirically demonstrating that these stable representations can be learned using stochastic gradient descent, opening the door to improved techniques for representation learning with deep networks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can become unstable when function approximation, off-policy data, and Bellman updates are combined. This paper investigates whether the state representation itself can provide stability. It formally establishes that nontrivial representations exist under which the standard SARSA algorithm remains stable even when learning off-policy.

The authors examine representations derived from a policy’s transition matrix, including proto-value functions. They assess them through three connected concerns: approximation error, stability, and how easily they can be estimated. For the general case of a defective transition matrix, a Schur basis provides convergence guarantees, but estimating that basis from samples is difficult.

When the reward function is fixed, an orthogonal basis of the associated Krylov subspace is identified as an even better choice. Experiments then show that stable representations can be learned with stochastic gradient descent. This makes representation learning a theoretically motivated route toward stability and suggests opportunities for deep networks, without claiming a general stability guarantee for arbitrary learned neural representations.
summary.tldr: Certain state representations guarantee stable off-policy SARSA, and experiments show stable representations can be learned through stochastic gradient descent.

title: Representations for Stable Off-Policy Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Recent successes of game-theoretic formulations in ML have caused a resurgence of research interest in differentiable games. Overwhelmingly, that research focuses on methods and upper bounds on their speed of convergence. In this work, we approach the question of fundamental iteration complexity by providing lower bounds to complement the linear (i.e. geometric) upper bounds observed in the literature on a wide class of problems. We cast saddle-point and min-max problems as 2-player games. We leverage tools from single-objective convex optimisation to propose new linear lower bounds for convex-concave games. Notably, we give a linear lower bound for $n$-player differentiable games, by using the spectral properties of the update operator. We then propose a new definition of the condition number arising from our lower bound analysis. Unlike past definitions, our condition number captures the fact that linear rates are possible in games, even in the absence of strong convexity or strong concavity in the variables.

paragraphs: Research on differentiable games often proposes algorithms and establishes how quickly they can converge. This paper studies the complementary question of fundamental iteration complexity: lower bounds that help describe limits on achievable convergence. Its focus is linear convergence, meaning geometric progress rather than an error that decreases by a fixed amount.

The authors formulate saddle-point and min-max problems as two-player games, then adapt tools from single-objective convex optimization to obtain lower bounds for convex-concave games. They also derive a linear lower bound for games with multiple players by analyzing spectral properties of the update operator, connecting convergence limits to the structure of the learning updates.

From this analysis, the paper proposes a new condition number for differentiable games. It captures the possibility of linear convergence even when strong convexity or strong concavity is absent from the variables. This matters because a measure of conditioning should reflect the convergence behavior that games can actually exhibit, including behavior that earlier definitions fail to capture.
summary.tldr: New convergence lower bounds motivate a game condition number that captures possible linear rates without strong convexity or concavity.

title: Linear Lower Bounds and Conditioning of Differentiable Games

abstract: In this work, we propose a novel method for generating 3D point clouds that leverage properties of hyper networks. Contrary to the existing methods that learn only the representation of a 3D object, our approach simultaneously finds a representation of the object and its 3D surfaces. The main idea of our HyperCloud method is to build a hyper network that returns weights of a particular neural network (target network) trained to map points from a uniform unit ball distribution into a 3D shape. As a consequence, a particular 3D shape can be generated using point-by-point sampling from the assumed prior distribution and transforming sampled points with the target network. Since the hyper network is based on an auto-encoder architecture trained to reconstruct realistic 3D shapes, the target network weights can be considered a parametrisation of the surface of a 3D shape, and not a standard representation of point cloud usually returned by competitive approaches. The proposed architecture allows to find mesh-based representation of 3D objects in a generative manner, while providing point clouds en pair in quality with the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: HyperCloud generates three-dimensional shapes through a network that produces the weights of another network. The second, or target, network transforms points sampled uniformly from a unit ball into points belonging to a shape. Generating a point cloud therefore means sampling input points and applying the shape-specific transformation one point at a time.

The hypernetwork uses an autoencoder architecture trained to reconstruct realistic shapes. Its output is a set of target-network weights, which the authors interpret as a parameterization of the object's surface. This allows the method to learn both an object representation and a representation of its three-dimensional surfaces, rather than returning only a conventional point-cloud representation.

The distinction matters because the learned object is associated with a transformation that can generate its geometry through sampling. The architecture also permits generative construction of mesh-based object representations. The authors report point-cloud quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods. The stated contribution combines competitive point generation with a surface-oriented representation that also supports meshes, rather than claiming an across-the-board improvement in point-cloud quality.
summary.tldr: HyperCloud generates shape-specific network weights that map sampled points into 3D objects and support both point-cloud and mesh representations.

title: Hypernetwork approach to generating point clouds

abstract: The Wasserstein distance has become increasingly important in machine learning and deep learning. Despite its popularity, the Wasserstein distance is hard to approximate because of the curse of dimensionality. A recently proposed approach to alleviate the curse of dimensionality is to project the sampled data from the high dimensional probability distribution onto a lower-dimensional subspace, and then compute the Wasserstein distance between the projected data. However, this approach requires to solve a max-min problem over the Stiefel manifold, which is very challenging in practice. In this paper, we propose a Riemannian block coordinate descent (RBCD) method to solve this problem, which is based on a novel reformulation of the regularized max-min problem over the Stiefel manifold. We show that the complexity of arithmetic operations for RBCD to obtain an $\epsilon$-stationary point is $O(\epsilon^{-3})$, which is significantly better than the complexity of existing methods. Numerical results on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate that our method is more efficient than existing methods, especially when the number of sampled data is very large.

paragraphs: Wasserstein distance provides a way to compare probability distributions, but approximating it becomes difficult in high dimensions. One proposed remedy compares sampled data after projecting them into a smaller space. Computing the projection robust version introduces another difficulty: the algorithm must solve a coupled maximization and minimization problem over the possible projection subspaces.

This paper develops a Riemannian block coordinate descent method for that computation. It starts with a new reformulation of the regularized problem. The Riemannian component handles the geometry of the Stiefel manifold, the constrained space used to represent projections, while block coordinate descent organizes the optimization into updates of different variable groups.

The authors prove an arithmetic-operation complexity of O(ε⁻³) for reaching an ε-stationary point, improving on the existing methods considered. This guarantee concerns approximate stationarity rather than a globally optimal solution. Experiments with synthetic and real datasets also show better computational efficiency, particularly when the number of sampled data points is very large.
summary.tldr: A geometry-aware block coordinate method computes projection robust Wasserstein distances more efficiently, with an improved approximate-stationarity guarantee.

title: A Riemannian Block Coordinate Descent Method for Computing the Projection Robust Wasserstein Distance

abstract: We consider the bilinear bandit problem where the learner chooses a pair of arms, each from two different action spaces of dimension $d_1$ and $d_2$, respectively. The learner then receives a reward whose expectation is a bilinear function of the two chosen arms with an unknown matrix parameter $\Theta^*\in\mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_2}$ with rank $r$. Despite abundant applications such as drug discovery, the optimal regret rate is unknown for this problem, though it was conjectured to be $\tilde O(\sqrt{d_1d_2(d_1+d_2)r T})$ by Jun et al. (2019) where $\tilde O$ ignores polylogarithmic factors in $T$. In this paper, we make progress towards closing the gap between the upper and lower bound on the optimal regret. First, we reject the conjecture above by proposing algorithms that achieve the regret $\tilde O(\sqrt{d_1 d_2 (d_1+d_2) T})$ using the fact that the action space dimension $O(d_1+d_2)$ is significantly lower than the matrix parameter dimension $O(d_1 d_2)$. Second, we additionally devise an algorithm with better empirical performance than previous algorithms.

paragraphs: In a bilinear bandit problem, a learner chooses two actions, one from each of two action spaces, and observes a reward. The expected reward depends on the pair through an unknown low-rank matrix. The challenge is to learn which pairs work well while limiting regret, the accumulated loss from choices that fall short of the best available reward.

The paper exploits the distinction between the number of coordinates needed to describe an action pair and the number needed to describe the unknown matrix. The former scales with d1+d2, while the latter scales with d1 times d2. This action-space analysis yields a regret upper bound proportional to the square root of d1 d2 (d1+d2) T, apart from polylogarithmic factors.

That bound removes the rank factor appearing inside a previously conjectured optimal rate, rejecting the conjecture and narrowing the gap between known upper and lower bounds. The authors also develop an algorithm with better reported empirical performance than previous methods. The work advances the regret analysis without claiming to fully determine the optimal rate.
summary.tldr: Analyzing the smaller action space yields improved bilinear-bandit regret bounds that reject a previous conjecture about the optimal rate.

title: Improved Regret Bounds of Bilinear Bandits using Action Space Analysis

abstract: Bi-level optimization model is able to capture a wide range of complex learning tasks with practical interest. Due to the witnessed efficiency in solving bi-level programs, gradient-based methods have gained popularity in the machine learning community. In this work, we propose a new gradient-based solution scheme, namely, the Bi-level Value-Function-based Interior-point Method (BVFIM). Following the main idea of the log-barrier interior-point scheme, we penalize the regularized value function of the lower level problem into the upper level objective. By further solving a sequence of differentiable unconstrained approximation problems, we consequently derive a sequential programming scheme. The numerical advantage of our scheme relies on the fact that, when gradient methods are applied to solve the approximation problem, we successfully avoid computing any expensive Hessian-vector or Jacobian-vector product. We prove the convergence without requiring any convexity assumption on either the upper level or the lower level objective. Experiments demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed BVFIM on non-convex bi-level problems.

We prove the convergence without requiring any convexity assumption on either the upper level or the lower level objective. Experiments demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed BVFIM on non-convex bi-level problems.

paragraphs: Bi-level optimization describes problems in which one optimization task depends on the solution of another. This nesting makes gradient-based solution methods attractive but can also make their computations expensive. The paper introduces BVFIM, a method that reformulates how the lower-level problem enters the upper-level objective.

The approach uses a regularized value function to represent the lower-level problem and incorporates it into the upper-level objective through a log-barrier construction. It then solves a sequence of differentiable, unconstrained approximation problems. This turns the nested formulation into a sequential programming procedure whose individual approximation problems can be handled with gradient methods.

A central computational benefit is that solving these approximations avoids expensive Hessian-vector and Jacobian-vector products. The authors also prove convergence without assuming that either level’s objective is convex, extending the theoretical reach of the approach to non-convex settings. Experiments demonstrate efficiency on non-convex bi-level problems. Together, these contributions connect a barrier-based reformulation with both a convergence result and a practical reduction in the derivative computations required.
summary.tldr: BVFIM solves non-convex bi-level problems through barrier-based approximations that avoid expensive derivative-vector products.

title: A Value-Function-based Interior-point Method for Non-convex Bi-level Optimization

abstract: Classical value iteration approaches are not applicable to environments with continuous states and actions. For such environments the states and actions must be discretized, which leads to an exponential increase in computational complexity. In this paper, we propose continuous fitted value iteration (cFVI). This algorithm enables dynamic programming for continuous states and actions with a known dynamics model. Exploiting the continuous time formulation, the optimal policy can be derived for non-linear control-affine dynamics. This closed-form solution enables the efficient extension of value iteration to continuous environments. We show in non-linear control experiments that the dynamic programming solution obtains the same quantitative performance as deep reinforcement learning methods in simulation but excels when transferred to the physical system.The policy obtained by cFVI is more robust to changes in the dynamics despite using only a deterministic model and without explicitly incorporating robustness in the optimization

paragraphs: Classical value iteration requires discretization when applied to continuous states and actions, which can make computation grow exponentially. This paper introduces continuous fitted value iteration, or cFVI, to extend dynamic programming to continuous environments. The method assumes a known dynamics model, making that model an explicit part of the learning setup.

The authors use a continuous-time formulation to derive the optimal policy in closed form for nonlinear control-affine dynamics. This analytical policy solution enables an efficient extension of value iteration without the same discretization burden. The stated dynamics structure is therefore central to how the method obtains its computational advantage.

In nonlinear control experiments, cFVI matches the quantitative performance of deep reinforcement learning methods in simulation and performs better when transferred to a physical system. Its learned policy also shows greater robustness to changes in dynamics. These are experimental findings despite using only a deterministic model and including no explicit robustness term in the optimization, highlighting a useful property of the tested solutions.
summary.tldr: cFVI uses known control-affine dynamics and a continuous-time policy solution to extend value iteration, with strong physical-transfer results in the reported experiments.

title: Value Iteration in Continuous Actions, States and Time

abstract: We introduce Hindsight Off-policy Options (HO2), a data-efficient option learning algorithm. Given any trajectory, HO2 infers likely option choices and backpropagates through the dynamic programming inference procedure to robustly train all policy components off-policy and end-to-end. The approach outperforms existing option learning methods on common benchmarks. To better understand the option framework and disentangle benefits from both temporal and action abstraction, we evaluate ablations with flat policies and mixture policies with comparable optimization. The results highlight the importance of both types of abstraction as well as off-policy training and trust-region constraints, particularly in challenging, simulated 3D robot manipulation tasks from raw pixel inputs. Finally, we intuitively adapt the inference step to investigate the effect of increased temporal abstraction on training with pre-trained options and from scratch.

paragraphs: Option learning organizes behavior through higher-level choices that can structure actions over time. Hindsight Off-policy Options, or HO2, learns these choices from trajectories by inferring which options were likely responsible for the observed behavior. It uses dynamic programming for this inference and backpropagates through that procedure to train all policy components together.

Because training is off-policy, the method can learn from trajectories beyond those produced by the policy currently being optimized. The paper reports that HO2 outperforms existing option-learning methods on common benchmarks. It also compares against flat policies and mixture policies with comparable optimization, helping distinguish the contribution of temporal abstraction from that of action abstraction.

The ablations highlight the importance of both forms of abstraction, alongside off-policy training and trust-region constraints. These effects are especially relevant in challenging simulated 3D robot manipulation tasks using raw pixel inputs. Finally, the authors modify the inference step to investigate stronger temporal abstraction, considering both training with pretrained options and learning from scratch.
summary.tldr: HO2 infers likely options from trajectories and differentiates through that inference to learn hierarchical policies efficiently from off-policy data.

title: Data-efficient Hindsight Off-policy Option Learning

abstract: As a prevalent distributed learning paradigm, Federated Learning (FL) trains a global model on a massive amount of devices with infrequent communication. This paper investigates a class of composite optimization and statistical recovery problems in the FL setting, whose loss function consists of a data-dependent smooth loss and a non-smooth regularizer. Examples include sparse linear regression using Lasso, low-rank matrix recovery using nuclear norm regularization, etc. In the existing literature, federated composite optimization algorithms are designed only from an optimization perspective without any statistical guarantees. In addition, they do not consider commonly used (restricted) strong convexity in statistical recovery problems. We advance the frontiers of this problem from both optimization and statistical perspectives. From optimization upfront, we propose a new algorithm named Fast Federated Dual Averaging for strongly convex and smooth loss and establish state-of-the-art iteration and communication complexity in the composite setting. In particular, we prove that it enjoys a fast rate, linear speedup, and reduced communication rounds. From statistical upfront, for restricted strongly convex and smooth loss, we design another algorithm, namely Multi-stage Federated Dual Averaging , and prove a high probability complexity bound with linear speedup up to optimal statistical precision. Numerical experiments in both synthetic and real data demonstrate that our methods perform better than other baselines. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work providing fast optimization algorithms and statistical recovery guarantees for composite problems in FL.

Experiments on synthetic and real data show better performance than the compared baselines, complementing the paper’s optimization and statistical guarantees.
summary.tldr: Two federated dual-averaging algorithms provide fast composite optimization and statistical recovery guarantees under their respective curvature conditions.

title: Fast Composite Optimization and Statistical Recovery in Federated Learning

abstract: To solve difficult tasks, humans ask questions to acquire knowledge from external sources. In contrast, classical reinforcement learning agents lack such an ability and often resort to exploratory behavior. This is exacerbated as few present-day environments support querying for knowledge. In order to study how agents can be taught to query external knowledge via language, we first introduce two new environments: the grid-world-based Q-BabyAI and the text-based Q-TextWorld. In addition to physical interactions, an agent can query an external knowledge source specialized for these environments to gather information. Second, we propose the ‘Asking for Knowledge’ (AFK) agent, which learns to generate language commands to query for meaningful knowledge that helps solve the tasks. AFK leverages a non-parametric memory, a pointer mechanism and an episodic exploration bonus to tackle (1) irrelevant information, (2) a large query language space, (3) delayed reward for making meaningful queries. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the AFK agent outperforms recent baselines on the challenging Q-BabyAI and Q-TextWorld environments.

paragraphs: An agent can learn about its surroundings by acting, but asking a useful question offers another route to information. This paper studies how reinforcement learning agents can acquire task-relevant knowledge through language. To make that capability testable, the authors introduce Q-BabyAI, a grid-world environment, and Q-TextWorld, a text-based environment.

In both environments, agents can interact physically and query an external knowledge source specialized for the environment. The proposed Asking for Knowledge agent, AFK, learns language commands that request useful information. Its design combines a non-parametric memory, a pointer mechanism, and an exploration bonus applied within episodes to address the challenges of irrelevant information, many possible queries, and rewards that arrive after a useful question.

Experiments show AFK outperforming recent baselines on both proposed environments. The result supports treating information requests as a learned part of task solving, alongside ordinary actions. The demonstrated capability concerns querying the specialized sources provided in these environments, where agents must discover which questions help them complete their tasks.
summary.tldr: AFK learns to ask useful language questions of external knowledge sources and improves task performance in two purpose-built reinforcement learning environments.

title: Asking for Knowledge (AFK): Training RL Agents to Query External Knowledge Using Language

abstract: Many of the successes of machine learning are based on minimizing an averaged loss function. However, it is well-known that this paradigm suffers from robustness issues that hinder its applicability in safety-critical domains. These issues are often addressed by training against worst-case perturbations of data, a technique known as adversarial training. Although empirically effective, adversarial training can be overly conservative, leading to unfavorable trade-offs between nominal performance and robustness. To this end, in this paper we propose a framework called probabilistic robustness that bridges the gap between the accurate, yet brittle average case and the robust, yet conservative worst case by enforcing robustness to most rather than to all perturbations. From a theoretical point of view, this framework overcomes the trade-offs between the performance and the sample-complexity of worst-case and average-case learning. From a practical point of view, we propose a novel algorithm based on risk-aware optimization that effectively balances average- and worst-case performance at a considerably lower computational cost relative to adversarial training. Our results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN illustrate the advantages of this framework on the spectrum from average- to worst-case robustness. Our code is available at: https://github.com/arobey1/advbench.

paragraphs: Minimizing average prediction loss can produce accurate models that remain vulnerable to input perturbations. Adversarial training addresses this by training against worst-case perturbations, but that objective can be overly conservative and reduce nominal performance. This paper proposes probabilistic robustness as an intermediate goal: robustness to most perturbations rather than every perturbation.

The framework changes the robustness requirement itself, allowing the learning objective to occupy a position between average-case and worst-case performance. The authors provide theoretical results overcoming performance and sample-complexity trade-offs associated with those two extremes. The distinction matters because a probabilistic robustness requirement does not claim protection against all possible perturbations.

For practical training, the paper introduces a risk-aware optimization algorithm that balances average and worst-case performance at considerably lower computational cost than adversarial training. Results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and SVHN illustrate advantages across that spectrum. Together, the framework and algorithm offer a way to select a less conservative robustness target while still explicitly accounting for perturbation risk.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic robustness targets most perturbations, balancing ordinary accuracy and robustness with lower training cost than adversarial training.

title: Probabilistically Robust Learning: Balancing Average and Worst-case Performance

abstract: Learned graph neural networks (GNNs) have recently been established as fast and accurate alternatives for principled solvers in simulating the dynamics of physical systems. In many application domains across science and engineering, however, we are not only interested in a forward simulation but also in solving inverse problems with constraints defined by a partial differential equation (PDE). Here we explore GNNs to solve such PDE-constrained inverse problems. Given a sparse set of measurements, we are interested in recovering the initial condition or parameters of the PDE. We demonstrate that GNNs combined with autodecoder-style priors are well-suited for these tasks, achieving more accurate estimates of initial conditions or physical parameters than other learned approaches when applied to the wave equation or Navier Stokes equations. We also demonstrate computational speedups of up to 90x using GNNs compared to principled solvers.

We also demonstrate computational speedups of up to 90x using GNNs compared to principled solvers.

paragraphs: Simulating a physical system starts with its conditions and parameters and predicts what happens next. This paper studies the reverse task: recovering initial conditions or physical parameters from a sparse set of measurements. The recovered quantities must be considered within dynamics governed by a partial differential equation, making this a PDE-constrained inverse problem.

The authors combine graph neural networks with autodecoder-style priors to solve these problems. The graph network provides a learned approach to representing the physical dynamics, while the prior contributes structure to the recovery task. This extends the use of graph networks beyond forward simulation to inferring the unknown quantities that explain observed behavior.

In applications involving the wave equation and Navier–Stokes equations, the combined method estimates initial conditions or physical parameters more accurately than other learned approaches. The paper also reports computational speedups of up to 90-fold compared with principled solvers. These are two distinct findings: improved recovery accuracy relative to learned alternatives and faster computation relative to principled numerical approaches in the demonstrated tasks.
summary.tldr: Graph neural networks with autodecoder-style priors recover PDE initial conditions or parameters from sparse measurements, with improved accuracy and reported speedups up to 90-fold.

title: Learning to Solve PDE-constrained Inverse Problems with Graph Networks

abstract: Human knowledge is largely implicit and relational — do we have a friend in common? can I walk from here to there? In this work, we leverage the combinatorial structure of graphs to quantify human priors over such relational data. Our experiments focus on two domains that have been continuously relevant over evolutionary timescales: social interaction and spatial navigation. We find that some features of the inferred priors are remarkably consistent, such as the tendency for sparsity as a function of graph size. Other features are domain-specific, such as the propensity for triadic closure in social interactions. More broadly, our work demonstrates how nonclassical statistical analysis of indirect behavioral experiments can be used to efficiently model latent biases in the data.

paragraphs: People have implicit expectations about relationships, such as who might share a friend or which locations might be connected. This paper uses graphs to quantify those expectations in social interaction and spatial navigation. The focus is on priors: the underlying expectations people bring to relational data.

The authors infer these priors through indirect behavioural experiments and analyse their graph structure. Some patterns are consistent across the domains, including how the tendency toward sparse connectivity relates to graph size. Other patterns depend on the setting. Social expectations show a propensity for triadic closure, the tendency for a shared connection to be accompanied by a connection between the other two parties.

These findings distinguish expectations that recur across relational domains from ones associated with a particular kind of relationship. The broader methodological contribution is to show how statistical analysis of indirect behaviour can efficiently reveal latent biases. Graphs provide a common language for this comparison, allowing implicit knowledge about friendships and navigation to be studied through properties of the connections people expect.
summary.tldr: Behavioural experiments reveal shared and domain-specific human expectations about graph structure in social relationships and navigation.

title: Quantifying Human Priors over Social and Navigation Networks

abstract: Learning to denoise has emerged as a prominent paradigm to design state-of-the-art deep generative models for natural images. How to use it to model the distributions of both continuous real-valued data and categorical data has been well studied in recently proposed diffusion models. However, it is found in this paper to have limited ability in modeling some other types of data, such as count and non-negative continuous data, that are often highly sparse, skewed, heavy-tailed, and/or overdispersed. To this end, we propose learning to jump as a general recipe for generative modeling of various types of data. Using a forward count thinning process to construct learning objectives to train a deep neural network, it employs a reverse count thickening process to iteratively refine its generation through that network. We demonstrate when learning to jump is expected to perform comparably to learning to denoise, and when it is expected to perform better. For example, learning to jump is recommended when the training data is non-negative and exhibits strong sparsity, skewness, heavy-tailedness, and/or heterogeneity.

paragraphs: Denoising-based generative models have been successful for images and studied for continuous and categorical data. This paper identifies difficulties with some other data types, including counts and nonnegative measurements. Such data can contain many zeros, strongly uneven values, heavy tails, or substantial variation across observations.

The proposed alternative, learning to jump, builds training objectives through a forward process that thins counts. A neural network then supports a reverse process that thickens counts, iteratively refining generated samples. This pairs a count-based forward transformation with a corresponding generation procedure, giving the model a different foundation from learning to remove noise.

The authors examine when learning to jump is expected to perform similarly to denoising and when it is expected to work better. They recommend it for nonnegative training data with pronounced sparsity, skewness, heavy tails, or heterogeneity. The contribution is therefore a data-sensitive generative recipe: the stated advantage depends on the characteristics of the distribution being modeled, rather than applying uniformly to every type of data.
summary.tldr: Learning to jump uses count thinning and thickening to model data whose nonnegative, sparse, or uneven distributions can challenge denoising methods.

title: Learning to Jump: Thinning and Thickening Latent Counts for Generative Modeling

abstract: A common training technique for language models is teacher forcing (TF). TF attempts to match human language exactly, even though identical meanings can be expressed in different ways. This motivates use of sequence-level objectives for dialogue response generation. In this paper, we study the efficacy of various offline reinforcement learning (RL) methods to maximize such objectives. We present a comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets, models, and metrics. Offline RL shows a clear performance improvement over teacher forcing while not inducing training instability or sacrificing practical training budgets.

We present a comprehensive evaluation across multiple datasets, models, and metrics. Offline RL shows a clear performance improvement over teacher forcing while not inducing training instability or sacrificing practical training budgets.

paragraphs: Teacher forcing trains a language model to match the wording of human responses. For dialogue, that creates a tension: several differently worded replies can express the same meaning. This paper investigates objectives that evaluate complete response sequences, motivated by the gap between matching a particular wording and producing an effective response.

The authors study several offline reinforcement learning methods for maximizing these sequence-level objectives. The work is an evaluation of their effectiveness across multiple datasets, models, and metrics. That breadth matters because the central question concerns whether this training approach is useful across the examined dialogue settings, rather than whether it helps one particular model on one evaluation.

The reported results show clear improvements over teacher forcing without introducing training instability or exceeding practical training budgets. Together, those findings address both response performance and the feasibility of the training process. They support offline reinforcement learning as a practical way to optimize whole-response objectives in the evaluated dialogue-generation settings, where exact wording alone can be an overly restrictive training target.
summary.tldr: Offline reinforcement learning improves dialogue response generation over teacher forcing in the evaluations while maintaining stable, practical training.

title: On the Effectiveness of Offline RL for Dialogue Response Generation

abstract: Due to the unsupervised nature of anomaly detection, the key to fueling deep models is finding supervisory signals. Different from current reconstruction-guided generative models and transformation-based contrastive models, we devise novel data-driven supervision for tabular data by introducing a characteristic – scale – as data labels. By representing varied sub-vectors of data instances, we define scale as the relationship between the dimensionality of original sub-vectors and that of representations. Scales serve as labels attached to transformed representations, thus offering ample labeled data for neural network training. This paper further proposes a scale learning-based anomaly detection method. Supervised by the learning objective of scale distribution alignment, our approach learns the ranking of representations converted from varied subspaces of each data instance. Through this proxy task, our approach models inherent regularities and patterns within data, which well describes data "normality". Abnormal degrees of testing instances are obtained by measuring whether they fit these learned patterns. Extensive experiments show that our approach leads to significant improvement over state-of-the-art generative/contrastive anomaly detection methods.

paragraphs: Unsupervised anomaly detection needs a training signal even when examples lack normal-or-abnormal labels. This paper creates such a signal for tabular data using a characteristic called scale. Here, scale describes the relationship between the dimensionality of a selected sub-vector of a data instance and the dimensionality of its representation.

The method forms representations from different subsets of an instance’s features and attaches scale labels to them. These transformations provide labeled examples for a proxy learning task. A scale-distribution alignment objective trains the model to learn rankings among representations drawn from different subspaces of each instance, exposing regularities within the data.

At test time, an instance receives an abnormality score according to how well it fits the learned patterns. The central idea is to learn normality through relationships among transformed representations, using supervision derived from the data itself. Extensive experiments report significant improvements over leading reconstruction-guided generative and transformation-based contrastive anomaly detectors. The findings support scale learning as a useful source of supervision for the studied tabular setting.
summary.tldr: Scale learning creates supervision from tabular feature subsets and detects anomalies by their mismatch with learned representation patterns.

title: Fascinating Supervisory Signals and Where to Find Them: Deep Anomaly Detection with Scale Learning

abstract: Time series pre-training has recently garnered wide attention for its potential to reduce labeling expenses and benefit various downstream tasks. Prior methods are mainly based on pre-training techniques well-acknowledged in vision or language, such as masked modeling and contrastive learning. However, randomly masking time series or calculating series-wise similarity will distort or neglect inherent temporal correlations crucial in time series data. To emphasize temporal correlation modeling, this paper proposes TimeSiam as a simple but effective self-supervised pre-training framework for Time series based on Siamese networks. Concretely, TimeSiam pre-trains Siamese encoders to capture intrinsic temporal correlations between randomly sampled past and current subseries. With a simple data augmentation method (e.g. masking), TimeSiam can benefit from diverse augmented subseries and learn internal time-dependent representations through a past-to-current reconstruction. Moreover, learnable lineage embeddings are also introduced to distinguish temporal distance between sampled series and further foster the learning of diverse temporal correlations. TimeSiam consistently outperforms extensive advanced pre-training baselines, demonstrating superior forecasting and classification capabilities across 13 standard benchmarks in both intra- and cross-domain scenarios.

paragraphs: Time-series pre-training aims to learn useful representations before task-specific training, potentially reducing labeling needs. Methods adapted from language or vision can distort or overlook temporal relationships when they randomly mask observations or compare entire series. TimeSiam makes the relationship between earlier and later segments central to its learning task.

The framework uses Siamese encoders on randomly sampled past and current subseries. With simple augmentation such as masking, it learns through past-to-current reconstruction, encouraging representations that capture time-dependent structure across diverse segment pairs. Learnable lineage embeddings distinguish the temporal distances between sampled segments, helping the model represent different kinds of temporal correlation.

The authors evaluate forecasting and classification across 13 standard benchmarks, including settings within a domain and across domains. TimeSiam consistently outperforms the advanced pre-training baselines in these evaluations. The findings support using temporal relationships as an explicit organizing principle for pre-training: the placement of segments in time becomes part of what the model learns, alongside the contents of the segments themselves.
summary.tldr: TimeSiam learns relationships between past and current time-series segments, improving forecasting and classification across 13 evaluated benchmarks.

title: TimeSiam: A Pre-Training Framework for Siamese Time-Series Modeling

abstract: In many practical applications, coarse-grained labels are readily available compared to fine-grained labels that reflect subtle differences between classes. However, existing methods cannot leverage coarse labels to infer fine-grained labels in an unsupervised manner. To bridge this gap, we propose FALCON, a method that discovers fine-grained classes from coarsely labeled data without any supervision at the fine-grained level. FALCON simultaneously infers unknown fine-grained classes and underlying relationships between coarse and fine-grained classes. Moreover, FALCON is a modular method that can effectively learn from multiple datasets labeled with different strategies. We evaluate FALCON on eight image classification tasks and a single-cell classification task. FALCON outperforms baselines by a large margin, achieving 22% improvement over the best baseline on the tieredImageNet dataset with over 600 fine-grained classes.

This paper asks how to use those broad labels to discover finer categories without receiving examples labeled at the finer level. FALCON is designed to extract that additional structure from coarsely labeled data.

The method jointly infers the unknown fine-grained classes and their relationships to the available coarse classes. Learning both together addresses two linked uncertainties: which detailed categories exist and how they fit into the broader labeling scheme. Its modular design also allows it to learn from multiple datasets that use different labeling strategies.

The authors evaluate FALCON on eight image classification tasks and one single-cell classification task. It outperforms the compared baselines by substantial margins, including a reported 22% improvement over the strongest baseline on tieredImageNet, which contains more than 600 fine-grained classes. These results show that coarse supervision can support discovering much more detailed class structure in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FALCON discovers fine-grained classes and their relationships to coarse labels without fine-grained supervision.

title: Fine-grained Classes and How to Find Them

abstract: Large language models have ushered in a new era of artificial intelligence research. However, their substantial training costs hinder further development and widespread adoption. In this paper, inspired by the redundancy in the parameters of large language models, we propose a novel training paradigm: Evolving Subnetwork Training (EST). EST samples subnetworks from the layers of the large language model and from commonly used modules within each layer, Multi-Head Attention (MHA) and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). By gradually increasing the size of the subnetworks during the training process, EST can save the cost of training. We apply EST to train GPT2 model and TinyLlama model, resulting in 26.7% FLOPs saving for GPT2 and 25.0% for TinyLlama without an increase in loss on the pre-training dataset. Moreover, EST leads to performance improvements in downstream tasks, indicating that it benefits generalization. Additionally, we provide intuitive theoretical studies based on training dynamics and Dropout theory to ensure the feasibility of EST.

Motivated by redundancy in their parameters, it trains sampled subnetworks whose size increases over time. This makes the amount of model computation used during training something that can evolve rather than remain fixed throughout the process.

The method samples subnetworks across model layers and within two common layer components: multi-head attention and multilayer perceptrons. Gradually increasing the sampled subnetworks' size reduces the training computation required. The authors also provide theoretical studies based on training dynamics and dropout theory to support the feasibility of this training approach.
